item.title: JAMA: Fluid eMTBR-tau243 as a Biomarker of Mixed 3-Repeat and 4-Repeat Tau Pathology
item.description:
Importance: Neurodegenerative diseases with abnormal tau protein aggregation in the brain (ie, tauopathies) can be classified by the tau isoform that accumulates: 3-repeat (3R), 4-repeat (4R), or mixed 3R/4R tauopathies, which include chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), some forms of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and Alzheimer disease (AD). The endogenously cleaved form of tau microtubule binding region containing the residue 243 (eMTBR-tau243) can be detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood and has been associated with AD tau pathology, but its specificity and biological interpretation in non-AD tauopathies remains unclear.

Objective: To evaluate biofluid eMTBR-tau243 in a range of tauopathies.

Design, setting, and participants: This case-control study included 4 biorepositories based in the US that contributed CSF and plasma samples from participants with and without tauopathies, many of whom had antemortem biofluid samples paired with autopsy or genetically defined neuropathology. Samples were analyzed between August 2023 and December 2025. Data analysis occurred from August 2024 to July 2026.

Exposure: CSF and plasma eMTBR-tau243 concentrations measured using a mass spectrometry-based assay.

Main outcomes and measures: Outcomes included mixed 3R/4R tauopathy (eg, AD and CTE) based on autopsy, frontotemporal lobar degeneration with MAPT variants (FTLD-MAPT), and CTE stage. Differences in biomarker levels between groups were evaluated using analysis of variance or analysis of covariance, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated to evaluate the discriminative performance of fluid eMTBR-tau243.

Results: Among the 229 participants (196 with CSF samples and 55 with plasma samples [22 with both]), mean (SD) age at fluid sample collection was 63 (13) years and 108 (47%) were female. Median (IQR) CSF eMTBR-tau243 was increased in 10 patients with AD (0.459 [0.246-0.801] fmol/mL) compared with 29 cognitively unimpaired controls (0.002 [0.001-0.005] fmol/mL) (adjusted P < .001), but other autopsy-confirmed non-AD tauopathies (which included 52 individuals with conditions including progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration) did not demonstrate an increase (0.015 [0.008, 0.039] fmol/mL). Six symptomatic FTLD-MAPT variant carriers with mixed 3R/4R tauopathy (R406W, V337M, and G389R) had increased median (IQR) CSF eMTBR-tau243 (0.140 [0.055-0.174] fmol/mL) compared with 15 4R tauopathy variant carriers including N279K and P301L (0.004 [0.001-0.044] fmol/mL) (P = .001). Median (IQR) plasma eMTBR-tau243 was increased in 11 patients with CTE (1.93 [0.42-3.68] fmol/L) compared with 20 cognitively unimpaired controls (0.29 [0.05-0.62] fmol/L) (adjusted P = .007), but did not increase as high as among 14 patients with AD (11.25 [2.29-19.38] fmol/L). Plasma eMTBR-tau243 distinguished CTE stage III and IV from controls (AUC, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.92-1.00), but not CTE stage I from controls (AUC, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.32-0.97).

Conclusions and relevance: This study found that plasma and CSF eMTBR-tau243 were increased in mixed 3R/4R tauopathies including AD, high-stage CTE, and a subset of genetic FTLD-MAPT, compared with cognitively unimpaired controls. Further validation in larger cohorts is needed to determine the clinical utility of eMTBR-tau243 as a potential diagnostic biomarker for CTE and other tauopathies beyond AD.

Horie K, Koppisetti RK, VandeVrede L, Asken BM, Li Y, Yen D

item.title: Crit Care: Impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on the occurrence of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia in trauma patients (antiVAP): a propensity score-weighted, retrospective cohort study
item.description:
Background: Short-course antibiotic prophylaxis has been associated with a reduced risk of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in selected populations, particularly patients with acute brain injury. However, its role in severely injured trauma patients remains controversial.

Methods: This multicentre, retrospective cohort study, conducted in 15 French trauma centres, included severely injured adults who required mechanical ventilation initiated within 24 h of admission and continued for at least 48 h. Propensity score-based analyses assessed the association between early antibiotic prophylaxis (initiated within the first 24 h of management and continued for up to 72 h) and patient outcomes. The primary outcome was early-onset VAP; secondary outcomes included late-onset VAP, extrapulmonary infections, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 30-day mortality.

Results: A total of 1,321 trauma patients were included. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered to 746 patients (56%), with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid used in more than 90% of cases. Early-onset VAP occurred in 240 of 746 patients (32%) who received antibiotic prophylaxis and in 195 of 575 (34%) who did not. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with early-onset VAP (weighted odds ratio [wOR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.66-1.22; p = 0.48). A cause-specific Cox model accounting for the competing risk of death before day 7 yielded similar results (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07; p = 0.19). Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with improve of secondary outcomes.

Conclusions: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis in severely injured trauma patients was not associated with a reduced risk of early-onset VAP.

Clinicaltrials: Gov ID NCT07059039 - Registration date: July, 10th 2025.

Foucrier A, Muchardt J, James A, Caffier C, Stan P, Ramonda V
Journal Article, Multicenter Study

item.title: Crit Care: Acute kidney injury and renal replacement therapy: a critical synthesis of metabolic derangements and nutritional implications
item.description:
Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects up to 50% of critically ill patients and is frequently complicated by severe metabolic derangements, requiring the initiation of replacement therapy (RRT) in 10-15% of cases. Despite substantial progress in the diagnosis of AKI and optimisation of RRT delivery, the nutritional management of these patients remains an underexplored area.

Main body: AKI is increasingly recognised as a systemic metabolic disorder extending beyond impaired renal clearance. Key metabolic alterations include mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated gluconeogenesis, increased proteolysis and altered amino acid metabolism, with accelerated nitrogen wasting. These abnormalities are further amplified by acute systemic stress states, including sepsis, systemic inflammation, trauma, burns, liver dysfunction and multiorgan failure. RRT introduces additional metabolic consequences through extracorporeal losses of amino acids and micronutrients. Conversely, citrate anticoagulation, glucose-containing dialysate, and lactate-buffered solutions represent sources of clinically relevant calories. Current nutritional recommendations are largely extrapolated from heterogeneous intensive care populations. Available evidence suggests that AKI primarily influences energy balance rather than energy expenditure, which appears broadly comparable to that of other critically ill populations. While evidence specific to AKI is limited, protein provision of approximately 1.2-1.3 g/kg/day is generally recommended during critical illness. However, higher intakes of up to 1.7-2.5 g/kg/day may be considered in patients receiving RRT to offset extracorporeal amino acid losses and increased protein catabolism. In this setting, emerging concepts such as metabolic tolerance and biomarker-guided metabolic phenotyping may facilitate individualised nutritional strategies.

Conclusions: AKI, particularly when requiring RRT, is associated with profound and dynamic metabolic disturbances that substantially influence energy and protein requirements, thereby making nutrition an integral component of organ support therapies. Future research should evaluate precision nutrition strategies that tailor nutritional support to the phase of critical illness, measured energy expenditure, metabolic tolerance, and RRT-related nutrient losses and gains. Such studies should prioritise patient-centred outcomes, including physical function and recovery, in addition to nutritional and metabolic endpoints.

Cutuli SL, Chapple LS, De Rosa S, Meersch-Dini M, Prowle JR, Stoppe C
Journal Article, Review

item.title: Chest: How I Do It: An Intensivist's guide to RV Failure and Right Ventricular Assist Devices
item.description:
Right ventricular failure (RVF) is a high-mortality form of cardiogenic shock frequently encountered in critical illness and is often underrecognized due to its heterogeneous presentation. This article presents a physiology-driven, stepwise approach to the diagnosis and management of acute RVF using a longitudinal case in the intensive care unit. We highlight practical bedside tools for recognition, including point-of-care ultrasound and invasive hemodynamics, and review targeted strategies for preload optimization, afterload reduction, and contractility support. Special emphasis is placed on airway management, vasoactive medications, and timely escalation to mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in appropriately selected patients. This bedside "How I Do It" guide is written for intensivists and pulmonary/critical care clinicians and translates advanced hemodynamic and device concepts into practical decision points for acute care management.

Sridhar M, Patel M, Manek G, Chowdhury J, Villalobos N, Soto F

item.title: Chest: Comparative Effectiveness of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists versus DPP-4 and SGLT2 Inhibitors in Patients with Bronchiectasis and Type 2 Diabetes
item.description:
Background: Bronchiectasis is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with limited disease-modifying therapies. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, but their impact on bronchiectasis outcomes remains unknown.

Research question: Is GLP-1RA use, compared with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i) or sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) use, associated with better clinical outcomes in patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes (T2D)?

Study design and methods: Using the TriNetX global federated research network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes who initiated GLP-1RA therapy between June 1, 2022, and May 30, 2025. We compared clinical outcomes, including all-cause mortality, bronchiectasis exacerbation, acute respiratory failure, and lower respiratory tract infections, with patients receiving DPP-4i) or SGLT2i using propensity score matching to balance baseline characteristics.

Results: After propensity score matching, 1,029 patients per group were included in the GLP-1RA versus DPP-4i cohort, and 2,255 patients per group in the GLP-1RA versus SGLT2i cohort. Compared with DPP-4i, GLP-1RA use was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 0.43; 95% CI, 0.33-0.56) and reduced risks of acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.36-0.58) and lower respiratory tract infection (HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.46-0.65). Similar benefits were observed compared with SGLT2i for all-cause mortality (HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.40-0.60), acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.39-0.55), and lower respiratory tract infection (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.68-0.86). Stratified analyses demonstrated consistent mortality benefits across demographic and clinical subgroups, with particularly pronounced effects in obese patients but there was no statistically significant reduction in bronchiectasis exacerbations.

Interpretation: Among patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes, GLP-1RA therapy was associated with significantly lower mortality and reduced respiratory complications compared with DPP-4i or SGLT2i. These findings suggest potential disease-modifying benefits of GLP-1RAs in bronchiectasis beyond glycemic control.

Liao KM, Chuang YM, Hsu WH, Kuo CY, Wu JY, Shiau BW
Journal Article
Full text · PubMed

item.title: Chest: The Burden of Chronic Cough in Patients With Interstitial Lung Disease: a US Survey-Based Analysis of Its Effects on Daily Life and Emotional and Social Well-Being
item.description:
Background: Chronic cough (≥8 weeks) is highly prevalent among patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and non-IPF interstitial lung disease (ILD) and imposes significant physical, social, and psychological burden. Research characterizing the burden of chronic cough in patients with IPF and non-IPF ILD from the patient perspective is limited.

Research question: What is the multidimensional burden of chronic cough in patients living with IPF or non-IPF ILD?

Study design and methods: An online cross-sectional survey was distributed to adults from June to July 2025 via the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation's US Community Registry. Eligibility required a self-reported diagnosis of IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough. Multiple-choice and open-text questions spanned six domains: demographics, disease history, cough characteristics, daily life impact, social/emotional and long-term impact, and healthcare experience.

Results: A total of 197 participants completed the survey: 75.63% reported a diagnosis of IPF, 21.32% reported non-IPF ILD, and 3.05% were awaiting further ILD diagnosis. Participants reported cough-related interference with daily activities (76.15%) and sleep disruption (79.69%) within the preceding week. Emotional burden was frequently reported: 95.94% of participants had cough-induced worry, 75.13% had depression, sadness, or low mood, and 67.01% reported avoiding social situations because of cough. Additionally, 60.91% of participants reported that chronic cough affected their platonic relationships, and 55.33% reported impact on their ability or desire to maintain physical or intimate relationships. To treat cough, participants reported using an average of 2.7 therapeutic classes historically and 2.0 classes currently, with many reporting limited or no relief.

Interpretation: Findings from this US survey of patients with IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough indicate that, among respondents, chronic cough burden manifests physically, psychologically, and psychosocially. Reports of limited relief from available therapies suggest an unmet need in managing chronic cough in this patient population.

Clinical trial registration: Not applicable.

Swigris J, Kulkarni T, Watterston C, Nakano A, Barrett K, Shore JE
Journal Article

item.title: J Emerg Med: Cannabis use Disclosure and Opioid Prescribing at Emergency Department Discharge
item.description:
Background: It is unclear whether documented cannabis use disclosure is independently associated with opioid prescribing practices when patients discharge from the emergency department (ED).

Objective: To examine associations between cannabis use disclosure and opioid prescribing as well as dose among adults with selected acute painful conditions.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients seen in the ED between 2021 and 2023 in a Southern California healthcare system. For patients with multiple ED visits, only the earliest encounter was included in the study. Eligible conditions included major/long-bone fractures, acute low-back/lumbar/sciatic conditions, and selected minor acute musculoskeletal injuries. The primary outcome was an opioid prescription at discharge. Among who were prescribed an opioid, secondary outcomes were total and daily prescribed morphine milligram equivalents (MME). Multivariable models adjusted for demographic, clinical, substance-use, utilization, year, and diagnosis variables.

Results: Among 3159 patients, 507 (16.0%) disclosed cannabis use. Opioids were prescribed to 27.6% of cannabis-disclosing and 31.3% of documented noncannabis patients (absolute difference, -3.6 percentage points; 95% CI, -7.9 to 0.6). Cannabis disclosure was not associated with discharge opioid prescribing after adjusting for covariates (adjusted odds ratio, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.67-1.11). Among opioid recipients, cannabis disclosure was not associated with total MME (adjusted mean ratio, 1.11; 95% CI, 0.92-1.34) or daily MME (1.07; 95% CI, 0.95-1.21).

Conclusions: Documented cannabis disclosure was not independently associated with opioid prescribing at ED discharge or prescribed opioid dose.

Clobes TA, Kraybill M, Himebaugh S, Jones B, Jaskolka M
Journal Article
Full text · PubMed

item.title: J Emerg Med: Cardioversion of Stable Atrial Fibrillation in the Emergency Department: Electrical Versus Pharmacological in the Era of Overcrowding
item.description:
Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a leading cause of emergency department (ED) visits. Optimizing the management of recent-onset AF is crucial to reduce length of stay (LOS) and improve ED resource utilization.

Study objectives: To evaluate differences in ED LOS between pharmacological (PC) and electrical cardioversion (ECV) in patients with recent-onset AF. Secondarily, to compare adverse event profiles of propofol versus midazolam.

Methods: This retrospective, single-center observational study analyzed ED patients with stable recent-onset AF who underwent PC or ECV. Patients with hemodynamic instability, combined sedatives, or concurrent clinical issues prolonging ED LOS were excluded from the primary analysis.

Results: A total of 575 patients were analyzed: ECV-propofol (n = 201), ECV-midazolam (n = 27), flecainide (n = 312), propafenone (n = 15), and amiodarone (n = 20). The overall ECV approach demonstrated a significantly shorter median LOS (114 min) compared with overall PC (130 min) (p = 0.006). In a propensity score matched analysis (excluding crossover pathways), ECV-propofol showed a numerically shorter LOS (106 min) versus flecainide (118 min), though not statistically significant (p = 0.086). However, a secondary analysis of 121 crossover patients revealed that pharmacological failures drove massive ED delays (median LOS 317 min). Adverse events in the ECV-propofol cohort (5%) were strictly minor and self-limited.

Conclusion: While uncomplicated PC with flecainide approaches the temporal efficiency of propofol sedation, the overall ECV strategy is associated with a significantly shorter ED LOS. By adopting structured propofol-based ECV protocols, emergency physicians can effectively avoid the enormous time delays that occur when initial pharmacological interventions fail.

Mariani A, Geniere Nigra S, Lorenzi L, Battaglini C, Francesconi R
Journal Article
Full text · PubMed

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Whole blood transfusion in adult patients with traumatic brain injury: A systematic review and meta-analysis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Whole blood (WB) transfusion may improve outcomes in trauma patients compared with component therapy, but evidence in traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains limited. We evaluated the clinical effectiveness of WB transfusion in adults with TBI requiring transfusion.

Methods: We searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP for studies published from January 2006 through August 31, 2026. Eligible studies included randomized trials and observational studies using propensity score matching or inverse probability of treatment weighting. Random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp adjustment was performed for mortality. Component-specific transfusion requirements were summarized qualitatively.

Results: Five studies were included in the systematic review, and four studies were included in the mortality meta-analysis. WB transfusion was not clearly associated with lower mortality (RR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.62-1.16; P = 0.19; I2 = 48.3%), with a 95% prediction interval of 0.48-1.49. Sensitivity analyses using alternative effect-size conversion methods, baseline risks, effect measures, and mortality definitions yielded consistent results. In exploratory leave-one-out analyses, pooled RRs ranged from 0.74 to 0.91, with all 95% CIs including 1. Three studies contributed component-specific transfusion data; red blood cells and plasma requirements were generally lower with WB, although this may partly reflect substitution by WB itself. The certainty of evidence was very low.

Conclusions: Current evidence is insufficient to determine whether WB transfusion reduces mortality after TBI because of the limited number of studies, clinical and methodological heterogeneity, risk of bias, and imprecision. Further randomized trials in clearly defined TBI populations are needed.

Nagamura T, Taniguchi H, Utsumi S, Yamada K, Terayama T, Mukherjee K
Journal Article, Review
Full text · PubMed

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the emergency department: Factors associated with outcome
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: Pediatric cardiac arrest is usually studied either before hospital arrival or after admission, although the emergency department (ED) team resuscitates both. We examined factors associated with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), recurrent arrest and mortality in an ED cohort including both out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCA) and in-ED cardiac arrests.

Methods: Retrospective cohort of all 83 children who received cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in a university pediatric ED over 14 years (January 2010-March 2024). The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge; multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with ED mortality.

Results: Median age was 35 months; 54.2% occurred out of hospital. ROSC was achieved in 42.2% and 30.1% survived the ED phase, but 9.9% survived to discharge. Epinephrine given later than 2 min was independently associated with ED mortality among the 27 patients with documented timing (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 7.73; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.27-46.97). Beyond 20 min of CPR, each additional minute was associated with ED death (aOR 1.32; 95% CI 1.01-1.73). Recurrent arrest after ROSC in the ED occurred in 42.9%, of whom 6.7% survived versus 38.9% without recurrence (p = 0.039). Survival did not differ by arrest location, initial rhythm or timing of advanced airway management.

Conclusion: Resuscitation in the ED restored spontaneous circulation in many children, but few survived to discharge. Time to first epinephrine was independently associated with ED mortality in this cohort, whereas prolonged resuscitation and recurrent arrest after ROSC in the ED identified children at very high risk.

Baran Ö, Eser Ö, Er A, Arayıcı ME, Duman M, Ulusoy E
Journal Article
Full text · PubMed

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Modified pneumonia risk score using lung ultrasound for the prediction of radiographic pneumonia in children
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: The diagnosis of pneumonia in children based on clinical findings is challenging. The Pneumonia Risk Score (PRS), a clinical prediction tool, estimates the risk of radiographic pneumonia. Most children are classified as moderate-risk and are recommended to undergo chest x-ray (CXR). We hypothesized that lung ultrasound (LUS) may add diagnostic value beyond the PRS for predicting radiographic pneumonia.

Methods: We studied a convenience sample of children 6 months to 18 years old enrolled in a prospective LUS registry who presented to the emergency department with acute respiratory complaints and underwent CXR and LUS. The primary outcome was radiographic pneumonia. Logistic regression included the five PRS clinical predictors, and LUS consolidation ≥1 cm with bronchograms was added to create the PRS + LUS model. We compared the area under the curve (AUC) of the PRS to the PRS + LUS, evaluated risk re-classifications, and proposed a novel diagnostic algorithm.

Results: Among 275 children, 58 (21%) had radiographic pneumonia. LUS consolidation was strongly associated with pneumonia (OR 28.68 [95% CI, 9.98 to 82.43]). The PRS + LUS demonstrated greater diagnostic accuracy than the PRS alone (AUC 0.85 [95% CI, 0.77 to 0.89] versus 0.70 [95% CI, 0.61 to 0.76]; P < 0.001). Using our proposed novel two-step diagnostic algorithm, the PRS + LUS was calculated for patients assigned a moderate-risk score by PRS, resulting in assigning an additional 120 (44%) patients a high- or low-risk score, decreasing the moderate-risk category.

Conclusion: Adding LUS to the PRS improves prediction of radiographic pneumonia and may reduce CXR use, particularly among patients with moderate risk.

Jarjour J, Neuman MI, Lipsett SC, Monuteaux MC, Hoffmann RM, Hirsch AW
Journal Article
Full text · PubMed

item.title: Crit Care Med: A Guytonian Atlas of Venous Return in Septic Shock: Reconstruction of Hemodynamic States
item.description:
Objectives: To reconstruct venous return physiology across published studies of septic shock and characterize the distribution of circulatory states represented in the literature.

Design: Exploratory physiologic reconstruction study.

Setting: Secondary analysis of published hemodynamic observations.

Patients: Adult patients with septic shock reported in studies containing sufficient information for reconstruction of mean circulatory filling pressure analogue (Pmca) and related parameters including venous return driving pressure (VRdP) and resistance to venous return (RVR).

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: A total of 150 observations were available. Median Pmca, central venous pressure (CVP), VRdP, and RVR were 17.3 mm Hg, 9.0 mm Hg, 7.9 mm Hg, and 1.04 mm Hg/min/L, respectively. Empirical quartiles identified four recurrent circulatory phenotypes: reduced filling pressure/gradient, preserved venous return, elevated venous pressure, and high-resistance venous return. The preserved venous return pattern demonstrated the highest median cardiac output (CO), whereas the high-resistance pattern exhibited the lowest flow despite comparable filling pressures. In exploratory adjusted analyses incorporating available vasopressor exposure and fluid-therapy context, VRdP remained strongly associated with CO (β, 1.03 L/min/mm Hg; 95% CI, 0.80-1.25; p < 0.001). When Pmca and CVP were entered separately, Pmca was positively associated with CO (β, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.79-1.25; p < 0.001), whereas CVP was inversely associated with CO (β, -1.03; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.80; p < 0.001).

Conclusions: Published hemodynamic observations in septic shock occupy distinct Guytonian phenotypes characterized by different combinations of circulatory filling pressure, venous pressure, and RVR. Reconstruction of venous return geometry may provide a physiologic framework for interpreting circulatory heterogeneity in septic shock.

Chalkias A, Mavridis T, Papagiannakis N, Katsifa K, Nikolaidis I, Laou E
Journal Article
Full text · PubMed

item.title: Crit Care Med: Association of Care Intensity With Survival and Long-Term Cost-Effectiveness in Sepsis Without Initial Organ Support After Emergency Admission: A Multicenter Cohort Study in Japan
item.description:
Objectives: To identify subgroups of patients hospitalized for community-acquired sepsis without initial organ support who may derive survival and cost-effectiveness benefits from ICU or high-dependency care unit (HDU) admission.

Design: Retrospective cohort study.

Setting: A 140-hospital Japanese database (April 2016-March 2024).

Patients: Adults admitted via emergency ambulance for community-acquired sepsis not requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, mechanical ventilation, catecholamines, or renal replacement therapy before or on the antimicrobial-initiation day.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: We compared ICU and HDU admissions, each vs. general ward (GW) admission, balancing patient characteristics using overlap propensity-score weighting. In-hospital mortality was estimated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs using modified Poisson regression. Cost-effectiveness was measured by the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in 3-year costs per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among 28,211 patients (GW, 18,349; HDU, 8,706; ICU, 1,156), ICU and HDU admissions were not associated with lower mortality overall (HDU vs. GW; RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.92-1.06 and ICU vs. GW; RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.92-1.22). However, HDU admission was associated with lower mortality among patients with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score greater than or equal to 6 (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.99) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score less than or equal to 12 (RR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.71-0.92). Under the Japanese (50,000 USD/QALY) and U.S. (100,000 USD/QALY) thresholds, ICU and HDU admissions were not cost-effective overall (ICERs > 200,000 USD/QALY). However, the HDU subgroup with GCS score less than or equal to 12 (ICER, 47,738 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 45,918-49,558) was cost-effective under both thresholds, and that with SOFA score greater than or equal to 6 (ICER, 55,319 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 52,018-58,624) met the U.S. threshold.

Conclusions: ICU or HDU admission was not associated with survival or economic benefits overall, whereas HDU subgroups (SOFA score ≥ 6 or GCS score ≤ 12) were associated with lower mortality and better cost-effectiveness. These findings may help optimize resource allocation.

Hashimoto Y, Inoue N, Yoshida M, Iketani R, Imai S
Journal Article
Full text · PubMed

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Effect of airway assistant training on intubation time during simulated prehospital airway management: A pilot study
item.description:
Objectives: Challenging airways are common in the out-of-hospital setting, where delays or failure to secure the airway can result in significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, this pilot study aimed to determine whether training paramedics in the role of airway assistant improves intubation time during a simulated regurgitating airway using suction-assisted laryngoscopy and airway decontamination (SALAD).

Methods: Twelve qualified paramedics were randomly allocated to one of two groups (n = 6) and paired with intensive care paramedics (ICPs). Airway assistants in Group 1 completed a one-hour airway assistant training program, whereas airway assistants in Group 2 received no training. Participants completed a standardized, timed simulation using a continuously regurgitating mannequin designed to replicate the challenges of out-of-hospital intubation. The primary outcome was time to successful intubation, defined as passage of the endotracheal tube through the vocal cords with cuff inflation.

Results: Airway assistant training significantly reduced intubation time. The untrained group recorded a median intubation time of 102.5 seconds (IQR 36), compared with 53 seconds (IQR 19) in the trained group. Group comparisons demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in intubation time (p = 0.009) and corresponded to a very large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.86; Hedges' g = 1.72). No association was observed between intubation time and the age or experience of either the airway assistant or the ICP. No esophageal intubations occurred in either group.

Conclusions: In this pilot study, training paramedics to perform the airway assistant role significantly reduced intubation time in a simulated regurgitating airway. These preliminary findings suggest that incorporating structured airway assistant training into prehospital education programs may improve airway management performance in challenging environments. Given the small sample size and simulated setting, larger studies are required to confirm these findings and determine whether the observed benefits translate to clinical practice.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Tumor Treating Fields and Quality of Life Among Patients With Locally Advanced Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: The PANOVA-3 trial demonstrated the survival benefit and tolerability of Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, but understanding the impact of TTFields therapy on quality of life (QoL) and pain is important for clinical decision-making.

Objective: To analyze the impact of TTFields therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel on QoL and pain outcomes using prospective data from PANOVA-3.

Design, setting, and participants: This is a prespecified secondary analysis of PANOVA-3, which was a global, open-label, multicenter, phase 3 randomized clinical trial in adult patients with previously untreated locally advanced unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma (LA-PAC). A total of 571 patients were randomized between May 1, 2018, and March 31, 2023, with follow-up completed October 31, 2024. Data analysis was performed from November 2024 to May 2025.

Intervention: Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive either TTFields therapy (150 kHz) with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel or gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. Nab-paclitaxel (125 mg/m2) and gemcitabine (1000 mg/m2) were administered intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of 28-day cycles. Duration of follow-up was 18 months.

Main outcomes and measures: QoL was measured using the European Organization for the Research and Treatment of Cancer Core Quality of Life Questionnaire and the 26-item pancreatic cancer module. End points were mean changes from baseline QoL scores, deterioration-free survival of QoL, and time to opioid use. An analysis of pain medication use was performed post hoc.

Results: At baseline, 562 patients (median [IQR] age, 67 [31-90] years; 295 [52.5%] female), including 279 of 285 patients in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm and 283 of 286 patients in the gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm, completed the EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaire. Global health status was stable during the 26-month follow-up in both study arms. Digestive symptoms, pain, and pancreatic pain were improved from 2 months after treatment initiation throughout treatment and follow-up in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm. TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel was associated with longer deterioration-free survival for global health status than gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone (median [IQR], 7.1 [3.5-14.8] vs 5.7 [2.3-11.5] months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.77; 95% CI, 0.61-0.97; P = .02). Longer deterioration-free survival was also observed for most items on the digestive symptoms scales (indigestion and altered bowel habit were similar between the 2 arms). Median (IQR) deterioration-free survival was significantly longer with TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel for pain (10.1 [4.0-20.9] vs 7.4 [3.5-14.5] months; HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.54-0.89; P = .003) and pancreatic pain (14.7 [6.2-46.2] vs 10.2 [5.6-18.2] months; HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.52-0.90; P = .006) as was median time to opioid use in the modified intention-to-treat population (9.3 [3.9-18.6] vs 6.7 [1.1-16.3] months; HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.55-0.93; P = .01).

Conclusions and relevance: This secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that TTFields therapy with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel improved QoL and provided clinically meaningful benefits in pain outcomes compared with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. This study's results suggest that TTFields therapy with gemicitabine and nab-paclitaxel is practice-changing for patients with unresectable LA-PAC.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03377491.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Clinician Training, Text Messages, and Human Papillomavirus Vaccination Among Children Aged 10 to 12 Years: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination rates among adolescents remain below recommendations.

Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician communication training and parent-targeted text messages at increasing HPV vaccination among children aged 11 to 12 years.

Design, setting, and participants: This doubly randomized, 2-level nested clinical trial was conducted from February 2022 to September 2024 among clinicians at 30 pediatric primary care clinics in Florida, children aged 10 to 12 years who had not received any of the 3 adolescent HPV vaccines, and their parents. Interventions occurred for 1 year, and vaccine records were collected for 2 years.

Interventions: Clinics were randomized 1:1:1 to 3 training groups: (1) the bundled approach, which presents the HPV vaccine in the middle of 2 other recommended vaccines; (2) the focused approach, which emphasizes cancer prevention; and (3) deferred, which offered clinicians the opportunity to participate in the focused training after the trial concluded. Clinicians in the first 2 groups completed a 1-hour communication training and a 5-minute booster session. Patients within clinics were randomized 1:1:1 to 3 text message groups, aligned with the communication strategies: (1) bundled, (2) focused, and (3) no text messages. Parents were sent text messages at the start of the study or prior to their child's 11th birthday as well as prior to appointments.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were HPV vaccine initiation (receipt of first dose) and completion (receipt of second dose). Analyses accounted for clinic-level clustering. Effects were analyzed as randomized and text messages as received.

Results: At baseline, 59 clinicians (44 [75%] female; 12 [20%] Asian, 21 [36%] Hispanic, and 21 [36%] non-Hispanic White) within 30 randomized clinics were included, with 17 randomized to the focused group, 21 to the bundled group, and 21 to the deferred group. A total of 7234 children were aged 10 (3576 [49%]), 11 (2617 [36%]), and 12 (1041 [14%]) years at study start (1673 [23%] Hispanic, 1001 [14%] non-Hispanic Black, and 1210 [17%] non-Hispanic White). A total of 28 clinics (93%), 50 clinicians (85%), and 6498 children (90%) completed the 2-year follow-up. The mean pre-post clinic-level difference for HPV vaccine initiation was 28.2 (95% CI, 25.3-31.1) percentage points and for completion was 16.1 (95% CI, 13.3-18.9) percentage points. Risk ratios for clinician training and text messaging did not differ between groups for initiation or completion. Among patients whose parents received text messages vs not, the risk ratio for initiation was 1.17 (95% CI, 1.08-1.26) and for completion was 1.29 (95% CI, 1.06-1.56).

Conclusions and relevance: In this study of Florida children aged 10 to 12 years, clinic-level HPV vaccination increased over time. No differences in HPV vaccination by random assignment of clinician training or text messages were detected. When received, text messages were associated with higher HPV vaccination.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05006833.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Body Mass Index Peak-Rebound Patterns and Inhibitory Control Among Young Children
item.description:
Importance: Childhood obesity has been linked with poor inhibitory control, and atypical body mass index (BMI) growth trajectories may identify children at higher risk for poor inhibitory control. Inhibitory control is also sexually dimorphic (male vs female), as maladaptive inhibitory control is more common in males.

Objective: To investigate the association between early childhood BMI peak-rebound patterns and inhibitory control development at 4 to 5 and 6 to 7 years and test whether there is a sexually dimorphic association.

Design, setting, and participants: The Programming Research in Obesity, Growth, Environment, and Social Stressors study is a prebirth cohort that recruited pregnant women receiving prenatal care through the Mexican Social Security Institute from July 2007 to February 2010 and followed up from pregnancy through age 8 years. Data were analyzed from November 2024 to December 2025.

Exposure: Repeated weight and length or height measurements were collected from birth to 8 years and mixed-effects models were used to characterize sex- and child-specific BMI trajectories and derive age and magnitude of the BMI peak (maximum inflection point during infancy) and rebound (minimum inflection point during early childhood).

Main outcomes and measures: Children completed the Conners Kiddie Continuous Performance Test, second edition, to assess inhibitory control at ages 4 to 5 and 6 to 7 years, and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess associations of age and magnitude of BMI peak and rebound with inhibitory control across the 2 time points. Sex-specific trajectories were evaluated by modeling interactions between child sex.

Results: Among 539 children included in the study, 278 (51.6%) were male; 277 (51.4%) were born to mothers with low socioeconomic status, and the mean (SD) gestational age at birth was 38.4 (1.6) weeks. After adjusting for covariates, a 1-SD higher BMI at peak was associated with higher T-scores for hit reaction time standard errors (β = 0.89; 95% CI, 0.20 to 1.58). A 1-SD higher age at rebound was associated with higher hit reaction time (β = 2.35; 95% CI, -0.01 to 4.72). However, age at peak and BMI at rebound were not associated with any inhibitory control measure. Children with early timing of peak and rebound exhibited higher T-scores for omission errors (β = 4.05; 95% CI, 0.96 to 7.13), while children with early timing of peak and late timing of BMI rebound had lower T-scores for hit reaction time (β = -4.16; 95% CI, -7.29 to -1.02) compared with those with normal timing of peak and rebound. In males, both older age and a higher magnitude of BMI rebound were associated with lower omission error T-scores, whereas in females, variations in age and magnitude of BMI patterns were associated with higher T-scores for hit reaction time and hit reaction time standard errors.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 539 children in Mexico, early-life BMI peak-rebound trajectories across childhood were associated with inhibitory control. These findings extend the literature beyond the well-established effects of BMI peak-rebound on metabolic conditions.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Access to Care and Practice Variation in the Assessment of Ankyloglossia
item.description:
Importance: Diagnosis and treatment of ankyloglossia has increased in recent years. A lack of universal evaluation and management guidelines may contribute to inconsistent practice patterns and variable access to care.

Objective: To evaluate access to care and practice pattern variation in the treatment of ankyloglossia as a source of breastfeeding difficulty across clinicians and sites of care in Ohio.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study of pediatric dentists and pediatric and general otolaryngologists providing treatment to pediatric patients in Ohio was conducted using a secret shopper approach from October 6, 2025, to January 5, 2026. All pediatric dentists and otolaryngologists providing treatment to pediatric patients were eligible for inclusion. Health care professionals were identified using lists obtained from the Ohio State Dental Board and the American Academy of Otolaryngology.

Exposure: Clinics were contacted via phone by a simulated patient's mother using a vignette describing a 2-week-old infant with breastfeeding difficulty characterized by painful latch and inquiring regarding ankyloglossia (ie, tongue tie) evaluation.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were time to first available appointment and procedure cost to patient on the day of service. Secondary outcomes included referral requirement, potential for same-day procedures, procedure technique, additional procedures discussed during scheduling, insurance acceptance, and total cost of consultation and procedure.

Results: A total of 175 clinics representing 487 health care professionals (299 dentists and 188 otolaryngologists) were contacted. The median (IQR) appointment wait time was 14 (7-28) days. For practices providing cost information, time-of-service cash payment was required by 31 of 36 dental offices (86%), while all otolaryngology practices (38 of 38; [100%]) billed medical insurance. Dental clinics were more likely to empirically recommend other procedures (eg, maxillary frenulum release) at the time of appointment scheduling (29 of 45 [64%]) than otolaryngology offices (1 of 38 [3%]) (P < .001). Across all practices, the median (IQR) cost of lingual frenotomy alone was $474 ($350-$545), while total cost (consultation and all recommended procedures) ranged from $200 to $1515.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of pediatric dental and otolaryngology clinics in Ohio, access to care for ankyloglossia was similar, but the anticipated cost of procedures varied widely, as did empiric recommendations for intervention beyond lingual frenotomy. Prospective patients should be aware of this heterogeneity and the potential for significant price differences for treatment.

Hunter MO, Lee K, Sanchez RE, Kistler I, Elmaraghy CA, Manning AM

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Work Hours, Emergency Department Context, and Workplace Violence Among Nurses
item.description:
Importance: Workplace violence is common in high-risk health care settings, with consequences for clinician well-being and care delivery. Less is known about multilevel work-system factors associated with workplace violence in emergency department (ED) nurses.

Objective: To characterize workplace violence among ED nurses and identify multilevel work-system factors associated with workplace violence.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study used nurse survey data combined with administrative and electronic medical record data collected in 2023 from nurses working in 11 EDs in a multisite health system in the southeastern US.

Exposure: Multilevel work-system factors, with primary exposures of interest including overtime, shift type, and ED type (freestanding vs in-hospital); additional covariates included individual, team, and ED-level characteristics.

Main outcomes and measures: Any self-reported workplace violence in the prior month (threats, physical violence, verbal abuse, unwanted sexual attention, or bullying) from patients, visitors, and/or coworkers. Associations were estimated using mixed-effects logistic regression with a random intercept for emergency department site and factor selection using cross-validated least absolute shrinkage and selectrion operator regression. Nurses in the supplemental staffing team were excluded from this analysis.

Results: Among 337 ED nurses (mean [SD] age, 34.9 [9.5] years; 289 [85.8%] female; 287 [85.2% white; mean [SD] nursing experience, 9.0 [8.2] years), 296 (87.8%) reported workplace violence in the prior month. Incidents of WPV involved patients or visitors (292 of 296 [98.6%]) and coworkers (60 of 296 [20.3%]). In adjusted mixed-effects models (n = 299), overtime was associated with higher odds of workplace violence (OR, 3.21; 95% CI, 1.30-7.93), while night shift (OR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.10-0.78) and employment in a freestanding ED (OR, 0.25; 95% CI, 0.09-0.76) were associated with lower odds.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of ED nurses, workplace violence was common and was associated with overtime and ED context. These findings support further evaluation of work-hour practices and context-specific approaches to workplace violence prevention.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Racial and Ethnic Differences in County-Level Availability of Uterine Cancer Clinical Trials
item.description:
Importance: Racial and ethnic disparities exist in clinical trial enrollment, but whether such disparities exist in geographic availability of uterine cancer trials is unknown.

Objective: To examine associations between race and ethnicity and county-level presence and rates of available uterine cancer clinical trials.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study linked Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Research Plus; Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov; and American Community Survey data of adult patients (aged ≥18 years) diagnosed with uterine cancer between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2021. The data analysis was performed between November 10, 2025, and September 9, 2026.

Exposures: Race and ethnicity categorized as American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black, Hispanic (any race), Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and White.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were county-level presence and rate of interventional uterine cancer trials. Hurdle models were used to estimate racial and ethnic differences in the odds of residing in a county with at least 1 trial and among patients in counties with trial availability, differences in rates of trials per person. Models accounted for county clustering and were adjusted for patient characteristics.

Results: Among 155 811 patients in the cohort (median [IQR] age at diagnosis, 62 [55-69] years; 1055 identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native [0.7%], 12 753 as Asian [8.2%], 16 303 as Black [10.5%], 23 177 as Hispanic [14.9%], 2175 as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander [1.4%], and 100 348 as White [64.4%] race and ethnicity), 121 525 (78.0%) resided in a county with at least 1 available trial. Trial availability was observed among 58.0% of American Indian or Alaska Native patients, 94.3% of Asian patients, 77.7% of Black patients, 86.1% of Hispanic patients, 90.3% of Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander patients, and 74.1% of White patients. Compared with White patients, higher odds of residing in counties with at least 1 available trial were found for Asian (odds ratio [OR], 5.83; 95% CI, 4.83-7.12), Black (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.07-1.30), Hispanic (OR, 2.18; 95% CI, 1.80-2.63), and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (OR, 3.34; 95% CI, 2.17-5.66) patients, whereas American Indian or Alaska Native patients had lower odds (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.39-0.61). Among patients in counties with at least 1 trial, fewer available trials per person were found for Asian (rate ratio [RR], 0.69; 95% CI, 0.65-0.74), Hispanic (RR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.52-0.61), and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.80-0.95) patients compared with White patients.

Conclusions and relevance: This cohort study of patients with uterine cancer found that racial and ethnic patterns in geographic trial availability differed by how availability was measured. The presence of any trial may not fully capture geographic access to clinical trial opportunities.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Neighborhood Exposome at Birth and Trajectories of Epigenetic Age Acceleration Across Childhood
item.description:
Importance: Epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) has been linked to increased disease risk in adults, yet its developmental trajectories and early-life neighborhood determinants remain poorly understood.

Objective: To examine whether there are associations between the neighborhood exposome at birth and EAA trajectories from early childhood through adolescence.

Design, setting, and participants: This longitudinal cohort study used data from Project Viva, a prebirth cohort that enrolled pregnant women in eastern Massachusetts from April 22, 1999, to July 31, 2002. Participants included 570 children with available peripheral blood DNA methylation data, complete neighborhood characteristics, and complete covariates. Data were analyzed from August 19, 2024, to August 21, 2026.

Exposures: Neighborhood exposome profiles at birth derived from 22 census tract-level characteristics across 4 domains (area deprivation, social fragmentation, population density, and environmental quality) using self-organizing maps.

Main outcomes and measures: EAA was calculated at 3, 8, and 13 years of age using the Horvath, Skin & Blood, and Wu epigenetic clocks. Trajectories were identified using latent class linear mixed models. Associations between neighborhood profiles and EAA trajectories were estimated using multinomial mixed models.

Results: Among 570 children (mean [SD] age at early childhood, 3.2 [0.4] years; 305 [53.5%] male), 3 EAA trajectory groups (stable, increasing, and decreasing for the Horvath and Skin & Blood clocks or low-baseline for the Wu clock) and 3 neighborhood profiles were identified. Compared with profile 1 (suburban, lowest adverse exposures [n = 278]), children born into profile 2 (urban, high residential instability and single-person households, and highway proximity [n = 168]) had greater odds of increasing EAA for the Wu clock (adjusted odds ratio, 1.67 [95% CI, 1.03-2.69]). Profile 3 (urban, high socioeconomic deprivation and pollution [n = 124]) showed no associations.

Conclusions and relevance: In this longitudinal cohort study, birth into neighborhoods characterized by high residential instability and single-person households and highway proximity was associated with increasing Wu EAA trajectories across childhood. These findings suggest that early-life neighborhood conditions, encompassing both social and physical environmental factors, may represent targets for interventions aimed at reducing long-term disease risk. Further research is needed to clarify the implications of these findings for later health and prevention.

item.title: Crit Care Med: The Impact of Early Changes in Albumin Levels on Long-Term Kidney and Mortality Outcomes in Patients With Acute Kidney Injury Undergoing Continuous Kidney Replacement Therapy
item.description:
Objectives: To investigate the association between early changes in the levels of serum albumin during continuous kidney replacement therapy (CKRT) and long-term dialysis dependence and mortality in patients with acute kidney injury who survived for 90 days or more days after CKRT initiation.

Design: A multicenter retrospective cohort study.

Setting: Eight university-affiliated tertiary hospitals in South Korea participating in the LINking health medical records, biospecimens, and biosignals in Korean patients with Acute kidney injury consortium cohort.

Patients: The study involved 1087 adult patients with acute kidney injury who survived for 90 or more days after CKRT initiation between January 2017 and June 2022.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Based on albumin levels at CKRT initiation and on day 7, patients were categorized into the persistent, resolved, new-onset, and no hypoalbuminemia groups. A composite of progression to end-stage kidney disease and all-cause mortality within 365 days was the primary outcome. The composite outcome occurred in 33.4% (363/1087) of the patients. The adjusted odds ratio (aOR) for the primary outcome was significantly higher in all groups when compared with the no hypoalbuminemia group (persistent: aOR, 2.64; 95% CI, 1.73-4.04; p < 0.001; resolved: aOR, 2.27; 95% CI, 1.38-3.75; p < 0.001; new-onset: aOR, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.06-2.68; p = 0.028). No hypoalbuminemia group was associated with the most favorable prognosis, whereas persistent hypoalbuminemia was associated with the worst outcomes.

Conclusions: During CKRT, early albumin level changes are associated with long-term kidney failure and mortality risk. Persistent hypoalbuminemia predicts the worst outcomes. Even in patients without baseline hypoalbuminemia, early decline in albumin is associated with worse prognosis.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Dynamics of Mitochondrial Structure, Biogenesis and Function in Skeletal Muscle of Critically Ill Patients
item.description:
Objectives: To define the timing and phenotype of mitochondrial ultrastructural remodeling and electron transport chain (ETC) function in skeletal muscle during early critical illness.

Design: Secondary analysis of a prospective observational study with serial muscle biopsies.

Setting: Adult ICU.

Patients: Thirty-three mechanically ventilated ICU patients (median age, 49 yr; 27% women) with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment greater than or equal to 9 on three consecutive days; skeletal muscle biopsies of the vastus lateralis muscle at ICU day 5 (n = 29) and day 15 (n = 22). Healthy subjects served as controls.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Vastus lateralis biopsies were analyzed by electron microscopy with stereology, quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), Western blotting, and spectrophotometric ETC enzyme assays (reported per tissue weight and normalized to citrate synthase [CS]). Intact mitochondrial profiles were reduced vs. controls (fold change vs. controls: day 5, 0.24 [0.18-0.34]; p = 0.039 and day 15, 0.20 [0.16-0.33]; p = 0.011) and disturbed profiles increased (day 5, 5.62 [3.20-7.17]; p < 0.001 and day 15, 5.20 [3.67-6.36]; p = 0.001), with reduced volume density of intact mitochondria (day 5, 0.33 [0.20-0.49]; p = 0.009 and day 15, 0.32 [0.21-0.50]; p = 0.005). Inner mitochondrial membrane surface-to-volume ratio was reduced at day 5 (0.69 [0.49-0.89]; p = 0.022) and remained unchanged at day 15. Complex III tissue activity was reduced at day 5 (85.6 [22.1-133.3] vs. 151.4 [100.5-205.0]; p = 0.015) and day 15 (50.5 [36.0-69.8]; p = 0.001), remaining reduced after CS normalization (day 5, 0.83 [0.34-1.49]; p = 0.040 and day 15, 0.87 [0.65-0.93]; p = 0.007). Complex IV activity remained reduced before and after CS normalization at both time points (all p < 0.001). CS activity declined by day 15 (56.3 [52.7-65.1] vs. 95.6 [80.1-133.0]; p = 0.001 and day 15 vs. day 5; p = 0.041). qRT-PCR and Western blot supported reduced ETC components and altered biogenesis signaling.

Conclusions: Skeletal muscle mitochondrial ultrastructure is altered by ICU day 5 and remains abnormal at day 15, with persistent complex III/IV dysfunction after CS normalization. These findings define an early sustained mitochondrial remodeling phenotype in skeletal muscle during critical illness.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Language Concordance in Critical Care: A Systematic Review
item.description:
Objectives: Language barriers are associated with differences in care delivery processes and outcomes in critical care settings, with differences despite language assistance services. Less is known about outcomes associated with language concordant care. Language concordance is a linguistic match between a patient's preferred language and the language used by their care team. We undertook a systematic review to examine the measurement and impact of language concordant care delivery during critical illness, inclusive of the critical care recovery period after hospitalization.

Data sources and study selection: A systematic review was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Embase, and Cochrane of English-language publications from database inception to March 3, 2026. Studies that investigated adults in critical care and post-ICU recovery clinic settings that included measurement of language concordance were included. Study quality was evaluated by the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist.

Data synthesis: Of 1,682 unique records identified, 11 were eligible for inclusion (128,181 total patients; mean [sd] age, 68.4 [17.9 yr]; 72,872 [56.9%] male and 55,082 [43.1%] female). Six studies assessed clinical decision-making. Reported outcomes included code status changes, family conferences, communication complexity, delirium, length of stay, mechanical ventilation, and mortality. Due to significant heterogeneity in study analyses and reported outcomes, data were not pooled for quantitative analysis.

Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that language-concordant care may influence clinically meaningful processes of critical care, warranting interventional studies to guide care delivery recommendations.

Danesh V, Royce S, Godoy SE, Mirabal-Beltran R, Sanchez K, Arroliga AC

item.title: West J Emerg Med: Shoulder Dislocation Reduction Using Inhaled Nitrous Oxide in the Emergency Department: Retrospective Case Series
item.category: The western journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Inhaled nitrous oxide (iNO) offers rapid onset analgesia with a favorable safety profile yet remains underused for shoulder dislocation reductions in the emergency department (ED). The objective of this study was to evaluate the use and outcomes of iNO for shoulder reduction in the ED, including whether intravenous (IV) access was required, whether successful reduction could be accomplished without additional analgesic or sedative medications under procedural sedation, and the rate of adverse effects from iNO.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective chart review of shoulder dislocation reductions using iNO at two high-volume EDs over three years (2019-2022). Data collected included age, sex, indication, procedural success, IV placement, medications administered, and adverse events and was stored in a password-protected database. The primary endpoint was successful reduction with iNO as the primary procedural analgesic; secondary endpoint was occurrence of any adverse events.

Results: Of 138 patients, 125 (90.6%; 95% CI, 0.84-0.95) achieved successful reduction with iNO alone without escalation to procedural sedation; 102 patients (74%) did not require IV access. Adverse events were rare (2/138 or 1.4% [95% CI, 0.02-0.05]): one patient experienced transient agitation (a known side effect of N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonism), and one had vomiting. Both were self-limited without hemodynamic changes.

Conclusion: This retrospective case series, the largest of its kind to date examining iNO for shoulder dislocation reduction, demonstrated a 90.6% success rate with minimal adverse events and reduced resource utilization compared to procedural sedation. These findings support further prospective investigation of iNO for shoulder dislocation as well as other orthopedic reductions and painful ED procedures.

item.title: West J Emerg Med: Assessment of Combined Food and Nutrition Insecurity Screening in the Emergency Department: A Brief Report
item.category: The western journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Emergency department (ED) food insecurity (FI) screening traditionally identifies insufficient access to food but does not account for diet quality. We evaluated the incremental yield of adding a nutrition insecurity (NI) screener to routine FI screening.

Methods: This single-center observational study enrolled adult ED patients from April-September 2025. Participants completed the 2-item Hunger Vital Sign and a 1-item NI screener. Our primary measure was incremental yield of NI screening beyond FI screening, defined by the number of NI-positive/FI-negative patients identified. Secondary outcome measures included FI and NI prevalence, screening concordance, and number needed to screen. Screening fidelity was supported through structured training of research associates and standardized phrasing.

Results: Of 1,120 patients, 13.6% (95% CI, 11.6-15.7%) screened positive for FI and 11.4% (95% CI, 9.7-13.5%) for NI. While the measures showed substantial agreement (κ = 0.67), they identified significantly different populations (McNemar P = .01). Specifically, 28 patients (2.5%) screened NI-positive but FI-negative, yielding an 18.4% relative increase in identified at-risk patients compared to only screening for FI.

Conclusion: Dual screening identified a clinically relevant NI-only subgroup whose diet-quality barriers were not captured by FI screening alone. Incorporating NI into ED social needs assessments may improve identification of diet-related risk and guide medically tailored interventions.

item.title: West J Emerg Med: Caring for Patients Anywhere, Anyhow: How Emergency Department Crowding and Boarding Shapes Professional Identity in Emergency Medicine Training
item.category: The western journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Emergency department (ED) boarding is a well-documented crisis associated with adverse patient outcomes, healthcare worker burnout, and moral injury. Although prior work has documented operational and educational impacts, including reductions in resident productivity and procedural exposure, less is known about how sustained boarding shapes professional identity formation. We sought to explore how sustained ED boarding shapes the learning experiences and professional identity formation of emergency medicine (EM) residents, as perceived by both residents and the attending physicians who train them.

Methods: Using a constructivist paradigm, we conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with residents and attending physicians from a 4-year EM residency program with rotations across 5 clinical sites, between July and August 2025. Two researchers independently coded transcripts and iteratively refined a shared codebook, continuing until additional interviews were unlikely to add new insight, guided by the concept of information power. We used reflexive thematic analysis, treating researchers' clinical and analytic judgment as a resource for identifying patterns of meaning, and prioritized participants' own construction of meaning over the frequency of any single idea, consistent with an interpretive phenomenological approach.

Results: We interviewed 13 emergency physicians: 6 residents and 7 attending physicians (range: 1-30+ years after residency). Three overarching themes emerged: (1) Educational challenges and opportunities-boarding fragments diagnostic ownership, narrows the acuity spectrum, and limits authentic undifferentiated encounters, although attending physicians adapt through structured hypotheticals and micro-teaching); (2) Shifts in the clinical environment-operational and structural adaptations create educational dead space, constrain the therapeutic alliance, and generate role ambiguity around boarded patients); and (3) Moral strain and suffering-moral injury and combined suffering is not peripheral to training but embedded within it, shaping how residents interpret professional responsibility and integrity. The three themes exist in a triangular relationship, with suffering at the foundation.

Conclusion: Boarding appeared to function as a formative context for professional identity formation, not merely a disruptive one. Residents described learning systems-level practice, advocacy, and emotional regulation, often through loss and moral injury, alongside attending physicians navigating the same. These findings suggest that recognizing boarding as a structural condition of training may reorient the responsibility of graduate medical education: formalizing adaptive teaching strategies, creating structured opportunities to process moral strain, and committing to advocacy that treats boarding as the educational crisis it is.

item.title: West J Emerg Med: Sex Differences in Time to Triage in the Emergency Department: A Retrospective Cohort Study
item.category: The western journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Efficient triage in emergency departments (ED) is crucial for timely patient care, as evidence indicates that time to triage could affect treatment outcomes. Sex differences have been observed in different healthcare areas. The objective of this study was to determine whether sex differences exist in a patient's time to triage and the magnitude of any observed differences at presentation to the ED of a Jerusalem hospital.

Methods: This retrospective study used anonymized data from adult ED visits between January 1 to September 30, 2024, at an ED in Jerusalem. Our primary outcome measure was the mean time to triage, defined as the interval between documented patient arrival and the first encounter with a triage nurse. Our secondary outcome measures included the proportion of patients triaged within 15 minutes, stratified by sex, ED division, and Emergency Severity Index (ESI) level.

Results: The study analyzed 30,447 adult ED visits over nine months. Mean time to triage was 10.9 minutes for women versus 10.3 minutes for men (absolute difference, 0.6 minutes; P < .001). Women were less likely to be triaged within 15 minutes (75.2% versus 76.9%; absolute difference, 1.7%; P < .001). Median time to triage was 6.0 minutes (interquartile range [IQR]) for men, 1.0-15.0 vs 7.0 minutes (IQR, 1.0-15.0) for women. Among patients with ESI levels 3-5, women had lower odds of triage within 15 minutes (odds ratio [OR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.73-0.84; P < .001), while no significant sex differences were observed for ESI levels 1-2 (OR 1.30; 0.90-1.88; P = .17). Differences were most pronounced in ED triage to the ambulatory care area (absolute difference, 1.8%; OR, 0.95) and minimal in acute care (absolute difference, 0.5%; OR, 0.84), with no significant difference in the shock-trauma unit. Both sexes had similar triage rates within 60 minutes (99.2%).

Conclusion: Although we found statistically significant sex differences in time to triage, the absolute difference of 0.6 minutes is not clinically meaningful. The near-universal triage within 60 minutes suggests that early triage prioritization differences do not translate into clinically significant delays. Within this ED, triage processes function similarly for men and women. Future research should evaluate downstream processes (eg, time to physician evaluation) to determine aspects of ED care that may demonstrate clinically important sex-based disparities.

item.title: West J Emerg Med: Machine Learning Versus Traditional Statistical Models for Emergency Department Volume Forecasting
item.category: The western journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Emergency department (ED) crowding harms patient care and strains hospital operations. Forecasting daily patient arrivals can help ED medical directors, department chairs, and hospital administrators plan staffing and bed capacity in advance, rather than reacting after a surge has already occurred. This study compared five computer-based forecasting methods, including three machine learning models (eXtreme gradient boosting [XGBoost], light gradient boosting machine [LGBM], and long short-term memory [LSTM]) and two traditional statistical models (autoregressive integrated moving average [ARIMA] and seasonal ARIMA [SARIMA]), to determine which most accurately predicts ED patient volume seven days in advance, using eight years of daily visit data from an academic freestanding ED.

Methods: This retrospective study analyzed 3,202 consecutive days of daily patient volume (March 27, 2017, to December 31, 2025) from an academic freestanding ED with approximately 31,102 annual visits. Each model used the preceding 365 days of data to forecast the subsequent 7 days, repeated across the study period to reflect the weekly cycle by which most EDs plan staffing. Our primary measure of accuracy was mean absolute error (MAE), defined as the average number of patients per day by which a forecast missed the actual volume. Secondary measures included root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), the coefficient of determination (R2, a score from 0 to 1 reflecting how well predictions tracked actual day-to-day volume), and the percentage of forecasts accurate within 5, 10, 15, and 20 patients, thresholds selected for their relevance to staffing decisions. The best-performing model on initial metrics, XGBoost, served as the reference model for statistical comparison using the Diebold-Mariano (DM) test, which determines whether an observed difference in accuracy between two models is statistically meaningful or attributable to chance.

Results: Among 453 rolling weekly forecast windows, SARIMA, XGBoost, and LGBM demonstrated the lowest absolute errors and best forecasting of patient volume, with MAE values of 9.60 (95% CI, 9.29-9.91), 9.61 (95% CI, 9.31-9.91), and 9.64 (95% CI, 9.33-9.94) patients/day, respectively; these three models therefore missed the actual daily patient count by approximately 9 to 10 patients, on average. Models ARIMA and LSTM were less accurate, with mean MAE values of 10.54 (95% CI, 10.21-10.87) and 12.01 (95% CI, 11.63-12.39) patients per day. Relative to the XGBoost reference (MAPE 13.82%), ARIMA (MAPE 14.93%) and LSTM (MAPE 17.27%) showed a marked decrease in predictive accuracy. For operational planning, the top-performing models (SARIMA, XGBoost, and LGBM) correctly predicted daily volume within a margin of 20 patients in 90.3% to 90.6% of instances, while LSTM performed less well and reached this threshold in only 83.3% of forecasts. Statistical testing confirmed these differences were unlikely due to chance, with XGBoost significantly outperforming ARIMA (DM = -6.09, P < .001) and LSTM (DM = -6.96, P < .001).

Conclusion: Models SARIMA, XGBoost, and LGBM performed comparably well, and all three would provide reliable, operationally useful forecasts for ED staffing and resource allocation decisions. A traditional statistical method, SARIMA, which is simpler and less resource-intensive to implement, performed as well as the newer machine learning methods evaluated in this study. This finding suggests that hospitals do not necessarily need to invest in more complex artificial intelligence tools to obtain accurate ED volume forecasts.

item.title: West J Emerg Med: Emergency Medicine Reimagined: Development of the Patient Rights Index for Emergency Medicine
item.category: The western journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Emergency medicine has evolved beyond episodic acute care to encompass a growing range of clinical, social, and system-level responsibilities. This scholarly perspective proposes the Patient Rights Index in Emergency Medicine (PRI-ED), a conceptual framework designed to organize recurring domains through which emergency departments promote access to care, patient safety, relief of suffering, autonomy, and dignity.

Methods: The PRI-ED was developed through iterative domain generation informed by clinical observation, professional experience, and targeted review of peer-reviewed literature, policy analyses, and professional organizational reports. No primary data collection, systematic review, formal consensus process, or empirical validation was performed.

Results: We identified 12 domains that represent recurring clinical, operational, and system-level challenges encountered in emergency medicine. These domains were organized within a standardized framework linking domain-specific objectives, intervention strategies, measurable indicators, and relevant policy or funding mechanisms.

Conclusion: The PRI-ED is a proposed conceptual framework for organizing and evaluating domains in which emergency medicine intersects with access, safety, autonomy, relief of suffering, and dignity. The framework is intended to inform future implementation, evaluation, and policy discussion and requires feasibility testing and outcome validation before effectiveness can be determined.

item.title: West J Emerg Med: Dedicated Vertical Physician Pilot in a Rotational Patient Assignment Emergency Department
item.category: The western journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Emergency department (ED) vertical patient pathways (VPP) assign patients to a dedicated care area with chairs, avoiding the use of traditional ED beds. The effect of reassigning a dedicated vertical emergency physician (EP) onto an established rotational patient assignment (RPA) system, which prospectively assigns arriving patients to EP queues, is unknown. We sought to describe operational outcomes and staff satisfaction with trialing this role.

Methods: We conducted a single-center, hypothesis-generating exploratory pilot at a 56-bed tertiary-care ED in which one 8.75-hour EP shift on five Mondays was repurposed into an 8.75-hour dedicated VPP role within a chair-based vertical patient care area while the rotational patient assignment system remained in place; three prior comparable Mondays served as comparison. Primary outcome was discharged-patient ED length of stay (LOS); secondary outcomes included VPP upgrades to a bed, patient numbers seen by the dedicated shift, and staff satisfaction. We report descriptive analyses.

Results: We analyzed 529 discharged-patient encounters: 199 (37.6%) during the preintervention period and 330 (62.4%) during the postintervention period. Median ED LOS for discharged patients did not demonstrate a consistent directional change, decreasing by seven minutes (3.1%) in the overall ED (226 vs 219 minutes) and increasing by 18.5 minutes (13.0%) among patients initially evaluated via the VPP (142.5 vs 161 minutes). The dedicated VPP EP saw three more patients per shift (21.4%; median 17 vs 14), and VPP upgrades fell from 15/68 (22.1%) to 5/130 (3.8%). Timeliness and communication were rated favorably by 4/4 VPP physician respondents and 10/12 and 16/17 registered nurse/allied health respondents, respectively; 3/4 VPP physician respondents vs 1/29 non-VPP physician respondents supported continuing the model.

Conclusion: Reassigning an existing EP to a dedicated vertical EP role within an ongoing rotational patient assignment system was not accompanied by shortened discharged-patient length of stay. Fewer VPP upgrades and a modest increase in patients seen by the dedicated shift were observed, but patient selection and acuity limit interpretation. Staff reported favorable teamwork within the vertical space, whereas non-VPP physicians reported less manageable workloads and little support for continuing the model.
