item.title: Lancet: Empirical tuberculosis treatment in infants living with HIV hospitalised with severe pneumonia in Africa (EMPIRICAL): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, 2 × 2 factorial, controlled superiority trial
item.description:
Background: Mortality among infants with severe HIV-associated pneumonia remains high globally. The EMPIRICAL trial evaluated whether empirical tuberculosis treatment (eTB-T) improves survival compared with the currently recommended microbiologically and clinically guided strategy.

Methods: This multicentre, open-label, group-sequential designed, 2×2 factorial, randomised, controlled, superiority trial was conducted in 19 hospitals across Côte d'Ivoire, Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Infants aged 28-365 days admitted with severe HIV-associated pneumonia, without a current tuberculosis diagnosis or contact, were centrally and individually randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) using a secure web-based system stratified by site and severity. A computer-generated block randomisation schedule was used, with fixed blocks of eight allocations (two allocations to each factorial treatment group) within each stratum. Participants received standard of care (SoC) comprising treatment for bacterial (WHO-recommended antibiotics) and Pneumocystis jirovecii (cotrimoxazole and steroids) pneumonia, SoC plus 15 days of oral valganciclovir (16 mg/kg per 12 h), or SoC plus 6 months of tuberculosis treatment (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, plus isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 subsequent months), or both interventions combined. Here, we report the comparison between the eTB-T (ie, SoC plus tuberculosis treatment and SoC plus oral valganciclovir plus tuberculosis treatment) and non-eTB-T (ie, SoC or SoC plus 15 days of oral valganciclovir) groups. Nasopharyngeal aspirates, stools for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing, and urine for tuberculosis lipoarabinomannan assay were collected at recruitment. In the non-eTB-T groups, tuberculosis treatment was initiated if microbiological results collected at recruitment yielded positive results or if, during follow-up, the treating clinician suspected tuberculosis on clinical grounds, including radiological findings, in accordance with routine clinical practice and guidelines. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality (at 15 days and 360 days). Survival was estimated using flexible parametric models with covariate-adjusted conditional estimates; missing data were imputed by chained equations. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03915366) and is now complete.

Findings: Between March 15, 2020, and Jan 31, 2024, 563 participants were enrolled; 558 were analysed after excluding five patients who did not meet eligibility criteria. 276 participants were allocated to the eTB-T groups (n=140 eTB-T and n=136 valganciclovir plus eTB-T) and 282 to the non-eTB-T groups (n=142 SoC and n=140 valganciclovir). 17 (6%) of 276 in the eTB-T groups and 20 (7%) of 282 in the non-eTB-T groups were lost to follow-up. Median age was 4·4 months (IQR 3·2-7·4) and 274 (49%) of participants were female and 284 (51%) were male. In the non-eTB-T groups, 130 (46%) of 282 participants eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment at a median of 4·0 days (IQR 3·0-15·0) after recruitment due to positive microbiological findings in 55 (20%) cases (53 confirmed by tuberculosis lipoarabinomannan assay and two by nasopharyngeal aspirates Xpert MTB/RIF) or clinical decision in 75 (27%) cases. There was no evidence of interaction between valganciclovir and eTB-T (adjusted hazard ratio 1·19, 95% CI 0·73-1·95; pheterogeneity=0·4836). At 12 months, 132 (48%) of 276 participants in eTB-T groups and 121 (43%) of 282 participants in non-eTB-T groups died. In the eTB-T groups, the adjusted hazard ratio for death was 1·12 (95% CI 0·87-1·43; p=0·3868). At 15 days, the odds ratio was 1·24 (95% CI 0·83-1·84; p=0·2950). Serious adverse events did not differ between groups (1·19, 0·82-1·73; p=0·3523). There were no treatment-related deaths. The most common adverse events were elevation of transaminases (72 [26%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 74 [26%] in the non-eTB-T group), anaemia (163 [59%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 169 [60%] in the non-eTB-T groups), and infectious disease requiring antimicrobial treatment (161 [58%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 176 [62%] in the non-eTB-T groups).

Interpretation: In contrast to empirical treatment with valganciclovir, there was no evidence that eTB-T was superior to a clinically and microbiologically guided strategy in reducing all-cause mortality among infants with HIV-associated pneumonia. However, the high proportion of infants who eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment during follow-up in the non-eTB-T groups might have reduced the contrast between strategies and attenuated the ability to detect differences in outcomes.

Funding: European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Multimodal Nonopioid Analgesia Versus Opioid-First Approaches for Acute Pain in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
item.description:
Background: The opioid crisis has prompted emergency departments (EDs) to adopt multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia for acute pain; however, comparative effectiveness and safety vs. opioid-first approaches remain incompletely characterized across common ED presentations.

Objective: To evaluate whether multimodal nonopioid or opioid-sparing analgesic strategies provide analgesia comparable or superior to opioid-first regimens for adults presenting to EDs with acute pain. Safety (opioid exposure and treatment-related adverse events) was assessed as a secondary aim.

Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from 2010 to 2026 in PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase enrolling adults (≥18 years) with acute pain from renal colic, trauma/musculoskeletal injury, or primary headache (migraine, tension-type, or cluster) treated in hospital-based EDs. Eligible interventions compared multimodal or opioid-sparing regimens with opioid-only or opioid-dominant regimens. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2.

Results: Seventeen RCTs (n = 7288) were included. Evidence was unevenly distributed, as 13 trials (76%; n = 5248) evaluated musculoskeletal trauma. Ibuprofen-acetaminophen achieved pain relief comparable to opioid-acetaminophen combinations for musculoskeletal pain. For migraine, prochlorperazine-diphenhydramine outperformed hydromorphone, with 86% achieving mild or no headache at 1 h vs. 52%. For renal colic, intramuscular diclofenac and intravenous paracetamol provided analgesia equivalent or superior to morphine with lower adverse event rates.

Conclusion: Multimodal nonopioid and opioid-sparing strategies generally provided comparable or superior analgesia to opioid-first regimens while reducing opioid exposure and adverse events, aligning with current guidelines. Because these conditions differ clinically and evidence was uneven and synthesized descriptively, the findings should be interpreted by condition rather than cumulatively.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Effect modification by arterial pH on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with shockable rhythm: A multicenter registry study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Arterial pH on emergency department (ED) arrival predicts outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but its effect on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) and neurological outcomes is unclear. We evaluated this association in patients with an initial shockable rhythm and assessed whether pH modified it.

Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the Korean Cardiac Arrest Research Consortium registry. Adults with presumed cardiac-origin OHCA, an initial shockable rhythm, ED cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and arterial blood gas data measured after ED arrival were included. Exposure was ECPR initiated in the ED; the primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome at discharge (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2). Arterial pH was categorized as low (≤6.85), medium (>6.85 and <7.05), or high (≥7.05). Multivariable logistic regression assessed ECPR-by-pH interaction, with optimal 1:2 propensity score matching as a sensitivity analysis.

Results: Of 2183 patients, 213 (9.8%) received ECPR and 154 (7.1%) had a favorable neurological outcome. The association between ECPR and favorable outcome differed across pH categories (p for interaction = 0.004): adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 7.34 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.84-18.98) in the low-pH group, 2.07 (95% CI, 1.06-4.03) in the medium-pH group, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.37-1.94) in the high-pH group. The propensity score-matched analysis showed a similar pattern (p for interaction = 0.036).

Conclusions: Initial arterial pH modified the association between ECPR and neurological outcome after OHCA with an initial shockable rhythm. The association was strongest at low pH and not observed at high pH. Arterial pH may inform ECPR evaluation but should not determine treatment thresholds.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Defining organized cardiac motion and cardiac standstill in cardiac arrest using point of care ultrasound: A Delphi study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Aim: There are no widely accepted definitions of organized cardiac motion (OCM) and cardiac standstill (CS) using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) during cardiac arrest. We aimed to define these terms and provide guidance on the clinical application of these findings.

Methods: Statements defining OCM and CS were developed by a steering committee of experts after a comprehensive literature review aided by a librarian. A diverse panel of 20 experts was convened. Using Delphi methodology, the panel came to a consensus on definitions of OCM and CS after three rounds of voting.

Results: The panelists voted on 64 total statements pertaining to OCM and CS in cardiac arrest: 29 defining OCM, 23 defining cardiac standstill, and 12 examining clinical implications of OCM and CS. We defined OCM as coordinated contraction with change in left ventricular chamber size. Coordinated contraction with any change of the right ventricle may also be used if visualization of the left ventricle was not possible. Ventricular fibrillation, agonal motion, and isolated valvular movement were deemed not consistent with OCM. Cardiac standstill was defined as including the absence of all cardiac motion or the presence of isolated valvular movement alone. The panel recommended that POCUS can guide cardiac arrest resuscitation, and that these definitions are applicable to pediatric patients and the prehospital setting.

Conclusion: The expert panelists established consensus definitions of OCM and CS during cardiac arrest. These definitions can guide further research into POCUS use during cardiac arrest and aid ongoing efforts to standardize its use.

item.title: J Addict Med: Perspectives and Preferences of Patients With Substance Use Disorder on Urine Toxicology Testing in Pregnancy
item.description:
Objectives: Urine toxicology testing is a ubiquitous practice in pregnancy among patients with substance use disorder (SUD). However, little data exists on patient views of this consequential practice. We aimed to explore the perspectives of patients with SUD on the utility of urine toxicology testing in pregnancy and on toxicology processes to inform best practice.

Methods: We conducted semistructured interviews with 15 pregnant and postpartum patients with SUD receiving care at an urban interdisciplinary obstetric and SUD clinic. Interviews explored patient experiences with urine toxicology testing, perceptions of risks and benefits, and opinions on optimal testing practices, including perspectives on a recently implemented toxicology testing policy. Interviews were recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using a combined deductive-inductive methodology to identify themes.

Results: Participants supported urine toxicology testing as an accountability tool but expressed concerns about testing inaccuracy and its potential legal consequences. Many participants felt that confirmatory testing and a transparent, comprehensive consent process could mitigate these challenges. Experiences in a specialty SUD treatment program helped reduce testing stigma and improved overall care. The newly implemented urine toxicology testing policy, which included a detailed consent process, contrasted favorably with prior experiences of urine toxicology testing, where consent was often implied or incomplete.

Conclusions: Clinicians and policymakers considering urine toxicology testing practice changes during pregnancy should consider patient perspectives and preferences as they work to optimize health for patients and their families.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Prehospital Advanced Airway Management in Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study Using Time-Dependent Propensity Score Sequential Matching
item.description:
Objectives: Traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (TCA) has extremely poor outcomes, and the benefit of prehospital advanced airway management (AAM) remains uncertain, partly because previous observational studies may have been affected by resuscitation time bias. We examined the association between prehospital AAM and clinical outcomes in adults with TCA using a time-dependent analytic approach.

Methods: We conducted a nationwide retrospective observational cohort study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry linked with emergency medical services transport records from 2021 to 2023. Adults (≥18 years) with TCA were included. The exposure was successful prehospital AAM, including supraglottic airway placement or endotracheal intubation. The primary outcome was 30-day survival, and the secondary outcome was favorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2) at 30 days. We applied time-dependent propensity score sequential matching and estimated corrected risk differences (RDs) using generalized estimating equations with inverse-frequency weighting.

Results: Among 7,217 patients, 2,653 (36.8%) received prehospital AAM, of whom 2,637 were successfully matched within the analytic cohort. Thirty-day survival was 1.8% in the AAM group and 1.4% among matched controls (corrected RD, 0.6%; 95% confidence interval (CI), -0.1 to 1.2). Favorable neurological outcome occurred in 0.2% and 0.4%, respectively (corrected RD, -0.2%; 95% CI, -0.6 to 0.1). No significant timing-dependent association or prespecified subgroup heterogeneity was observed.

Conclusions: In this nationwide cohort study using time-dependent propensity score sequential matching, prehospital AAM was not significantly associated with improved outcomes in adults with TCA.

item.title: JAMA: Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Review
item.description:
Importance: Acute ischemic stroke, caused by thrombotic or embolic occlusion of a cervical or cerebral artery, leads to neurologic injury due to sudden disruption of blood flow to the brain. Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of disability and death and accounts for about 85% of strokes in the US.

Observations: Symptoms of acute ischemic stroke vary based on the area of the affected brain. Common presentations include sudden arm or leg weakness, aphasia or slurred speech, sudden loss of balance or coordination, sudden visual difficulties, and/or facial drooping. Patients with suspected stroke should be transported to the nearest emergency department for urgent brain imaging, typically noncontrast computed tomography (CT). Based on 2026 American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) guidelines, first-line therapy for patients with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours from symptom onset with disabling symptoms (eg, affecting the ability to perform activities of daily living) is intravenous thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) in those without intracranial hemorrhage or other contraindications to thrombolysis. The treatment window can be extended to 9 hours-and up to 24 hours in patients with large vessel occlusion (eg, involving the internal carotid artery or proximal middle cerebral artery [M1 segment]) who are unable to receive thrombectomy-based on identification of salvageable tissue using perfusion imaging with CT perfusion or magnetic resonance imaging. In appropriately selected patients with acute ischemic stroke, pooled randomized trial data show an approximately 10% absolute increase in the probability of a better functional outcome with intravenous thrombolysis. Based on 2026 AHA/ASA guidelines, endovascular thrombectomy, which involves clot removal with an intra-arterial mechanical device, is recommended for patients with large vessel occlusion within 6 hours of stroke onset (class 1 recommendation) and is recommended in selected patients with large vessel occlusion within 24 hours of last known well (class 1 recommendation). Endovascular therapy should be performed after intravenous thrombolysis unless patients have contraindications to thrombolytic therapy. Compared with medical management, which includes intravenous thrombolysis when indicated, endovascular thrombectomy produces an approximately 20% absolute increase in functional independence.

Conclusions and relevance: Acute ischemic stroke causes substantial disability and mortality. First-line therapy for patients with disabling acute stroke symptoms is intravenous thrombolysis (if no contraindications) within 4.5 hours of stroke onset and up to 24 hours in carefully selected patients not receiving mechanical thrombectomy; for large vessel occlusions, mechanical thrombectomy may be performed up to 24 hours after stroke onset in eligible patients.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Publicly Available Information on Insurance Coverage for Maternal-Fetal Surgery
item.description:
Importance: Maternal-fetal surgery has expanded rapidly in the US, but how insurance coverage supports delivery of this specialized, high-cost care has not been systematically characterized.

Objective: To characterize publicly ascertainable information about how Medicaid programs and large commercial insurers cover procedures used in maternal-fetal surgery.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional descriptive study analyzed insurance coverage policies in the US from March through August 2025. Medicaid programs and large commercial insurers were selected based on national market share.

Exposure: Insurance coverage policies for maternal-fetal surgery-related procedures were assessed using publicly available fee schedules and structured outreach to payer representatives.

Main outcomes and measures: Coverage status (covered, not covered, or data not available) for 19 maternal-fetal surgery-related Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) and Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) codes and 5 comparator codes.

Results: The study included 50 state Medicaid programs and 30 large commercial insurers. Among Medicaid programs, coverage was high for nonspecific or individual components of procedures (eg, intrauterine transfusion: 49 of 49 available determinations [100%]) but incomplete and highly variable for codes specific to comprehensive interventions (eg, 6 of 36 available determinations [16.7%] for in utero sacrococcygeal teratoma resection). Among 44 states with available determinations for both code types, mean (SD) coverage was higher for CPT codes than S-codes (86.3% [14.1%] vs 53.0% [37.0%]; P < .001), with consistent findings in sensitivity analyses. The median (range) proportion of MFS-related codes covered per state was 14.5 (0-19) of 19 codes (76.3%). Among 5 commercial insurers with data, all 5 (100.0%) reported coverage of all 4 S-codes representing comprehensive interventions.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, coverage of maternal-fetal surgery-related codes was incomplete and variable, and transparency in commercial coverage policies was limited. These findings suggest that coverage uncertainty may complicate health-system planning and financing for this increasingly used, high-cost care.

Wilpers A, Zapolin B, Francis K, Powne AB, Suba I, Zapolin D

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Procalcitonin- and Presepsin-Guided Antibiotics for Early-Onset Sepsis in Preterm Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Early administration of antibiotics in the absence of proven sepsis, such as for treatment of early-onset sepsis (EOS), has been associated with adverse outcomes in very preterm infants. Reference values for procalcitonin (PCT) and presepsin (P-SEP) have been established in preterm infants.

Objective: To determine whether PCT- and P-SEP-guided antibiotic treatment for EOS was noninferior to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity.

Design, setting, and participants: This randomized multicenter noninferiority clinical trial was conducted in 17 Italian neonatal intensive care units between June 1, 2023, and January 31, 2025, among preterm infants born at 25 weeks and 0 days to 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation.

Interventions: Enrolled infants were randomly allocated to receive either PCT- and P-SEP-guided antibiotic treatment, administered if PCT and P-SEP levels exceeded prespecified thresholds, or universal antibiotic treatment for EOS.

Main outcomes and measures: The composite primary outcome was defined as survival without late-onset sepsis (LOS), bronchopulmonary dysplasia, grade 3 or 4 intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), grade 2 or higher necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), or stage 3 or higher retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). The prespecified noninferiority margin was -5 percentage points. Both a primary intention-to-treat analysis and a secondary per-protocol analysis were performed, as recommended for noninferiority trials.

Results: The study enrolled and randomized 283 very preterm infants (mean [SD] gestational age, 30.2 [2.2] weeks; 161 girls [57%]); 143 received procalcitonin- and presepsin-guided treatment and 140 received universal antibiotic treatment. The primary outcome did not differ between the PCT- and P-SEP-guided treatment group and the universal antibiotic treatment groups (76 of 143 [53%] vs 77 of 140 [55%]; risk difference, -1.8 percentage points; 90% CI, -11.9 to 8.3 percentage points; P = .32). Noninferiority of PCT- and P-SEP-guided treatment compared with universal treatment was not demonstrated, because the lower bound of the 2-sided 90% CI crossed the prespecified noninferiority margin. The risk differences for LOS, IVH, NEC, PVL, ROP, and death were not significantly different between the groups. PCT and P-SEP values were not different between the groups. No patient developed EOS.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial conducted among neonates born between 25 weeks and 0 days and 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation, a PCT- and P-SEP-guided strategy for the treatment of EOS did not demonstrate noninferiority to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity. Within the limits of this study, these findings do not support the routine use of a biomarker-guided approach as an alternative to universal treatment for this high-risk population.

Trial registration: Clinicaltrials.gov identifier: NCT05796115.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities in Preschoolers With Bilateral Cerebral Palsy: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Intensive interventions for children with cerebral palsy (CP) have traditionally focused on the upper extremities, despite frequent impairments in gross motor function and the critical period of motor development occurring before age 5 years. Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities (HABIT-ILE) has demonstrated efficacy in improving manual dexterity and gross motor function in school-aged children, but evidence in preschool children with bilateral CP remains limited.

Objective: To determine whether early HABIT-ILE improves gross motor function more than usual unstructured motor activities in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP.

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter randomized clinical trial was conducted between December 2019 and December 2021. Recruitment was from European university hospitals, CP-specialized centers, and spontaneous applications at 4 sites: Brussels, Belgium; Brest and Angers, France; and Pisa, Italy. Children aged 12 to 59 months with spastic or dyskinetic bilateral CP who were able to follow instructions were included. Exclusion criteria were uncontrolled seizures, scheduled botulinum toxin injections or orthopedic surgery during the 6 months before or during the study period, severe visual or cognitive impairments, and contraindications to magnetic resonance imaging. Data were analyzed in May 2024.

Interventions: Children were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive 2 weeks of usual motor activity, including usual rehabilitation (control group), or 2 weeks (50 hours) of HABIT-ILE (HABIT-ILE group).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was Gross Motor Function Measure-66 (GMFM-66; range, 0-100, with lower scores indicating lesser gross motor ability). Secondary outcomes included Both Hand Assessment (BoHA), Melbourne Assessment 2, Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory-Computer Adaptive Test (PEDI-CAT), and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM). Assessments were performed at baseline (immediately before intervention) and 2 weeks and 3 months after baseline.

Results: Among 49 preschool children with CP (mean [SD] age, 40.18 [11.53] months; 18 girls [36.7%] and 31 boys [63.3%]), Gross Motor Function Classification levels were I in 5 children, II in 14 children, III in 17 children, and IV or V in 13 children and Mini-Manual Ability Classification levels were I in 10 children, II in 27 children, III in 7 children, and IV or V in 6 children. Change in mean (SD) GMFM-66 score from baseline to 3 months was significantly greater in the HABIT-ILE group (5.01 [2.52] logits) than the control group (0.70 [1.98] logits) (adjusted mean difference [aMD] in score, 4.33 logits; 95% CI, 3.03-5.62 logits; P < .001). Likewise, mean (SD) scores favored the HABIT-ILE group vs the control group for secondary outcomes of BoHA (5.32 [4.47] vs 0.13 [5.16]; aMD, 5.15; 95% CI, 2.23-8.08; P < .001), PEDI-CAT mobility domain (1.70 [2.18] vs -0.40 [4.38]; aMD, 2.27; 95% CI, 0.20-4.33; P = .03), and COPM performance (4.22 [1.61] vs 1.14 [1.35]; aMD, 3.55; 95% CI, 2.86-4.24; P < .001) and satisfaction (4.37 [1.38] vs 1.15 [1.63]; aMD, 3.11; 95% CI, 2.25-3.97; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial, early HABIT-ILE significantly improved upper and lower extremities motor performance in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP at 3 months after the intervention. These findings suggest that HABIT-ILE is effective in improving gross motor function in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP.

Trial registration: Clinicaltrial.gov Identifier: NCT04020354.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Cumulative Stress and Health Care Utilization Among US Service Members
item.description:
Importance: Military personnel experience unique occupational stressors, which, combined with other life stressors, may substantially impact their health readiness. Stress exposure is known to be associated with health and health care concerns in civilian populations, but little is known as to whether these associations are present among US service members.

Objective: To evaluate the association between individual stressors, cumulative stress exposure, and health care utilization (HCU) among a contemporary sample of US service members.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort analysis used self-reported survey data from the Millennium Cohort Study and up to 3 years of inpatient and outpatient HCU data from Military Health System electronic health records (2020-2023) from US active-duty service members who first completed a Millennium Cohort Study baseline survey in 2020 and 2021. Data were analyzed from January to May 2026.

Exposure: Self-reported stress exposure (adverse childhood experiences, stressful life events, discrimination, bullying, hazing, and combat experiences) was assessed in 2020 and 2021.

Main outcomes and measures: Inpatient, outpatient, and total HCU patient-days were calculated. Negative binomial regression models examined the HCU association with cumulative and individual stress exposures, adjusting for demographic and military characteristics.

Results: A total of 34 731 service members were included in the analytic sample (33 252 [95.8%] were young adults aged 17-34 years; 9906 [28.5%] were female). They spent a mean (SD) of 17.74 (19.10) days (median [IQR], 12 [2-23] days) in outpatient and 0.61 (4.98) days (median [IQR], 0 [0-0] days) in inpatient care across a mean (SD) follow-up period of 2.08 (0.84) years. Higher cumulative stress exposure was associated with greater total (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 1.54; 95% CI, 1.50-1.57), inpatient (IRR, 2.28; 95% CI, 2.21-2.35), and outpatient (IRR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.47-1.54) HCU. Individual stressors, particularly adverse childhood experiences and stressful life events, were also associated with greater HCU.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of contemporary US active-duty service members, increased stress exposure was positively associated with greater HCU. Identifying and triaging various stress exposures during outpatient visits can support better access to inpatient care for service members. In turn, these efforts may translate into better patient outcomes, medical readiness, and military health system improvements.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Eating Disorders in Individuals With Celiac Disease and Their Biological First-Degree Relatives
item.description:
Importance: Patients with celiac disease (CD) may face elevated risk of eating disorders, potentially due to genetic susceptibility and psychosocial factors of a gluten-free diet. However, up-to-date population-based evidence is scarce, and whether any excess risk extends to biological first-degree relatives (bFDRs) remains unclear.

Objective: To investigate the risk of eating disorders in patients with CD and their bFDRs, including parents, full siblings, and offspring.

Design, setting, and participants: A nationwide multigenerational cohort study of patients with celiac disease in Sweden, observed from January 2002 to December 2023. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to August 2026. From Sweden's 28 histopathology departments, patients with biopsy-confirmed CD diagnosed 2002 to 2023 were identified. Each patient was matched with fewer than or equal to 5 general population reference individuals; bFDRs of patients with CD and reference individuals were also identified.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was any eating disorder. The adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) for eating disorders diagnosed at age 6 years or older were estimated using Cox regression and flexible parametric survival models for the overall and time-varying estimates, respectively.

Results: This study included 37 853 patients with CD (23 704 [62.6%] female; median [IQR] age at index date 28.7 [11.7-53.0] years ) and 185 159 reference individuals. Over 10.9 years median follow-up (IQR, 5.9-15.8 years), 485 patients with CD and 1578 reference individuals were diagnosed with any eating disorder. CD was associated with an increased hazard for eating disorders (aHR, 1.39; 95% CI,1.27-1.53), most apparent during the first 5 years of follow-up. Over 20 years of follow-up, 1 extra eating disorder case was expected per 222 patients with CD. In contrast, there was no hazard elevation for any eating disorder among CD-bFDRs (53 435 parents: aHR, 0.82 [0.61-1.12]; 48 743 siblings: aHR, 1.11 [0.99-1.24]; 38 695 offspring: aHR, 1.05 [0.92-1.20]). Sensitivity analyses mitigating information bias and residual confounding largely aligned with main findings.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of patients with CD, a moderately increased eating disorders risk particularly during the first 5 years of follow-up was observed, although the absolute risk was low. This increased risk did not extend to bFDRs of patients with CD. Clinical vigilance toward disordered eating is important among patients with newly diagnosed CD.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Family Presence Policies in Pediatric Intensive Care Units
item.description:
Importance: Family presence supports critically ill children, yet pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) policies remain inconsistent, creating inequities in access to parents or caregivers. Clear guidance is needed to support equitable, child-centered policy development.

Objective: To generate evidence-informed and knowledge user-informed recommendations for family presence policies in PICUs.

Design, setting, and participants: This survey study, conducted through surveys and virtual meetings, used a modified Delphi consensus process. Candidate items were derived from family presence guidance documents and PICU family presence research (environmental scan; scoping review; surveys and interviews with patients, families, and health care professionals; and focus groups). Items were organized into themes covering policy priorities; policy-making responsibilities; baseline and emergency policies; and policy communication, enforcement, and revision. From February 2024 to February 2025, panelists completed 2 rating rounds and 1 virtual meeting, with follow-up meetings and member-checking to incorporate input across knowledge user groups. Knowledge users included former PICU patients, family members, clinicians, and policymakers (hospital and PICU administrators and infection prevention and control specialists) from across Canada.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcome was consensus-derived policy priorities and recommendations for PICU family presence during baseline operations and emergency situations.

Results: Forty-three knowledge users, including 5 patients, 12 family members, 21 clinicians, and 5 policymakers (35 self-reported women or girls [81.4%]), agreed on 10 policy priorities and 44 recommendations. Key messages included that children should be at the center of policy-related decision-making and always have access to at least 2 primary caregivers; families should determine sibling presence and assume responsibility for it; policies should recognize the importance of visitors beyond family for the child's well-being; and policies should be flexible, adapting to different situations while adhering to core priorities. Recommendations addressed who should make policies; communication, enforcement, and change processes; number, type (eg, parents or caregivers, siblings, and visitors), and timing of bedside presence; family movement and supports; and approaches to personal protective equipment and infectious symptoms to preserve family presence, including during emergencies.

Conclusions and relevance: This survey study with consensus-based recommendations for PICU family presence provided a framework for policy design in routine and emergency contexts. The recommendations emphasized the patient's best interest and continued access to at least 2 primary caregivers. They supported context-specific and unit-specific policy design and may be broadly applicable across children's hospitals.

item.title: JAMA: Izalontamab Brengitecan in Recurrent or Metastatic Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: The PANKU-Esophagus01 Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Effective therapy remains lacking for patients with advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) whose disease progressed after standard treatment. Izalontamab brengitecan, an epidermal growth factor receptor and human epidermal growth factor receptor 3 bispecific antibody-drug conjugate with a topoisomerase I inhibitor, Ed-04, has shown clinical activity in ESCC in a phase 1b study.

Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of izalontamab brengitecan compared with chemotherapy in patients with advanced ESCC who progressed after first-line programmed cell death 1 protein (PD-1)/programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy.

Design, setting, and participants: This phase 3, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted across 80 hospitals in China. Patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC that had progressed with first-line PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy were enrolled. Between March 19, 2024, and August 1, 2025 (final follow-up, October 17, 2025), a total of 704 patients were screened, and 497 were enrolled and randomized.

Interventions: Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either izalontamab brengitecan (n = 249; 2.5 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 every 3 weeks) or physician-selected chemotherapy (n = 248; irinotecan, paclitaxel, or docetaxel) every 3 weeks.

Main outcomes and measures: The dual primary end points were progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by blinded independent central review according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 and overall survival (OS).

Results: Of 497 patients who underwent randomization (median age, 61.0 years [range, 34-76]; 448 male patients [90.1%]), 493 received study treatment. At this interim analysis, izalontamab brengitecan demonstrated statistically significant improvement in both PFS and OS. Median PFS by blinded independent central review was 4.17 months (95% CI, 3.61-4.53 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 1.97 months (95% CI, 1.61-2.73 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.40-0.63; log-rank P < .001). Median OS was 9.79 months (95% CI, 7.89-11.01 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 7.20 months (95% CI, 6.18-7.82 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.48-0.82; log-rank P < .001). Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 212 of 249 patients (85.1%) with izalontamab brengitecan and 147 of 248 patients (59.3%) with chemotherapy and were predominantly hematologic.

Conclusions and relevance: Izalontamab brengitecan significantly improved PFS and OS vs chemotherapy in patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC whose disease had progressed after first-line treatment. These findings support izalontamab brengitecan as a new second-line treatment for this population in China.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06304974.

item.title: Crit Care Med: National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Care for Adults With Suspected Sepsis in the Emergency Department: A Hybrid Type 1 Effectiveness-Implementation Stepped-Wedge Randomized Controlled Trial Pilot Study (NEWS-1 TRIPS)
item.description:
Objectives: To increase the uptake of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle, we implemented a novel sepsis care model (National Early Warning Score [NEWS]-1 care), in which the Hour-1 Bundle is objectively triggered by a high NEWS-2 (≥ 5). We aimed to determine the feasibility of a full-scale type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial of this model.

Design: A pilot type 1 hybrid trial, comprising a stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial and mixed-methods implementation evaluation with staff focus group interviews and an anonymous survey guided by the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance framework.

Setting: Four emergency departments in Hong Kong.

Patients: Adult patients of 18 years or older with a clinical diagnosis of infection requiring hospitalization and a NEWS-2 greater than or equal to 5.

Interventions: Implementation of the Hour-1 Bundle when NEWS-2 was greater than or equal to 5.

Measurements and main results: The primary outcome was the feasibility of a full-scale hybrid trial, evaluated based on 14 progression criteria. Preliminary clinical effectiveness and safety were assessed, alongside implementation barriers and facilitators. During the implementation phase, compliance with lactate, blood culture, and antibiotics increased significantly. All progression criteria were met, except for suboptimal overall bundle compliance (56.1%). Exploratory intention-to-treat analysis (standard care group, n = 102; NEWS-1 group, n = 98) showed no significant between-group difference in 30-day all-cause mortality (standard care group, 3.9%; NEWS-1 group, 9.2%; absolute risk difference, 5.3%; 95% CI -1.6% to 12.1%); in-hospital, 90-day all-cause, or sepsis-related mortality; need for mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, intensive care, or surgery; or ventilator-free days and adverse events. Implementation evaluation identified 15 barriers and 13 facilitators.

Conclusions: The effectiveness of NEWS-1 care remained uncertain, though adverse events were rare. A full-scale hybrid stepped-wedge trial is feasible but requires a much larger sample size. Real-world implementation barriers and facilitators should be considered in sepsis management guidelines.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Global Prevalence of Obstetric Causes of Critical Illness in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Objectives: To determine the prevalence, risks, and outcomes of obstetric causes of critically ill pregnant women admitted to the ICU.

Data sources: We searched the PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Ovid, and ScienceDirect databases up to May 15, 2026.

Study selection: We included studies reporting primary data on critically ill pregnant and postpartum women (up to 48 d post-delivery) admitted to an ICU, with relevant obstetric risk factors and maternal outcomes.

Data extraction: Two reviewers independently performed data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment using the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The pooled prevalence was estimated using a random-effects model with 95% CIs.

Data synthesis: Of the 3,735 total records, 50 studies met the eligibility criteria, encompassing 7,756,232 women receiving obstetric care in tertiary hospitals across 20 countries, with 49,299 ICU admissions. Globally, 1.0% (95% CI, 0.8-1.3%) of pregnant and postpartum women experience critical illness and require admission to an ICU. The frequency varies according to the country's income levels, with the highest in low-income countries (4.1%) and the lowest in high-income countries (0.5%). Notably, 72.3% of ICU admissions were attributed to known obstetric causes, primarily obstetric hemorrhage (23.3%) and hypertension in pregnancy (26.9%). Nearly 33.3% of ICU patients required either respiratory or transfusion support, and the maternal mortality rate among ICU-admitted obstetric women was 8.5%.

Conclusions: Nearly one in 100 pregnancies require admission to intensive care due to critical illness, and nearly three-quarters of these admissions were due to direct obstetric causes, with high maternal morbidity and mortality. Obstetric hemorrhage and hypertensive disorders account for the majority of ICU admissions. Strengthening obstetric care in resource-limited settings through the expansion and optimization of intensive care services is essential for improving maternal and neonatal outcomes and reducing preventable morbidity and mortality.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Neurological Outcomes of Rhythm Transitions in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest With Initial Nonshockable Rhythms: A Nationwide Population-Based Study
item.description:
Objectives: To evaluate the prognostic implications of rhythm transitions between asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA) in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with initial nonshockable rhythms.

Design: Nationwide population-based observational study.

Setting: Nationwide OHCA Registry of South Korea, managed by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.

Patients: Consecutive adult (≥ 18 yr old) OHCA patients with nonshockable rhythms from January 1, 2016 to December 31, 2021.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Patients were categorized into four groups based on rhythm changes during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR): asystole-to-asystole (A-A), asystole-to-PEA (A-P), PEA-to-asystole (P-A), and PEA-to-PEA (P-P). The primary outcome was good neurologic outcome at hospital discharge, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1-2. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to adjust for measured confounding. In the primary IPTW model, weighted risks of good neurologic outcome were 0.101% in A-A, 0.231% in A-P, 0.384% in P-A, and 0.874% in P-P. Compared with A-A, the odds of good neurologic outcome were higher in A-P (odds ratio [OR], 2.28; 95% CI, 1.78-2.93; risk difference [RD], 0.130 percentage points), P-A (OR, 3.80; 95% CI, 3.01-4.80; RD, 0.283 percentage points), and P-P (OR, 8.70; 95% CI, 6.98-10.83; RD, 0.773 percentage points). Compared with A-P, P-A had higher odds of good neurologic outcome (OR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.39-1.99; RD, 0.153 percentage points).

Conclusions: Asystole conversion to PEA during CPR was associated with a better neurologic outcome than persistent asystole. Although transitioning from PEA to asystole was associated with lower odds of a good outcome compared with persistent PEA, it was associated with a better outcome than A-P transitions. Recognizing these patterns may provide prognostic context beyond a single rhythm assessment.

item.title: Crit Care Med: New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review of In-Hospital and Post-Discharge Outcomes
item.description:
Objectives: This systematic review and meta-analysis determines the incidence of new-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) in critically ill patients, risks of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism, anticoagulation therapy, and the proportion diagnosed with AF post-discharge.

Data sources: A search of registered databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and CINAHL) was performed from inception to April 20, 2026.

Study selection: Eligible studies included critically ill patients (≥ 18 yr old) who developed NOAF during admission to general ICUs or high-dependency units. NOAF was defined as AF in patients without prior history of AF.

Data extraction: Data were independently extracted from full-text versions of included studies by nonblinded reviewers.

Data synthesis: A Bayesian meta-analysis was conducted on 54 studies (367,896 patients) with a random-effects model using R (Version 4.3.3). Pooled incidence of NOAF in critically ill patients was 10.6% (95% credible interval [CrI], 8.6-12.9%). Absolute risk of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism was 7.1% (95% CrI, 4.5-11.0%), changing to 6.9% (95% CrI, 4.2-11.6%) after age and sex adjustment. Evidence from six studies reports that critically ill patients with NOAF had 1.94 times (95% CrI, 1.23-3.29) higher relative risk of systemic thromboembolism post-discharge than patients without NOAF, rising to 2.01 (95% CrI, 1.54-2.80) with adjustment. Absolute and relative risk are evaluated with follow-up durations ranging from 1.5 months to 5 years, with variable anticoagulation exposure. Anticoagulation rates were low: 32.9% in-hospital (95% CrI, 14.6-57.9%) and 35.9% post-discharge (95% CrI, 19.7-55.9%). On follow-up, 23.9% (95% CrI, 13.9-38.5%) of critically ill patients with NOAF were subsequently diagnosed with AF.

Conclusions: Our review suggests that NOAF during critical illness is associated with significantly increased risk of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism and subsequent AF diagnosis. However, rates of anticoagulation initiation remain low, highlighting the need for improved risk stratification and targeted strategies post-discharge.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Structured Patient and Family-Centered Rounding in the ICU is Associated With Increased Family Confidence in Staff Compassion and Perceived Quality of Information Shared
item.description:
Objectives: Determine whether inviting families to participate in structured, multidisciplinary rounding in the ICU can lead to improved quality of information shared and greater overall confidence in the care delivered to patients.

Design: Pre- and postimplementation observational study based on surveys provided by the Society of Critical Care Medicine-Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute initiative.

Setting: Academic teaching hospital with 21 medical (closed unit) and 25 surgical (open unit) ICU beds.

Subjects: Family members and care providers of critically ill adults of 18 years and older.

Interventions: Families and clinicians were surveyed before and after implementation of a quality initiative to promote greater patient and family-centeredness in daily ICU rounds, using a structured and scripted rounding template. Additional information was gathered regarding provider attitudes toward the incorporation of families in rounds.

Measurements and main results: In pre-and postintervention periods, 36 and 28 families were surveyed in the MICU, and 44 and 42 families were surveyed in the SICU, respectively. In pre-and postintervention periods, respectively, 53 and 48 clinicians were surveyed in the MICU, and 46 and 28 clinicians were surveyed in the SICU. Clinician perceptions improved favorably in the MICU, with statistically significant improvements falling under the category of family welcoming, presence, and participation in decision-making; less so in the SICU. Family perceptions improved in almost all parameters in the MICU, with statistical significance achieved in perceived interest in patient needs, control of agitation and pain, and consistency and honesty of information shared. Similar patterns were observed in the SICU but did not reach statistical significance.

Conclusions: Structured, multi-disciplinary rounding with regular inclusion of family members and bedside nurses was associated with significantly greater family confidence in the quality and honesty of information shared, and an increase in perceived compassion in the care provided by ICU staff. Clinician perceptions regarding family inclusion on rounds were generally positive.

item.title: Crit Care Med: The Impact of Hospital Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Volume and Its Distribution Across ICUs on Adult Patients' Outcomes: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry
item.description:
Objectives: Research from a prior era of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) found that higher hospital ECMO volume was associated with higher survival rates, but it did not examine whether distributing ECMO volume across multiple ICUs affected this relationship.

Design: Retrospective analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry.

Setting: ECMO centers contributing to the registry.

Patients: Adult patients required ECMO support from 2012 to 2023.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: We analyzed adult patients from the ELSO registry (2012-2023), adjusting for hospital factors and case mix using multivariable hierarchical logistic regression. The main outcome was in-hospital mortality. Hospital experience was measured by the annual number of adult ECMO cases and total ECMO hours. Volume-outcome associations were modeled for all centers and by total adult ICUs per center. We included 115,849 adults on ECMO across 495 hospitals. Model estimates showed small decreases in mortality odds with higher annual case counts (odds ratio [OR], 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97-0.99 per 10-case increase) and ECMO hours (OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr increase). Hospitals with one ICU had a median of 10 cases (interquartile interval [IQI], 3-25 cases), while those with four or more ICUs had a median of 50 (IQI, 28-91). Adjusted mortality was higher in centers delivering ECMO across four+ ICUs compared with one ICU (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.06-1.31), the annual case model (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06-1.26), and the annual ECMO hours model. Higher volume was associated with a reduction in the odds of mortality for hospitals with four+ ICUs compared with those with one ICU (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.96-1.00 per 10 cases and OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr).

Conclusions: Higher hospital ECMO volume is associated with reduced mortality. Hospitals with more adult ICUs that perform ECMO may experience higher mortality, which may be explained by increased patient complexity and is offset by the higher center volume. More research is needed to better understand the optimum design of ECMO centers.

item.title: Crit Care Med: A Telemedicine Intervention for Spontaneous Awakening and Breathing Trials in Small and Large ICUs
item.description:
Objectives: To evaluate the effect of a tele-critical care (TCC) daily audit-and-feedback intervention on spontaneous awakening trial and spontaneous breathing trial protocol compliance.

Design: Pre-post quality improvement study.

Setting: Single health system composed of 14 hospitals in the Midwestern United States.

Patients: A total of 8909 patients of 18 years or older receiving mechanical ventilation via endotracheal tube for more than 1 calendar day between October 01, 2022 and September 20, 2024.

Interventions: Daily in the early afternoon, TCC nurses reviewed mechanically ventilated patients to determine whether a spontaneous awakening trial and spontaneous breathing trial had occurred. They contacted the bedside nurse if no trial had occurred and no weaning exclusion criteria were noted during a manual chart review.

Measurements and main results: The coprimary outcomes were the proportion of ventilator days during each ventilator episode with documentation of spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials. Linear mixed effects models were used to examine the effect of the intervention on each outcome stratified by ICU size (large ≥ 15 beds or small < 15 beds). Spontaneous awakening trial documentation improved over time throughout the entire period, but the rate of improvement increased significantly after the telemedicine intervention (preintervention slope: 0.2% increase per 30 d; 95% CI, -0.2% to 0.6% and postintervention slope: 1.4% increase per 30 d; 95% CI, 1.0% to 1.9%; p < 0.001 for intervention-time interaction). The telemedicine intervention was associated with a step increase in spontaneous breathing trial documentation in small ICUs (absolute increase, 12.8%; 95% CI, 8.7-16.9%) but not in large ICUs (absolute increase, -0.1%; 95% CI, -1.8% to 1.6%; p = 0.02 for intervention-ICU size interaction).

Conclusions: The telemedicine intervention was associated with increased spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials selectively in small ICUs. Telemedicine may have promoted practice standardization in small ICUs where exposure to ventilated patients was infrequent. Local ICU characteristics may impact the effectiveness of TCC interventions.

item.title: Am J Respir Crit Care Med: Optimizing Sepsis Time Zero Definitions Through Associations between Antibiotic Timing and Mortality
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Sepsis performance measures require operational definitions of "time zero", but SEP-1's heterogeneous organ dysfunction criteria may not all identify patients vulnerable to harm from antibiotic delays.

Objectives: To determine which SEP-1 organ dysfunctions identify patients in whom antibiotic delays are associated with increased mortality.

Methods: We analyzed adults with suspected infection using electronic health record data from 145 U.S. hospitals (2018-2023). We estimated associations between antibiotic timing (1-3 vs. 0-1h and 3-6 vs. 0-3h) and in-hospital mortality for each SEP-1 organ dysfunction criterion, alone and in combination: hypotension, elevated lactate, respiratory failure, renal dysfunction, hyperbilirubinemia, thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy. We used inverse probability weighting to adjust for baseline and time-varying confounders.

Measurements and main results: Among 1,849,729 encounters with suspected infection, 624,416 had ≥1 organ dysfunction and received antibiotics within 6h of time zero. Antibiotics at 1-3 vs. 0-1h were associated with higher mortality when time zero was defined by hypotension (aRR 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03-1.10) or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L (aRR 1.10; 1.05-1.15), but not for other dysfunctions alone or in combination. Among patients without hypotension or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L, antibiotics at 3-6 vs. 0-3h were only associated with higher mortality in patients with acute respiratory failure (aRR 1.11; 1.05-1.18).

Conclusions: Mortality associations with antibiotics beyond 1 hour were most evident when sepsis time zero was defined by hypotension or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L, and with antibiotics beyond 3 hours when defined by acute respiratory failure. These findings could inform refinements to sepsis time zero definitions to better guide antibiotic urgency and performance measurement.

item.title: Crit Care: Conflict in intensive care units: a conceptual framework for patient, family, team, and inter-service disagreement
item.description:
For clinicians, conflict in the intensive care unit (ICU) is both common and expected owing to the nature of critical illness and its treatment. Examination of conflict in this context has been conceptually diffuse. Studies of moral distress, psychological safety, ethical climate, and other fields offer valuable insights that can be challenging to synthesize cohesively, due to differences in concepts, methods, and disciplinary perspectives. This narrative review integrates this literature using a task-process-relationship framework from organizational psychology. Conflict in the ICU arises in two principal arenas: between clinical teams and patients, families, or surrogates, and within and across clinical teams. Patients who retain decision-making capacity are a distinct and often overlooked party to conflict, as the focus has primarily been on the families and surrogates who speak for those who cannot. The task-process-relationship framework suggests a recurring escalation pattern for both arenas. Genuine task disagreements about treatment, prognosis, or goals of care can become destructive in the presence of process gaps or failures. These include role ambiguity, inconsistent messaging, and perceived unfairness. From there, conflict can enter the relationship domain wherein mistrust or identity threat makes resolution far harder, and two implications follow. First, much of what clinicians may describe as a "difficult family" can often be a response to antecedent process failures rather than a purely interpersonal problem, emphasizing the importance of engineering robust processes and systems in the ICU to avoid conflict reaching the relationship domain. Second, family and team conflict are linked in that unresolved team disagreement can reach families as contradictory recommendations and mixed messaging. Challenging family situations can expose team misalignment and damage collegial relationships. Evidence-based interventions, organized by conflict type and escalation stage, suggest that the most promising investments are structural, namely those built into rounds, improving role clarity, ensuring pre-conference team alignment, and fostering ethical climate. When conflict becomes entrenched, formal supports such as mediation and ethics consultation are matched to the nature of the dispute. While disagreement in intensive care is inevitable, destructive conflict is not.

Jabaley CS, Brummell Z, Benoit DD, Kentish-Barnes N, Metaxa V

item.title: Crit Care: Early albumin use and mortality in critically III children with severe hypoalbuminemia: a target trial emulation study
item.description:
Background: Hypoalbuminemia is highly prevalent in critically ill children and is an established independent risk factor for mortality. Whether albumin supplementation is associated with improved survival remains unclear, particularly in pediatric populations where causal evidence is sparse.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study used data from the Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database, a single-center pediatric-specific critical care database in China, and adopted a target trial emulation (TTE) framework. Children whose first albumin measurement within 24 h of ICU admission was below 30 g/L were included (N = 1,649). Time zero was defined as the first detection of albumin below 30 g/L. The exposure was receipt of at least one dose of human albumin within 24 h after time zero. Primary outcomes were 7-day and 28-day all-cause mortality, estimated using IPTW-weighted Cox proportional hazards models with doubly robust adjustment. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding was assessed by E-value.

Results: Among 1,649 children, 374 (22.7%) received early albumin therapy. After doubly robust adjustment, early albumin therapy was associated with reduced 7-day mortality (HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.24-0.74; P = 0.003; E-value = 4.21). The association with 28-day mortality was not significant (HR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.45-1.36; P = 0.393). Relaxing the hypoalbuminemia threshold to below 35 g/L attenuated the 7-day association (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.39-1.05). Extending the treatment window to 48 h further attenuated the association (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.40-1.91). A significant interaction was observed between vasoactive agent use and albumin therapy (P for interaction = 0.045), with the strongest association among children not receiving vasoactive agents (HR, 0.17; 95% CI, 0.04-0.70).

Conclusions: In critically ill children with severe hypoalbuminemia, early albumin therapy was associated with reduced 7-day mortality. This association showed clear threshold- and time-dependence, suggesting that any potential benefit may concentrate within a narrow clinical window early in the disease course. Prospective confirmation is needed.

Trial registration: Not applicable. This is a retrospective observational study using de-identified data; the study protocol was not prospectively registered in a clinical trials registry.

Zhang YZ, Xie C, Nie MS, Sun JJ, Zhao X, Wang K

item.title: Crit Care: Using capnography to differentiate airway from gastrointestinal placement of nasogastric tubes: a prospective multicentre diagnostic accuracy study
item.description:
Background: Patient safety incident reports and case reports have repeatedly highlighted factors contributing to inadvertent airway placement of nasogastric tubes, including misleading pH readings, insufficiently documented placement checks, and misinterpretation of radiographs. The study aimed to: (i) evaluate the diagnostic performance of capnography compared with radiography for detecting inadvertent airway placement of nasogastric tubes; and (ii) estimate the average cost incurred when radiography is used alone versus when capnography is used in conjunction with radiography.

Methods: A multicentre, prospective, observational diagnostic study was conducted. The diagnostic accuracy of capnography was examined using three end-tidal carbon dioxide thresholds (> 5 mmHg, > 10 mmHg, > 15 mmHg), with radiographic confirmation as the reference standard. For each threshold, true positives, false negatives, true negatives, and false positives were determined. Cost savings per patient were estimated using a bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrapping method with 20,000 replications.

Results: A total of 508 participants were recruited from 39 study sites across 21 hospitals, including medical or geriatric wards, intensive care units, and emergency departments. Most participants (n = 485; 95.5%) had end-tidal carbon dioxide readings ≤ 5 mmHg. Radiography confirmed correct gastric placement in 452 cases (89.0%), with one case (0.2%) of inadvertent airway placement. Estimated cost savings per patient, were HK$210.3, HK$214.5, and HK$217.5 for the three respective end-tidal carbon dioxide thresholds, based on a hypothetical strategy in which radiographic confirmation was performed only when the end-tidal carbon dioxide value exceeded a predefined threshold, compared with a radiography-only strategy in which all patients underwent radiographic confirmation of nasogastric tube placement.

Conclusions: Given the favourable outcomes and the simplicity of capnography measurement, capnography can be considered a first-line tool for excluding airway placement of nasogastric tubes, used alongside pH testing of aspirates.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, Number NCT05817864 (Registration date: 18 April 2023).

item.title: Crit Care: The evolution of biocontainment unit care for high-consequence infectious diseases: progress, lessons learned, and future directions
item.description:
Biocontainment units (BCUs) are specialized facilities designed to treat patients with high-consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) which are pathogens with high mortality rates, limited treatment options, and significant potential for healthcare-associated transmission. Since the opening of the first modern BCU in 1971, these units have evolved from simple isolation environments into advanced centers capable of delivering comprehensive critical care while maintaining rigorous infection control. This evolution has been driven from the lessons learned from past outbreaks of Ebola, Marburg, Middle Eastern Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), among other emerging infectious threats. Four key domains contribute to the care of patients with HCIDs - laboratory capabilities, critical care delivery, healthcare workforce readiness, and safe patient transport. Improvements in diagnostic capabilities have allowed for earlier disease recognition while greater access to routine laboratory tests better inform clinical decision making. Clinical care capabilities now match those seen in intensive care units while maintaining infection control standards. Training of specialized workforce and multidisciplinary staffing models have improved bedside care and operational readiness. Meanwhile, innovations in ground and air transport have enhanced the ability to safely transfer HCID patients to facilities best suited to provide care. This review synthesizes the evolution of BCU capabilities globally, examining advances in critical care, diagnostics, investigational therapeutics, workforce models, and patient transport.

item.title: Crit Care: Sigh ventilation versus conventional protective ventilation in cardiac surgery: a proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial
item.description:
Background: Lung protective ventilation is crucial for preventing ventilator-induced lung injury in cardiac surgery. The protective role of a low tidal volume (VT) has been established, whereas the added protection afforded by lung recruitment remains uncertain. We investigated whether sigh breaths could provide additional lung protection, when added to protective ventilation with low VT.

Methods: This randomized, assessor-blinded, phase 2 proof-of-concept trial enrolled 192 patients undergoing elective on-pump cardiac surgery from February to August 2024. Patients were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive sigh ventilation (sigh breaths plus protective ventilation with low VT; 96 patients) or conventional ventilation (protective ventilation with low VT; 96 patients). Sigh breaths targeting a plateau pressure of 35 cmH2O (or 40 cmH2O for BMI >35 kg/m2) were delivered once every 6 min. Perioperative respiratory mechanics and gas exchange were monitored. The primary outcome was postoperative oxygenation, a marker of lung injury, as measured by the time-weighted average SpO2/FiO2 ratio during the first postextubation hour. There were 9 predefined secondary outcomes, including the severity of respiratory failure within postextubation day 7.

Results: All 192 patients completed the trial (53% male; median age, 64 [55-72] years). Perioperatively, sigh ventilation produced sustained improvements in oxygenation and respiratory system compliance, together with reductions in driving pressure and mechanical power (All P interaction<0.001). After extubation, the mean time-weighted SpO2/FiO2 ratio was higher in the sigh ventilation group (380 ± 86 vs 338 ± 93; mean difference 42.1, 95% CI [16.7 to 67.5]; P=0.001). The severity and occurrence of respiratory failure was reduced in the sigh ventilation group compared with conventional ventilation group (common odds ratio for lower severity 2.2; 95% CI [1.2 to 3.8]; P=0.007). There was no difference in adverse events of interest between groups.

Conclusions: In patients undergoing on-pump cardiac surgery, adding sigh breaths was safe and resulted in a statistically significant improvement in postoperative oxygenation. Nevertheless, the clinical importance of this finding is uncertain because oxygenation was adequately maintained in both groups. Reduction in driving pressure and mechanical power, together with findings in secondary outcomes, suggest additional lung protection and justify future trials.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06248320); registered on January 30, 2024.

Wang Z, Chen H, Chen T, Cheng Q, Huang S, Zha Z

item.title: Crit Care: Dynamic reprogramming of alveolar epithelial-immune cell interactions in ARDS: from mechanisms to clinical translation
item.description:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by disruption of the alveolar-capillary barrier and refractory hypoxemia. Despite advances in supportive care, effective targeted therapies remain lacking. A major challenge to therapeutic success is the marked heterogeneity of ARDS, in which distinct biological mechanisms may drive different etiologies, inflammatory subphenotypes, and disease stages. Increasing evidence suggests that alveolar epithelial cells (AECs) are not merely passive targets of injury but active regulators of immune responses. Dynamic interactions between AECs and macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes occur throughout the course of ARDS and contribute to inflammatory amplification, tissue repair, and aberrant remodeling. In this review, we summarize epithelial-immune interaction patterns across the inflammatory exudative, proliferative repair, and fibrotic phases of ARDS. We further discuss how disease stage transitions, immunometabolic regulation, and ARDS heterogeneity shape these interaction networks. Based on these findings, we present an AEC-centered dynamic reprogramming framework that organizes current evidence on how epithelial-immune interactions change during ARDS progression. We also discuss candidate biomarkers, approaches for clinical stage and phenotype identification, therapeutic opportunities, and current evidence limitations, aiming to provide a conceptual framework for stage-specific and precision interventions in ARDS. We further contextualize existing and controversial immunomodulatory strategies, including corticosteroids and IL-6/IL-1 blockade, within this dynamic framework to illustrate how disease stage and patient phenotype may influence therapeutic responses. Throughout the review, we distinguish evidence derived from experimental models from observational data in human ARDS and separately identify human interventional evidence and therapies supported by current clinical guidelines.

Gao C, Wang Q, Tan Z, Yang Y, Su L, Long Y

item.title: Chest: Pragmatic Clinical indicators of Tuberculosis Transmission Risk: a Household Contact Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: Interrupting TB transmission is a priority in high-burden settings. Identifying highly infectious people with TB may guide targeted interventions.

Research question: Can readily available clinical characteristics (eg, lung cavitation, cough duration, modified Bandim TB score) indicate the transmission risk in participants with TB?

Study design and methods: We conducted an observational cohort study in Lima, Peru, enrolling 4,500 index participants. Of the 4,044 people with microbiologically confirmed TB, 3,109 had at least 1 household contact (HHC), yielding 12,767 HHCs. Index participants underwent chest radiograph and TB symptom assessment, from which we derived a modified Bandim TB score. We assessed HHCs for TB infection at baseline and 6 months, and for incident TB disease over 12 months. We analyzed associations between index participant indicators and TB outcomes in HHCs using modified Poisson regression with generalized estimating equations, adjusting for relevant covariates.

Results: Among child HHCs, baseline TB infection risk increased with greater cavitary extent (adjusted trend P = .005) and longer cough duration (adjusted trend P = .002), with similar trends at 6 months. Among cavitation categories, multiple-quadrant involvement was associated with the highest baseline infection risk (adjusted prevalence risk ratio, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.10-2.39), but not with incident disease (adjusted cumulative risk ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 0.56-2.60). Among cough duration categories, ≥ 56 days showed the highest baseline infection risk (adjusted prevalence risk ratio, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.18-2.13), but not incident disease (adjusted cumulative risk ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 0.85-1.99). The modified Bandim TB score was not associated with transmission risk.

Interpretation: Our results show that in this large household cohort, cavitary extent on chest radiograph and cough duration in people with TB were associated with increased TB transmission risk and showed dose-response relationships with TB infection. These simple, readily available indicators may help target preventive interventions in high-burden settings; however, associations with incident TB remain uncertain.

item.title: Chest: Associations between temperatures, extreme temperature events, and onset of acute exacerbations of COPD: a time-stratified case-crossover study in China
item.description:
Background: Non-optimal temperatures and extreme temperature events may trigger acute exacerbations of COPD (AECOPD), but most evidence is admission based, potentially misclassifying exposure timing and obscuring susceptible groups.

Research question: Are non-optimal temperature and extreme temperature events associated with AECOPD onset, and which patients are most susceptible?

Study design and methods: We used the Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Registry (ACURE) data and assigned residential temperature exposure using ERA5-Land, a reanalysis dataset of European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Cold spells (CS) were defined as consecutive days below location-specific low-temperature thresholds, and compound cold spells (CCS) as concurrent daytime and nighttime cold spells. Associations with reported symptom onset were estimated using a time-stratified case-crossover design, conditional logistic regression with distributed lag nonlinear models. Subgroup and cytokine analyses assessed susceptibility and inflammation.

Results: Among 5,634 patients with AECOPD (mean age, 69.4 ± 9.5 years; 78.8% male), lower temperature was associated with higher odds of AECOPD onset, whereas higher temperature was not. The strongest associations occurred for CS lasting ≥3 days and CCS lasting ≥2 days over lag 0-3 days, with ORs of 1.84 (95% CI, 1.22-2.78) and 4.31 (95% CI, 2.07-8.97), respectively. Nearly half had delayed admission within 14 days. Using admission rather than onset dates attenuated estimates by 88.8% for CS and 84.8% for CCS. Associations were stronger among older adults, men, smokers, patients with severe AECOPD in the past year or previously diagnosed COPD, and those using combination inhaler in the preceding year. CS were also associated with higher TNF-α, IL-6, and CXCL-11 concentrations.

Interpretation: Lower temperature and extreme cold events, particularly CCS, were associated with AECOPD onset. Symptom-onset timing may better capture temperature-related associations than admission timing. These findings highlight the need for targeted cold-weather prevention strategies to reduce AECOPD burden.

Trial registry: ClinicalTrials.gov; NO.: NCT02657525.
