item.title: Lancet: Trevogrumab (anti-GDF8) with or without garetosmab (anti-activin A) for prevention of muscle loss during semaglutide-induced weight reduction in people with obesity (COURAGE): a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial
item.description:
Background: Rapid weight loss, as induced by GLP-1 receptor agonists, is accompanied by pronounced muscle loss. GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A (ActA), acting via ActRIIA/B receptors, are negative regulators of muscle mass. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of antibodies blocking GDF8 (trevogrumab) and ActA (garetosmab) on semaglutide-induced weight and muscle loss.

Methods: COURAGE is a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial. This multicentre (60 sites), US-based trial enrolled participants aged 18-80 years with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2). In part A, participants were treated for 26 weeks with semaglutide (titrated to 2·4 mg subcutaneously weekly) in addition to a randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) concomitant treatment: placebo, trevogrumab 200 mg, trevogrumab 400 mg, or trevogrumab 400 mg and garetosmab 10 mg/kg. Trevogrumab was administered subcutaneously weekly and garetosmab was administered intravenously every 4 weeks. Part A also included a subsequent semaglutide withdrawal period, at which point participants (randomly assigned at baseline 1:1 within each group) received either trevogrumab 400 mg or placebo for an additional 26 weeks. In part B, participants were treated with semaglutide for 52 weeks and randomly assigned (1:2:2) to concomitant treatment with placebo, trevogrumab 25 mg, or trevogrumab 75 mg. Groups were stratified according to sex, BMI (<35 kg/m2vs ≥35 kg/m2), and participation in an exploratory MRI substudy assessing thigh muscle volume. Study participants, the principal investigators, and study site personnel were masked to all randomisation assignments throughout the study. Primary endpoints were percent change in lean mass, fat mass, and bodyweight from baseline to week 26 (part A) or week 52 (part B). Efficacy and safety analyses were done in all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of a study drug (efficacy, as randomly assigned; safety, as treated). COURAGE is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06299098, and is currently active, not recruiting.

Findings: 975 participants were enrolled between June 21, 2024, and April 14, 2025. Mean age was 49·0 years (SD 13·2) and mean BMI was 36·7 kg/m2 (SD 5·0); 627 (64%) of 975 participants were female and 348 (36%) were male. In part A (n=605, of whom n=599 received at least one dose of study drug), a substantial decrease in lean mass was observed in the semaglutide plus placebo group at week 26 (-6·6% [95% CI -7·4 to -5·7]); the estimated treatment difference (ETD) versus semaglutide plus placebo was +3·1% (95% CI 1·9 to 4·3) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg, +2·7% (1·5 to 4·0) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg, and +4·5% (3·1 to 5·9) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg. In part B (n=376), lean mass percent change from baseline to week 52 for semaglutide plus placebo was -7·3% (-8·8 to -5·8); the ETD versus semaglutide plus placebo was +1·5% (-0·3 to 3·3) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 25 mg, and +3·1% (1·3 to 4·9) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 75 mg. Change from baseline in fat mass in part A was -15·6% (-17·4 to -13·9) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg group (-3·4% [-5·9 to -0·9]) and the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-11·7% [-14·4 to -9·0]) in part A. No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in fat mass compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Percent change in bodyweight in part A was -10·6 (-11·6 to -9·7) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant for the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-2·7 [-4·1 to -1·2]). No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in bodyweight compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Semaglutide plus trevogrumab (25 mg, 75 mg, 200 mg, or 400 mg) was generally well tolerated with a safety profile similar to semaglutide plus placebo; however, semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg had a high incidence of serious adverse events (14 [9%] of 149) and treatment discontinuations (48 [32%] of 149). Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most commonly reported, and they occurred with similar incidence across treatment groups. Muscle spasms occurred more frequently in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (61 [41%] of 149) compared with the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg or 400 mg groups (23 [8%] of 299) and semaglutide plus placebo groups (seven [5%] of 151). Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity. Two deaths occurred during the study, both in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group; a causal association between treatment and these events was not identified.

Interpretation: This study establishes proof of concept for GDF8 inhibition by trevogrumab alone as a generally well tolerated strategy to preserve lean mass during GLP-1 receptor agonist-induced weight loss. Although the addition of ActA inhibition by garetosmab further improved body composition and weight loss, the combination did not have favourable safety and tolerability. Further study is required to understand whether improved body composition during weight loss might preserve physical function and overall metabolic health.

Funding: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

Mosenzon O, Rosenstock J, Raya JG, Grimsby JS, Calle RA, Cannon K

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Applications of intravenous magnesium Sulfate in the emergency department: A narrative review
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Intravenous (IV) magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) has a variety of indications within the emergency department (ED) with evidence for its use continuing to evolve. It is used for common presentations such as headache/migraine, arrhythmias, severe respiratory exacerbations, and refractory hypokalemia while remaining the mainstay of treatment for preeclampsia/eclampsia. Evidence also supports its use for the management of shivering during targeted temperature management and a potential role for analgesia.

Objective: The focus of this review is to provide an update on the literature regarding the use of IV MgSO4 for common presentations in the ED for adults and provide an evidence-based approach to its utilization.

Discussion: The most robust trials suggest that IV MgSO4 serves a supporting role in the management of headache/migraine and may be used as an adjunct for rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rate. Magnesium sulfate should be reserved for patients experiencing severe respiratory exacerbations who fail to respond to initial therapy and may have a role in patients experiencing shivering during targeted temperature management. Routine empiric use in the management of hypokalemia is not suggested and evidence supporting its use for analgesia is limited. Intravenous MgSO4 remains first-line for preeclampsia/eclampsia and is the drug of choice in Torsades de Pointes. There was a low risk of adverse events across all studies evaluated with no serious events reported.

Conclusion: Intravenous MgSO4 is an adjunct for a myriad of indications in the ED. Additional high-quality research is needed to identify patients who benefit most from IV MgSO4.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Beyond alcohol cue reactivity: A novel test of task-based event-related potentials as a measure of individual differences in natural reward cue processing in alcohol use disorder
item.description:
Background: Incentive salience attribution (ISA) is the process by which reward-associated cues take value themselves. Translational work has observed individual ISA differences that predict behavior - suggesting prognostic potential for alcohol/substance use disorders. With human basic science observing ISA differences with natural reward (e.g., food) cues, this study tested if natural reward (rather than disorder-triggering) cues can also be used to assess ISA in alcohol use disorder (AUD).

Method: 30 individuals with AUD and heavy drinking at screening did a validated task wherein pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral content-depicting pictures were seen along with 1) low-salience cues that predicted M&M rewards, and 2) alcohol-related comparator images. To capture ISA heterogeneity as before, k-means clustering was applied to an electroencephalographic late positive potential (LPP) salience index.

Results: As in prior work, clustering identified "Cue > Pleasant" (C>P; n = 14) and "Cue < Pleasant" (C<P; n = 16) groups who showed enhanced or reduced LPPs for reward-predicting cues relative to pleasant-depicting pictures. Beyond cue responding, C>P and C<P groups each showed enhancement for pleasant and unpleasant, compared to neutral, pictures and did not show LPP enhancement - but did show enhanced earlier P300 - for alcohol images. Finally, groups did not differ in task-based M&M consumption or average weekly drinking but did differ in drinking recency (more C<P individuals drank within 2 days of their session).

Conclusions: Results 1) provide proof-of-concept for assessing ISA in AUD without cuing alcohol, and 2) motivate further work to fully test predictiveness of disorder-relevant variables (e.g., drinking during alcohol availability; treatment outcomes).

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: "He's a social creature… he just had no one to share anything with." Social isolation among deaths attributed to acute stimulant toxicity in San Francisco, CA
item.description:
Background: Notwithstanding data suggesting social isolation may play a role in mortality from acute drug toxicity, few studies have explicitly explored the association.

Methods: We analyzed qualitative data from a mixed methods psychological autopsy study of 101 deaths attributed to stimulants in San Francisco, CA. Sociodemographic measures and drugs involved in death were obtained from death records. Interviews were conducted with 141 informants and transcribed and coded using a qualitative codebook. We conducted a thematic analysis of interview excerpts related to loneliness and social isolation.

Results: We identified three interconnected themes: social isolation following major life changes or traumatic events, the bidirectional relationship between social isolation and substance use, and social isolation proximal to death. Informants described decedent isolation as both a driver and consequence of stimulant use. Social isolation was exacerbated by major life changes and anticipated stigma. Many informants described decedents using substances alone due to isolation or feelings of shame, which precluded the presence of a bystander able to respond to their fatal event.

Conclusion: We found that social isolation played a major role in stimulant deaths in our sample. Social isolation both contributed to and resulted from stimulant use and associated stigma and shame. Efforts to prevent stimulant deaths should prioritize reducing isolation and strengthening social connection through nonjudgemental environments.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Impulse control as a mediator between mental health and substance use across diverse adolescent and young adult samples
item.description:
Background: Substance use (SU) and substance use disorders (SUD) are common and often co-occur with psychopathology including depression, anxiety, and emotional dysregulation (ED). The specific role of ED components, including impulsivity, and their links to various substances has not been fully studied. This research examines how impulse control relates to anxiety, depression, and SU in adolescents and young adults (AYA).

Methods: The study involved baseline data from 1246 participants aged 14-30 (M=20.07, SD=4.48) from behavioral health clinics, juvenile justice, juvenile rehabilitation, and high schools across four projects focused on opioid and other SU prevention. Analyses tested whether impulse control challenges mediated the indirect effects of depression and anxiety on SU (alcohol, cannabis, opioids).

Results: We fitted group structural mediation models in which mental health factors (depression or anxiety) predicted impulse control, which in turn predicted SU (alcohol, cannabis, opioids). Generally, AYA with high depression or anxiety had higher SU rates for alcohol and cannabis, and the associations were partly mediated by challenges in impulse control.

Conclusion: AYA with depression or anxiety are more likely to exhibit increased impulsivity and SU, and impulsivity further raised the risk of SU among those with depression or anxiety. Hence, careful monitoring of symptoms related to anxiety, depression, and impulsivity may help identify AYA at the highest risk for developing problematic SU and SUD.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Are Muscle Relaxants an Effective Treatment for Patients With Acute Low Back Pain?
item.description:
Background: Acute low back pain (LBP) is a common condition evaluated and managed in the healthcare setting. While numerous treatment options exist, the efficacy varies, and it is important to balance the benefits with the risk of harm. Muscle relaxants are commonly prescribed in practice, yet it is important to understand the effectiveness to inform their continued use.

Clinical question: Are muscle relaxants an effective treatment for patients with acute low back pain?

Evidence review: Studies retrieved included four randomized controlled trials and two meta-analyses. These studies provide estimates of the effectiveness and safety of muscle relaxants in patients with acute LBP. The data found muscle relaxants do not improve symptom resolution or function in emergency department (ED) patients with acute LBP.

Conclusion: Based upon the available literature, muscle relaxants are not associated with improved outcomes for acute LBP and should not be routinely prescribed in the ED setting.

item.title: N Engl J Med: Intismeran Autogene plus Pembrolizumab for Resected Stage IIB to IV Melanoma
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Intismeran autogene (intismeran) is an individualized neoantigen therapy that is designed to induce new T-cell responses and expand preexisting T-cell responses against patient-specific tumor neoantigens, which may potentially improve the efficacy of adjuvant therapy in patients with melanoma.

Methods: In this phase 3, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned patients with completely resected stage IIB to IV cutaneous melanoma in a 2:1 ratio to receive intramuscular intismeran (at a dose of 1 mg) or placebo every 3 weeks for nine doses; all the patients received intravenous pembrolizumab (at a dose of 400 mg) every 6 weeks for nine cycles. The primary end point was investigator-determined recurrence-free survival, assessed in a time-to-event analysis. Key secondary end points included investigator-determined distant-metastasis-free survival (assessed in a time-to-event analysis) and safety.

Results: A total of 1137 patients underwent randomization: 757 to the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 380 to the placebo-pembrolizumab group. The median follow-up was 24.6 months. Recurrence-free survival at 24 months was 82.2% in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 70.0% in the placebo-pembrolizumab group (two-sided P<0.001); the piecewise hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 1.49) before 6 months and 0.42 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.58) after 6 months. Distant-metastasis-free survival at 24 months was 88.5% with intismeran-pembrolizumab and 80.2% with placebo-pembrolizumab (two-sided P = 0.002); the piecewise hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% CI, 0.58 to 1.79) before 6 months and 0.50 (95% CI, 0.34 to 0.73) after 6 months. Adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 23.6% of the patients in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 20.3% of the patients in the placebo-pembrolizumab group. Eight patients (1.1%) in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group died from an adverse event; five of the deaths occurred before intismeran was administered.

Conclusions: Adjuvant therapy with intismeran plus pembrolizumab significantly prolonged recurrence-free survival and distant-metastasis-free survival as compared with pembrolizumab alone in patients with completely resected, high-risk cutaneous melanoma. (Funded by Merck Sharp and Dohme and Moderna; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05933577.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Preventing Malaria Infections and Moving toward Malaria Elimination
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Malaria continues to be a major health challenge worldwide, causing an estimated 282 million cases of illness and 610,000 deaths in 2024, predominantly among African children. Despite recent stagnation in the progress of malaria prevention, the landscape is undergoing rapid transformation. This review examines current and emerging approaches to preventing malaria infection and supporting malaria elimination, including vector control, transmission-blocking interventions, chemoprevention, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines. Next-generation insecticide-treated nets, expanded use of seasonal malaria chemoprevention, and the introduction of RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M vaccines are already reshaping control strategies. Looking ahead, long-acting injectable chemoprevention, transmission-blocking medicines and vaccines, and improved surveillance-driven deployment may further accelerate progress. As funding becomes constrained and decision making shifts increasingly to countries where malaria is endemic, effective malaria prevention will depend on locally tailored, integrated combinations of interventions supported by strong surveillance, regulatory capacity, and national leadership.

item.title: N Engl J Med: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism after Total Hip or Knee Replacement
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Studies comparing aspirin with anticoagulants for venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty have had conflicting results.

Methods: In a comparative-effectiveness noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned patients undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty to receive aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days. The composite primary effectiveness outcome (death from any cause or symptomatic VTE) and primary safety outcome (bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction) were evaluated through 6 months in a blinded fashion. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference was 0.69 percentage points.

Results: Among 18,883 participants who had undergone randomization, 15,317 (7214 with hip arthroplasty and 8103 with knee arthroplasty) were included in the primary per-protocol analysis. A primary effectiveness outcome event occurred in 77 of 6090 participants (1.26%) in the aspirin group, in 52 of 4231 (1.23%) in the warfarin group, and in 47 of 4996 (0.94%) in the rivaroxaban group; a primary safety outcome event occurred in 177 (2.91%), 142 (3.36%), and 174 (3.48%), respectively. In pairwise comparisons, 6-month risks of a primary effectiveness outcome event were 1.24% and 0.94% for aspirin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.30 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.20 to 0.81); 1.24% and 1.01% for aspirin versus warfarin (difference, 0.23 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.34 to 0.81); and 1.13% and 1.10% for warfarin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.03 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.57 to 0.63). Risks of a primary safety outcome event were 3.70% and 3.02% for rivaroxaban versus aspirin (difference, 0.68 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.41); 3.65% and 2.88% for warfarin versus aspirin (difference, 0.77 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.58); and 3.59% and 3.61% for rivaroxaban versus warfarin (difference, -0.02 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.89 to 0.85). Intention-to-treat analyses yielded similar results.

Conclusions: Aspirin prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty was not noninferior to rivaroxaban or warfarin with respect to death or symptomatic VTE. Warfarin and rivaroxaban were not noninferior to aspirin for safety. (Funded by the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute; PEPPER ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02810704.).

item.title: JAMA: HOPO 14-1, an Oral Actinide Chelator: A Phase 1 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Current treatments approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for internal actinide contamination (pentetate calcium trisodium and pentetate zinc trisodium) require intravenous injection or nebulized inhalation under medical supervision and have limited radionuclide coverage. HOPO 14-1, an oral form of 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO), is the first shelf-stable, broad-spectrum actinide chelator in clinical development that does not require intravenous access or trained personnel. In preclinical models, 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO) removed a broad range of actinides, and its oral route supports scalable emergency medical use.

Objective: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetic parameters, and excretion of a single dose of HOPO 14-1 in healthy adults.

Design, setting, and participants: This was a phase 1 nonrandomized clinical trial including 42 healthy adults (6 per dose level) with evaluations for 14 days after administration of a single dose and conducted at a single site in the US. Participants were recruited and screened between March 2023 and July 2025 and follow-up was completed in August 2025.

Intervention: Single oral dose of HOPO 14-1 administered at 1 of 7 dose levels (100 mg, 200 mg, 500 mg, 1200 mg, 2500 mg, 5000 mg, or 7500 mg) with follow-up through day 14 after dose administration.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes were the incidence and severity of adverse events, drug-related adverse events, and serious adverse events. The secondary outcomes were plasma pharmacokinetic parameters and cumulative urinary and fecal excretion.

Results: Of the 42 healthy adults enrolled (median age, 43 [IQR, 34-51] years; 64% female), all received a single dose of HOPO 14-1 (administered across all dose levels as assigned). There were no serious adverse events or dose-limiting toxic effects. The drug-related adverse events included diarrhea (31%), vomiting (14%), headache (12%), and fatigue (7%); all were mild to moderate in severity. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the principal tolerability findings and most evident at the highest doses. The plasma pharmacokinetic parameters demonstrated rapid absorption (median time of maximum plasma concentration, 0.86 [range, 0.53-1.60] hours to 1.90 [range, 1.40-2.90] hours) and dose-dependent increases in systemic exposure, with greater than proportional increases at higher doses. Fecal excretion was the primary route of elimination; urinary excretion was minimal.

Conclusions and relevance: Single oral doses of HOPO 14-1 up to 7500 mg were administered without dose-limiting toxicity or serious adverse events in healthy adults. Gastrointestinal tolerability defined the practical single-dose ceiling. These findings establish the first human safety and pharmacokinetic profile of a novel, orally administered actinide chelator and support further clinical evaluation of HOPO 14-1 as a countermeasure for internal radionuclide and heavy metal contamination. Development of a deployable and population-level emergency intervention addresses a long-standing unmet need with important implications for public health preparedness.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05628961.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Civil Society Organization-Led Home Visit Intervention to Reduce Unintentional Child Injury in Rural China: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Unintentional injuries are a leading cause of childhood death and disability, but evidence on scalable home visit interventions in rural settings is limited.

Objective: To evaluate whether a civil society organization-led home visit intervention can reduce unintentional injuries among children and improve caregiver and household safety.

Design, setting, and participants: This outcome assessor-blinded cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 24 rural communities in Guizhou and Shaanxi, China, from May 6 to October 1, 2025. After baseline assessment, communities were randomized as clusters in a 1:1 ratio. Participants were households with children aged 3 to 12 years.

Interventions: Control communities received routine social worker home visits; intervention communities received routine services plus 3 monthly structured visits with home safety and first aid tool kits and a follow-up visit at month 4.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was caregiver-reported cumulative child unintentional injury incidence during 4 months, a subjective outcome with caregivers unblinded to group allocation. Secondary outcomes were caregiver knowledge, safety attitudes, and supervisory behaviors, with scores ranging from 0 to 40, 0 to 8, and 0 to 80, respectively, with higher scores indicating better knowledge, more positive safety attitudes, and more appropriate supervisory behaviors, respectively, and household environmental hazards, with scores ranging from 0 to 230 and higher scores indicating more household environmental hazards and a less safe home environment. Generalized estimating equations accounted for clustering.

Results: Among 24 randomized clusters, caregivers (mean [SD] age, 45.4 [13.0] years; 271 [75.3%] female) and children (mean [SD] age, 8.6 [2.3] years, 198 [55.0%] female) from 360 households were enrolled, with 180 each randomized to intervention and control groups. After baseline, 9 households withdrew with missing outcome data; all 360 households were included in the intention-to-treat analyses with multiple imputation. Injury occurred in 21 of 178 households (11.8%) with observed outcomes in the intervention group and 33 of 173 (19.1%) in the control group. The intervention was associated with lower injury odds (adjusted odds ratio, 0.36 [95% CI, 0.18-0.73]; P = .005). At month 4, adjusted mean differences favored the intervention for supervisory behaviors (17.08 [95% CI, 14.71-19.46] points) and household environmental hazards (-36.66 [95% CI, -42.87 to -30.46] points).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cluster randomized clinical trial of households with children aged 3 to 12 years, a civil society organization-led home visit intervention reduced caregiver-reported unintentional injuries and improved caregiver supervisory behaviors and household safety during the 4-month intervention period. Longer follow-up is needed to assess durability of the response.

Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2500098928.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Avoidable Mortality in Adults With Down Syndrome or With Other Intellectual Disabilities
item.description:
Importance: Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause of Alzheimer disease. Adults with Down syndrome experience higher mortality than the general population. However, the avoidable causes and their associated factors remain unclear.

Objective: To compare the proportion and causes of avoidable mortality in adults with Down syndrome, adults with other intellectual disabilities, and the general population, and to identify factors associated with avoidable death.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based retrospective cohort study used data from the Learning From Lives and Deaths mortality review and the Office for National Statistics in England from 2016 to 2023. It included adults with Down syndrome (n = 3381), other adults with intellectual disabilities (n = 15 347), and the general population (n = 4 163 160).

Exposures: Down syndrome status, ethnicity, socioeconomic deprivation, co-occurring health conditions, COVID-19 pandemic period.

Main outcomes and measures: Proportion and causes of avoidable, treatable, and preventable deaths according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development/Eurostat criteria; odds of avoidable death estimated using logistic regression; and age at avoidable death using Cox regression. Factors associated with avoidable death and age at death were also evaluated.

Results: Among 3381 adults with Down syndrome (1892 male [56.0%]; median [IQR] age at death, 59.5 [54.3-64.2] years), 1589 (47.0%) died from avoidable causes. Among 15 347 adults with other intellectual disabilities (8675 male [56.5%]; median [IQR] age at death, 63.8 [51.7-73.4] years), 6885 (44.9%) died from avoidable causes. Both proportions were substantially higher than in the general population (22.0%) (both P < .001). Treatable deaths were more common (972 [28.7%] vs 3847 [25.1%] vs 317 968 [7.6%]), with epilepsy and pneumonia as the leading treatable causes. Down syndrome was independently associated with higher odds of avoidable death (aOR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.06-1.25) and earlier age at avoidable death (aHR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.40-1.58). Minoritized ethnic background, asthma, diabetes, and osteoporosis were each independently associated with higher odds of avoidable death, and minoritized ethnic background and greater socioeconomic deprivation with earlier age at avoidable death.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of adults with Down syndrome and other adults with intellectual disabilities in England, avoidable mortality exceeded that of the general population. For the adults with Down syndrome, epilepsy and pneumonia were the dominant treatable causes. These findings support proactive integrated neurological care, including epilepsy review with dementia monitoring, pneumonia prevention, and respiratory vaccination, alongside targeted interventions for minoritized ethnic groups and socioeconomically deprived groups.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Importance of Angina Pectoris by Coronary Artery Disease Severity
item.description:
Importance: Angina pectoris remains a common clinical manifestation, but contemporary population-based data on its long-term prognostic significance are limited.

Objective: To evaluate the long-term importance of angina pectoris in association with coronary artery disease (CAD) severity determined by coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) in a general population.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based cohort study included participants from the Swedish Cardiopulmonary Bioimage Study who had completed the Rose Questionnaire and underwent valid CCTA from November 2013 to October 2018, excluding participants with prior myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure, or coronary revascularization. Follow-up continued through September 2024. Data analyses were conducted between August 2025 and January 2026.

Exposures: Angina (defined by the Rose Questionnaire) and CAD (categorized as no findings, nonobstructive CAD [<50% stenosis], or obstructive CAD [≥50% stenosis]) according to CCTA findings.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was MI or coronary death. The secondary outcome was major adverse cardiac events (MACE), defined as MI, coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, or death from coronary disease or heart failure. Associations were evaluated using Cox regression with sequential multivariable adjustment and stratification by CAD category and presented as hazard ratios (HRs).

Results: This study included 24 176 individuals (median [IQR] age, 57 [54-61] years; 12 225 female [50.6%]; 1615 with hyperlipidemia [6.8%]; 4374 with hypertension [18.3%]; 703 with diabetes [2.9%]). Angina was present in 720 participants (3.0%). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 7.7 (6.9-8.6) years, 293 primary events occurred. Angina was associated with a higher incidence of MI or coronary death compared with no angina (21 participants [2.9%] vs 272 participants [1.2%]; HR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.60-3.90). Event rates increased across CAD categories, with no evidence of interaction between angina and CAD severity. After multivariable adjustment, angina remained independently associated with the primary outcome (HR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.04-2.63). Similar associations were observed for MACE (adjusted HR, 2.34; 95% CI, 1.73-3.16).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of a contemporary general population, angina pectoris was associated with adverse cardiac outcomes, independent of CAD severity assessed by CCTA. These findings suggest that symptom assessment remains relevant in cardiovascular risk stratification because it provided incremental prognostic information that may reflect underlying coronary microvascular dysfunction or vasomotor disorders.

Welén Schef K, Dworeck C, Johnston N, Sederholm Laweson S, Söderberg S, Tornvall P

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Circulating Tumor DNA in Oligoprogressive Prostate Cancer Treated With Stereotactic Radiotherapy: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis of a Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is increasingly used for oligoprogressive prostate cancer, but the duration of disease control is highly variable.

Objective: To evaluate time to progression based on circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) prior to SBRT.

Design, setting, and participants: Between October 17, 2018, and February 1, 2023, the phase 2 prospective, single-arm, nonrandomized clinical TRAP (Targeted Radiotherapy in Androgen-Suppressed Prostate Cancer Patients) trial evaluated SBRT to treat 81 patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and 2 or fewer metastases and imaging evidence of progression while receiving an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI). Plasma DNA was collected at 1 or 2 points prior to SBRT and centrally tested for ctDNA using the next-generation sequencing assay PCF_SELECT. Data were collected prospectively using electronic trial case report forms. Data were extracted November 26, 2025. The median follow-up was 24.5 (IQR, 23.7-36.3) months.

Exposures: Progressing metastases were treated with SBRT, and patients were followed up with clinical assessments, serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) tests, and imaging.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome measure was time to progression, defined as an increase in serum prostate-specific antigen level of 25% or greater from the post-SBRT nadir, radiologic or symptomatic progression, clinician decision to stop ARPI, or death from any cause. The secondary outcomes were time to next therapy or death from any cause. All end points were measured from time of final SBRT treatment.

Results: Of 77 patients with evaluable blood samples taken prior to SBRT, 19 (24.7%) were in the ctDNA-positive group. The 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate was 21.1% (95% CI, 6.6%-41.0%) for the ctDNA-positive group compared with 58.3% (95% CI, 44.5%-69.8%) for the ctDNA-negative group. The median PFS was 3.0 (95% CI, 2.7-5.9) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 7.8 (95% CI, 5.9-11.4) months for the ctDNA negative group (log rank test, P = .003 at 5% significance level). The median time to initiation of a new therapy or death was 15.3 (95% CI, 4.7-26.0) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 29.6 (95% CI, 17.8-37.6) months for the ctDNA-negative group. The median overall survival was 27.2 (95% CI, 19.2 to undefined) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 33.6 (95% CI, 28.4-38.2) months for the ctDNA-negative group.

Conclusions and relevance: These findings suggest that for patients with oligoprogression and no ctDNA, SBRT and continued ARPI could be considered a valid option for prolonging disease control.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03644303.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Cord Serum Neonicotinoid-Related Biomarkers and Neurodevelopment From Early to Middle Childhood
item.description:
Importance: Despite widespread neonicotinoid insecticide use, evidence on prenatal exposure and neurodevelopment beyond early childhood remains limited.

Objective: To examine whether cord serum concentrations of the neonicotinoid-related biomarkers dinotefuran and desmethyl-acetamiprid (dm-ACE) are associated with domain-specific neurodevelopment from infancy through middle childhood.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study included individuals randomly selected from eligible Hamamatsu Birth Cohort for Mothers and Children Study participants born between December 2007 and March 2012 in Japan; assessments spanned ages 10 months to 9 years. Data were analyzed between October 2025 and September 2026.

Exposures: Cord serum dinotefuran and dm-ACE concentrations measured at birth and categorized into quartiles.

Main outcomes and measures: Outcomes were standardized scores for 5 Mullen Scales of Early Learning (MSEL) domains at ages 10 to 32 months and 4 Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (WISC-IV) indices at age 9 years. Associations were examined using linear regression and expressed as mean MSEL or WISC-IV differences in SD units at quartile 3 (Q3) and Q4 concentrations (combined Q1-Q2 was the reference).

Results: Among 200 individuals, 102 (51.0%) were male and 13 (6.5%) were born preterm; 185 (92.5%) to 195 (97.5%) were included in age-specific MSEL analyses and 178 (89.0%) in WISC-IV analyses. Dinotefuran groups included 96 individuals (48.0%) in Q1 and Q2, 47 (23.5%) in Q3, and 57 (28.5%) in Q4. dm-ACE groups included 82 (41.0%) in Q1 and Q2, 63 (31.5%) in Q3, and 55 (27.5%) in Q4. Early childhood associations across neurodevelopmental scale scores varied by age and concentration group, and there were no associations after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. At age 9 years, Q3 dinotefuran concentration was associated with lower WISC-IV Processing Speed Index scores compared with Q1 to Q2 scores (mean difference, -0.50 [95% CI, -0.81 to -0.20] SDs; q = .01), and Q4 dm-ACE concentration was associated with lower Perceptual Reasoning Index scores (mean difference, -0.47 [95% CI, -0.81 to -0.14] SDs; q = .03).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of infants and children in Japan, small differences in some neurodevelopmental scale scores in early childhood were observed in association with dinotefuran and dm-ACE cord serum concentrations, but there were no associations after FDR correction. At age 9 years, dinotefuran was associated with lower processing speed and dm-ACE with lower perceptual reasoning. Overall, these findings suggest domain- and age-specific associations rather than a uniform or sustained pattern across development; confirmation in larger cohorts is needed.

Nagata A, Okumura A, Takahashi N, Nomura Y, Harada T, Iwabuchi T

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Bisphosphonates vs Denosumab After Low-Trauma Fractures
item.description:
Importance: Patients are at high risk of refracture and death in the immediate period following low-trauma fracture, but comparative evidence for antiresorptive therapies is limited.

Objective: To compare refracture and all-cause mortality between patients who initiated nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (N-BPs) and denosumab therapy after fractures.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used sequential target trial emulation of monthly trials among treatment-naive adults 50 years or older through the 12 months after incident low-trauma fracture with a new-user, active-comparator design. Linked administrative health data from the population of New South Wales, Australia, was used. Women entered from January 1, 2011, to June 30, 2018, and men from January 1, 2014, to June 30, 2018, both with 3 years of follow-up. Data were analyzed from December 1, 2025, to May 31, 2026.

Exposures: N-BP (alendronate, risedronate or zoledronic acid) vs denosumab.

Main outcomes and measures: Three-year all-cause mortality and refracture. Primary analyses estimated intention-to-treat (ITT) associations with inverse probability weighting. Secondary analyses included per-protocol and Fine-Gray competing-risk analyses. Hazard ratios (HRs) greater than 1.00 indicated higher risk with N-BP.

Results: The cohort included 15 099 participants (overall mean [SD] age, 77.2 [9.2] years), of whom 12 529 (83.0%) were women and 2570 (17.0%) were men (79.9 [8.4] years). All-cause mortality rates with N-BP vs denosumab were 48.1 vs 48.9 per 1000 person-years in women and 123.0 vs 116.4 per 1000 person-years in men, with no clear association in women (ITT HR, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87-1.10]) or men (ITT HR, 1.09 [95% CI, 0.93-1.25]). Refracture rates were 52.7 vs 46.5 per 1000 person-years in women and 70.5 vs 58.8 per 1000 person-years in men. Initiation of N-BP therapy was associated with higher refracture risk in women (ITT HR, 1.14 [95% CI, 1.05-1.26]) and men (ITT HR, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.03-1.42]). Competing-risk estimates were similar; per-protocol estimates were higher in women (HR, 1.30 [95% CI, 1.09-1.55]) and men (HR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.10-1.98]). Risks were strongest following nonhip-nonvertebral (NHNV) fractures in women (HR, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.06-1.38]) and men (HR, 1.54 [95% CI, 1.10-2.15]).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study emulating a target trial, initiation of N-BP and denosumab therapy was associated with similar mortality, whereas initiation of N-BP was associated with higher refracture risk, particularly after NHNV fractures.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Estimation of mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 COVID-19 Vaccine Effectiveness in Older US Veterans
item.description:
Importance: The mRNA-1283 vaccine, a novel mRNA vaccine targeting immunodominant spike regions, was first used during the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season. Older adults remain at elevated risk for severe COVID-19 outcomes, and clinical evidence of estimated vaccine effectiveness can inform seasonal vaccination policy.

Objective: To compare the estimated effectiveness of mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 vaccines against medically attended COVID-19 illness and COVID-19-associated hospitalization among US veterans aged 65 years or older.

Design, setting, and participants: This was a retrospective matched cohort study emulating a target trial. US veterans aged 65 years or older who were enrolled in a national, integrated Veterans Health Administration (VHA) health care system and received an LP.8.1-formulated mRNA-1283 or BNT162b2 vaccine between August 27, 2025, and January 31, 2026, were followed up for up to 150 days or through May 1, 2026.

Exposure: Receipt of LP.8.1 mRNA-1283 or BNT162b2 vaccine.

Main outcome and measures: The primary outcome was medically attended COVID-19 illness, defined by a positive SARS-CoV-2 test result linked to medical care or antiviral treatment or a primary COVID-19 diagnosis. Matching was performed on home county and calendar week of vaccination, followed by inverse probability of treatment weighting. Secondary outcomes included the individual component event of hospitalization. Measures were absolute and relative differences in 150-day cumulative incidence among patients receiving mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 vaccine, computed as the estimated relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) percentage and absolute risk difference (ARD) per 10 000 persons, adjusted for demographic and clinical factors.

Results: The cohort included 60 340 mRNA-1283 and 321 845 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (mean [SD] age, 76.8 [6.7] years; 94.2% male). Among the 294 499 participants in the final matched sample, medically attended COVID-19 occurred in 86 of 55 349 mRNA-1283 vaccine recipients (0.16%) and 672 of 239 150 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (0.28%), corresponding to estimated rVE of 35.9% (95% credible interval [CrI], 20.4%-49.7%) and an adjusted ARD of -10.0 (95% CrI, -14.3 to -5.6) events per 10 000 persons. COVID-19-associated hospitalization occurred in 11 mRNA-1283 vaccine recipients (0.02%) vs 114 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (0.05%) (estimated rVE, 47.0% [95% CrI, 5.4%-74.8%]; adjusted ARD, -2.2 [95% CrI, -3.8 to -0.2] events per 10 000 persons).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of older US veterans during the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season, mRNA-1283 vaccination was associated with lower risks of medically attended COVID-19 outcomes and COVID-19 hospitalizations compared with BNT162b2 vaccination. The findings suggest that the mRNA-1283 vaccine may offer more clinically meaningful protection for older adults at high risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes and could inform seasonal vaccine selection.

McConeghy KW, Skov B, DeVone F, Wilson A, Araujo AB, Vicic N

item.title: Crit Care Med: Characterization of Urgent ICU Consultations in the Evaluation of Processes of Care and the Outcomes of Children in Hospital (EPOCH) Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Objectives: Urgent ICU consultation is intended to elicit advice and consider ICU transfer. Our objective was to describe the nature and outcomes of ICU consultations across a global cohort.

Design: This is a secondary analysis of patients with one or more ICU consultations. A care episode was defined as consecutive urgent ICU consultations until an ICU admission or at least 2 weeks without an urgent ICU consultation. We describe consultation outcomes for the last care episode. Late escalations were defined by a Children's Resuscitation Intensity Scale score greater than 2.

Setting: Twenty-one centers participating in the Evaluation of Processes of Care and the Outcomes of Children in Hospital (EPOCH) cluster-randomized trial.

Patients: There were 4288 urgent ICU consultations in 3625 care episodes for 3000 patients with a median (interquartile range) age of 25 months (5-99 mo).

Interventions: In the parent EPOCH trial, hospitals were randomized to Bedside Pediatric Early Warning System or usual care; no intervention was assigned in this secondary analysis.

Measurements and main results: The outcomes of the 3000 last care episodes were in-consultation death in three (0.1%) and urgent ICU admission in 1477 (49.2%). Among 3000 first, 400 second, and 68 third consultations, the proportions of ICU admission were 42%, 44%, and 47%. The proportions of ICU admissions that were late escalation were similar across groups: 18% for first and second urgent ICU consultations, and 25% for third urgent ICU consultations. among patients having a second urgent ICU consultation, patients who had received resuscitation interventions in their first urgent ICU consultation (and remained on the ward) had more frequent resuscitation events (23.2% vs. 3.4%, p < 0.01) and had a similar frequency of late escalation (31.8% vs. 15.6%, p = 0.07) and ICU admission (51.1% vs. 43.1%, p = 0.40) compared with patients without resuscitation in their first urgent ICU consultation.

Conclusions: Urgent consultation to the ICU is common during pediatric hospitalization. Repeated ICU consultation was associated with a similar frequency of late escalation. Resuscitation measures were provided in one of 12 ICU consultations where patients were not admitted to ICU and were a risk factor for late escalation in subsequent consultations.

Pisesky A, Szadkowski L, Tomlinson G, Frndova H, Joffe AR, Parshuram CS

item.title: Crit Care Med: Low Physical Activity and Reported Barriers Among Survivors of Critical Illness: A Mixed-Method Study
item.description:
Objectives: To examine physical activity levels in survivors of critical illness across 6 months, and to understand the barriers and facilitators of physical activity.

Design: Prospective, longitudinal, convergent mixed-methods study.

Setting: Functional testing laboratory.

Patients: Adults admitted to the ICU for at least 72 hours with acute respiratory failure or sepsis.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Patients wore an accelerometer starting at hospital discharge, at 3- and 6-month follow-up to quantify daily step counts. At 6 months, physical function and patient-reported outcomes were collected in-person, with a subset of participants completing semi-structured interviews. Eighty-two patients were enrolled, with 67 (82%) having physical activity data with median age of 60 years (interquartile range [IQR], 52-66 yr), 54% male, and ICU stay 9.0 days [IQR, 5.8-17.0 d]. The median daily steps were 1358 (IQR, 742-2799) in 50 patients at baseline, 2305 (IQR, 1081-3898) in 54 patients at 3 months, and 2826 (IQR, 1609-4781) in 44 patients at 6 months. Higher comorbidity burden and earlier measurement associated with lower step counts. At 6 months, patients walked a mean of 344 ± 169 meters on the 6-minute walk test and reported being sedentary a median of 300 min/days (150-480 min/d). Eleven participants completed interviews, yielding three themes: 1) "a marathon, not a sprint": the extended ICU recovery trajectory; 2) engagement in physical activity is highly regulated by personal context; 3) value-driven and motivation-informed physical activity decisions. Mixed-methods integration demonstrated that qualitative themes expanded upon quantitative findings to explain nonlinear recovery patterns, contextualizing persistent sedentary behavior, and revealing that motivational and behavioral gaps are not captured by accelerometry.

Conclusions: Survivors showed gradual improvement in daily steps over 6 months yet remained below recommended activity levels. Survivorship and attrition biases may lead to overestimation of step counts, further warranting larger studies. Integrating quantitative and qualitative data reveals modifiable contextual factors that may inform the design of pragmatic physical activity interventions.

Fresenko LE, González-Seguel F, Johnson AM, Slone SA, Morris PE, Salyer AL

item.title: Crit Care Med: Evaluation of Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 Performance Across Demographic Subgroups: An External Validation Using MIMIC-IV
item.description:
Objectives: To evaluate the discrimination and calibration of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-2 score for ICU mortality across demographic subgroups defined by age, sex, race and ethnicity, primary language, and insurance status.

Design: Retrospective cohort study.

Setting: Single academic medical center in the northeastern United States (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA), using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV database (version 3.1), 2008-2022, a dataset external to the SOFA-2 development cohort.

Patients: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) with at least one ICU admission. The first ICU admission of the first qualifying hospitalization per patient was analyzed.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: First-day SOFA-2 scores were calculated from the worst values recorded during the first 24 hours of ICU admission across six organ systems, with ICU mortality as the primary outcome. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration using intercept and slope, with subgroup differences in AUROC estimated by bootstrap resampling. Among 64,015 ICU patients (mean [sd] age, 64.6 [17.1] yr; 56.1% male; 66.1% White), overall AUROC was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.76-0.77). Discrimination declined significantly with age: AUROC, 0.85 (0.83-0.87) for ages 18-44 years vs. 0.72 (0.70-0.73) for ages 75 or older (ΔAUROC, -0.14 [95% CI, -0.16 to -0.11]), with systematic underprediction in older patients. Discrimination was significantly decreased among non-English speakers (ΔAUROC, -0.04) but did not differ across documented racial/ethnic groups. Patients with missing demographic information had markedly higher mortality than the overall cohort rate of 7.2% (14.1% for missing race/ethnicity; 23.1% for missing language).

Conclusions: SOFA-2 demonstrated good overall performance but with clinically meaningful variation across subgroups, particularly with age and language. Patients with missing demographic data experienced markedly higher mortality. These findings argue for routine equity evaluation as a complement to traditional validation of clinical prediction tools.

Ellen J, Hao S, Gao CA, Pilar Arias MD, Viola M, Wong AI

item.title: Crit Care Med: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Objectives: To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial investigating guanfacine for ICU delirium, including assessment of recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, and data completeness, while estimating treatment effects to inform future trial design.

Design: Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial conducted from November 2020 to February 2023.

Setting: Surgical and Trauma ICUs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Hospital.

Patients: One hundred critically ill adults with Confusion Assessment Method-ICU-confirmed delirium randomized 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo.

Interventions: Patients received 2 mg guanfacine or matching placebo nightly for up to 14 days, or until ICU discharge or delirium resolution.

Measurements and main results: Primary feasibility outcomes included protocol adherence (target ≥ 90%), retention (target ≥ 80%), recruitment rate (target ≥ 2 patients/mo), and data completeness (target ≥ 95%). Most feasibility targets were achieved: protocol adherence was 100%, retention was 100%, and data completeness was 100%. Recruitment was significantly impacted by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, achieving 0.9 patients/wk during active recruitment periods.For clinical outcomes, in unadjusted analyses, median delirium and coma-free days were higher with guanfacine than placebo (2 [interquartile range [IQR], 0-6] vs. 1 [IQR, 0-4]; p = 0.02); however, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for prespecified baseline covariates. ICU and hospital length of stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly between groups. No hemodynamic differences or safety concerns were observed.

Conclusions: This pilot study successfully supports feasibility for a definitive trial, with excellent protocol adherence, adequate retention, and preliminary signals that warrant further evaluation. Although adjusted analyses were not statistically significant, the observed unadjusted difference in delirium and coma-free days and favorable safety profile support progression to a multicenter trial informed by these pilot estimates.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials
item.description:
Delirium is an abnormal mental status, commonly occurring among critically ill patients, in which a person's attention and awareness change acutely. Delirium is associated with negative outcomes, including death. Furthermore, a longer duration of delirium is associated with long-term cognitive impairment in survivors of critical illness. Hence, there is a need for novel interventions that reduce the duration of delirium; however, measuring and analyzing "duration of delirium" as an endpoint in randomized trials is challenging due to the episodic nature of delirium and the competing events of coma and death, which can bias analyses of duration of delirium. Given these challenges, delirium trials have adopted one of two composite endpoints: delirium- and coma-free days, defined as the number of days alive without delirium or coma for both survivors and nonsurvivors, and an alternative composite that ranks death as the worst state and orders days alive without delirium or coma among survivors. To date, these composite endpoints have not been rigorously evaluated. Hence, herein we use data from the Maximizing Efficacy of Targeted Sedation and Reducing Neurologic Dysfunction (MENDS) trial to motivate the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, discuss how to define the effect of treatment on each composite endpoint and their clinical interpretability, and present a method for visualizing how the treatment effects accrue over the course of follow-up. Based on these analyses, we provide practical recommendations for the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, which could be extended to other randomized trials that rely on similar composite endpoints.

Smith BB, Pandharipande PP, Ely EW, Girard TD, Needham DM, Colantuoni E

item.title: Crit Care Med: Normocapnia Versus Mild Hypercapnia During Lung Protective Ventilation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Target Trial Emulation
item.description:
Objectives: This trial emulation aimed to answer the question: Among patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) who receive lung protective ventilation with low tidal volume, is normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia?

Design: Target trial emulation.

Setting: Hospitals of the ARDS Network and Prevention and Early Treatment of Acute Lung Injury (PETAL) Network.

Patients: Patients with ARDS enrolled in seven ARDS Network and PETAL Network randomized controlled trials.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: A target trial was emulated, assigning participants in a 1:1 ratio to normocapnia (target Paco2 35-45 mm Hg) or mild hypercapnia (target Paco2 50-55 mm Hg) for 4 days following the initiation of lung protective ventilation. The primary outcome was 90-day in-hospital mortality. Of 5367 potentially eligible subjects, 292 patients were assigned to normocapnia and 292 to mild hypercapnia. Separation in Paco2 values was preserved over the 4-day period of emulated intervention. Both groups had median pH greater than or equal to 7.33. Bicarbonate levels, driving pressure, tidal volume, and dead-space fraction did not differ clinically significantly between groups, while median respiratory rate was 33.0 breaths/min in the normocapnia vs. 28.0 breaths/min in the mild hypercapnia group (p < 0.001). Death within 90 days occurred in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the normocapnia group and in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the mild hypercapnia group (log-rank p = 0.842). This result persisted in subgroups such as older (≥ 65 yr) and obese (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m2) patients.

Conclusions: Among patients with ARDS who received lung protective ventilation, normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate was not associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia. As this finding is derived from a trial emulation, it should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for significant residual bias.

Giannakoulis VG, Papoutsi E, Gkirgkiris K, Diakonikolaou Z, Kalamara E, Katsogianni A

item.title: Crit Care Med: Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study
item.description:
Objectives: During sepsis, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released and elevated due to cell injury, augments the immune response, and may contribute to organ dysfunction. Delirium is common and deleterious during sepsis, but little is known about the relationship between mitochondrial injury and delirium during sepsis. We sought therefore to examine associations between ccf-mtDNA and delirium and other clinical outcomes during sepsis.

Design: Multicenter, prospective cohort study.

Setting: Medical and surgical ICUs in university and community hospitals in Nashville, TN.

Patients: Four hundred eighty patients with sepsis plus shock and/or acute respiratory failure.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: We measured ccf-mtDNA in plasma collected on multiple days (study days 1, 3, and 5) during sepsis and assessed participants bid for delirium and coma using the validated Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale. We then assessed survivors' cognitive function 3 and 12 months after hospital discharge using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99-1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, -1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, -0.36; 95% CI, -2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes.

Conclusions: In this multicenter, prospective cohort study, higher levels of ccf-mtDNA were associated with lower odds of delirium, a result that contradicted our hypothesis. This provocative finding should be interpreted cautiously until replicated and explained by future studies.

Onyemekwu CA, Mart MF, Prendergast NT, Toth KM, Tan X, Gu X

item.title: Crit Care Med: Alarm Fatigue Across Critical Care Domains: Comparative Insights and Independent Predictors From a Cross-Sectional Multicenter Survey Study
item.description:
Objectives: Alarm fatigue, the desensitization to excessive false alarms, threatens patient safety and staff performance across critical care domains. It is unclear whether alarm fatigue differs between hospital departments. This study compared alarm fatigue among staff in the ICU, cardiac telemetry ward (CTW), and operating room (OR), and, secondarily, identified its independent determinants.

Design: Cross-sectional, multicenter survey study.

Setting: ICUs, a CTW, and ORs.

Patients: A total of 514 healthcare professionals working in the ICU, CTW, and OR.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Alarm fatigue was assessed using the Dutch-translated Charité Alarm Fatigue Questionnaire, which includes alarm stress and alarm coping subscales. Participants also rated their self-perceived alarm fatigue on a 1-10 scale and the percentage of perceived false alarms. Telemetry staff reported the highest self-perceived alarm fatigue (B = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.06-1.24; p = 0.032) and perceived false alarms (B = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.23-1.30; p = 0.005), while OR staff reported the lowest (B = -1.01; 95% CI, -1.59 to -0.43; p < 0.001). Second, physicians (B = -0.13; 95% CI, -0.25 to -0.01; p < 0.031) and less experienced staff (< 3 mo; B = -0.34; 95% CI, -0.68 to -0.01; p = 0.046) reported lower alarm fatigue.

Conclusions: Alarm fatigue varied significantly across departments and professions, being highest in telemetry staff and lowest among physicians and less experienced personnel. Targeted department-specific interventions and longitudinal research are necessary to mitigate alarm fatigue and enhance patient safety.

Le Pera T, Gerardu VCA, van Bussel BCT, Bukowski M, Kloeze C, de Kok JWTM

item.title: Lancet: A blended digital parenting intervention for the prevention of sexual violence, exploitative sex, and maltreatment of children at scale in Tanzania: a cluster-randomised, controlled trial
item.description:
Background: Childhood sexual, physical, and verbal violence are global public health priorities, affecting 1 billion children each year. ParentApp integrates sexual violence prevention into WHO-UNICEF's open-access Parenting for Lifelong Health programme, using innovative blended digital delivery. We aimed to test the efficacy of ParentApp in preventing sexual violence and maltreatment against adolescent-aged children and improving preventive mechanisms such as family mental health and adolescent-caregiver relationships.

Methods: This cluster-randomised, controlled trial was conducted in 80 Tanzanian sub-wards. Participants were primary caregivers aged 18 years and older and their adolescents (aged 10-17 years). Sub-wards were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either ParentApp (intervention group) or a control WASHApp programme. Clusters were randomly assigned in blocks of six, stratified by urban versus rural location. Statisticians carrying out randomisation and data analysts were masked; it was not possible to mask participants or researchers. Intervention groups received a low-cost Android phone installed with ParentApp, a 12-module offline-first app, with one in-person orientation session and remote support via WhatsApp group chats, at a delivery cost of US$6 per family at scale, or $10 with 20% smartphone provision. Control groups received a low-cost Android phone installed with WASHApp, a 12-module offline-first app for water, sanitation, and hygiene, with one in-person orientation session. The primary outcomes were adolescent sexual violence victimisation and maltreatment and high-risk situations for sexual violence, assessed in all participants irrespective of uptake and engagement at 5 months and 18 months post-baseline. The trial was registered on March 14, 2023, with OSF (https://osf.io/t9fxz) and is completed.

Findings: Between May 11 and Oct 9, 2023, 2692 caregiver-adolescent dyads were screened for study eligibility; 2396 adolescents (1217 [50·8%] female and 1179 [49·2%] male) and 2396 caregivers (1795 [74·9%] female and 601 [25·1%] male) were recruited. 2145 (89·5%) adolescents and 2252 (94·0%) caregivers were retained in the study and included in analyses at 18 months. Adolescent girls in ParentApp clusters had a substantial reduction in past-month sexual violence victimisation compared with those in control clusters (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0·43 [95% CI 0·21-0·86]; p=0·018), with no effect for boys (1·21 [0·59-2·43]; p=0·60). Past-month maltreatment (physical abuse, verbal abuse, and neglect) was lower in ParentApp clusters than in control clusters (adolescent report IRR 0·92 [0·88-0·96]; p<0·0001, caregiver report 0·87 [0·82-0·92]; p<0·0001). Past-month exposure to high-risk situations for sexual violence was lower in ParentApp clusters than in control clusters (adolescent girls IRR 0·87 [0·77-0·97]; p=0·012, adolescent boys 0·85 [0·79-0·91]; p<0·0001, caregiver report 0·81 [0·75-0·88]; p<0·0001). There were no reported adverse events.

Interpretation: A low-cost blended digital parenting programme in countries such as Tanzania could simultaneously reduce childhood sexual violence (for girls) and maltreatment and sexual violence risk situations (for girls and boys).

Funding: UK Research and Innovation Global Challenges Research Fund, The Oak Foundation, The LEGO Foundation, The European Research Council, and an anonymous donor.

item.title: Lancet: Reframing disease elimination: an update from the Lancet Commission on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
item.description:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with increasing global burden driven by population growth and ageing, persistent harmful exposures, and substantial health inequities. The Lancet Commission on COPD articulated an ambitious vision for disease elimination with prevention, early detection, and intervention. This Review revisits that vision, assesses progress since 2022, and calls for a broader commitment to lifelong lung health as an update of the Commission. Across seven sections, this Review advances a unified framework integrating the biology of lung development and ageing, precision medicine, patient-centred outcomes, and regulatory reform. COPD is not a single, uniform disease; rather, a biologically complex condition shaped by genetic, developmental, environmental, infectious, and behavioural factors across the entire life course. Effective prevention and care should therefore move beyond the detection and treatment of late physiological impairment toward earlier disease recognition, biological stratification, and interventions to preserve lung health, reduce symptoms, and prevent morbidity and premature mortality. The Review charts a path from reactive, late-stage management toward proactive, equitable, precision-based prevention and care. The central premise is unequivocal: the global burden of COPD can be substantially reduced. Success should be measured not only by gains in lung function and survival but also by improvements in daily functioning, quality of life, and wellbeing. In this expanded vision, COPD is no longer viewed solely as a chronic disease to be managed but as a preventable and modifiable condition within a broader commitment to lifelong lung health.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Tenecteplase for isolated central retinal artery occlusion secondary to internal carotid artery dissection: A case report
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is a blinding neuro-ophthalmologic emergency. Internal carotid artery dissection (ICAD) is a rare but underrecognized etiology of CRAO, frequently missed at initial presentation due to absence of pathognomonic clinical signs. While early intravenous thrombolysis confers benefit in CRAO, evidence for tenecteplase (TNK) in ICAD-associated cases remains exceedingly sparse. A 44-year-old previously healthy woman presented with isolated acute left CRAO after routine jogging. Intravenous TNK (0.25 mg/kg) administered within 3 h of onset achieved complete visual recovery the next day. Cervicocephalic vascular imaging confirmed left ICAD. Six-month follow-up after dual antiplatelet therapy demonstrated favorable recanalization, stable visual function, and no cerebral or ocular ischemic events occurred. This case suggests that intravenous TNK thrombolysis within the therapeutic window can yield favorable visual outcomes and acceptable safety in patients with ICAD-associated CRAO. For patients with acute visual loss occurring after exercise, ICAD must be actively suspected. Prompt cervicocephalic vascular etiological assessment alongside emergency care, delivered via multidisciplinary stroke pathways for improved long-term prognosis.

Shen Y, Jiang X, Shi Z, Zhang L

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Comparative safety, efficiency, and diagnostic accuracy of YEARS, PEGeD, age-adjusted D-dimer, and fixed D-dimer strategies for excluding pulmonary embolism in the emergency department: a systematic review and meta-analysis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: D-dimer-based strategies, including fixed D-dimer, age-adjusted D-dimer (AADD), YEARS, and pulmonary embolism graduated D-dimer (PEGeD), have been developed to exclude pulmonary embolism (PE). This systematic review and meta-analysis compared their diagnostic accuracy, safety, and efficiency in emergency department (ED) patients with suspected PE.

Methods: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to July 2026. Outcomes included diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) safety (diagnostic failure rate), and efficiency (imaging avoidance). Bivariate random-effects models were used in pooling diagnostic accuracy outcomes and imaging avoidance rates were expressed as percentages.

Results: Twenty-four studies involving 63,583 patients were included. The pooled analysis demonstrated a sensitivity of 98.3% (95% CI, 97.3 to 99.1), 96.5% (95% CI: 94.3 to 98.2), 91.8% (95% CI: 87.2 to 95.4), and 91.0% (95% CI: 79.5 to 95.9), and a pooled specificity of 22.0% (95% CI: 12.8 to 38.8), 34.7% (95% CI: 20.0 to 51.7), 51.6% (95% CI: 32.5 to 71.5), and 43.6 (95% CI: 23.0 to 69.5) for fixed D-dimer, AADD, YEARS, and PEGeD algorithm, respectively. Pooled imaging avoidance rates were 15% (95% CI: 0 to 42) for fixed D-dimer, 16% (95% CI: 0 to 45) for AADD, 51% (95% CI: 23 to 79) for YEARS, and 53% (95% CI: 25 to 81).

Conclusion: Across studies, all D-dimer strategies showed high pooled sensitivity, with variable specificity and imaging avoidance rates. Diagnostic failure rates were reported in a limited number of studies, limiting conclusions regarding clinical safety.

Shaban EE, Abosamak MF, Elmelliti H, Shaban A, Shaban A, Jobran AWM

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Fentanyl and xylazine precipitated withdrawal in Swiss Webster mice
item.description:
Background: In recent years, α2-adrenoreceptor (α2AR) agonists have become common adulterants of illicit fentanyl supplies. One such drug is xylazine, a veterinary anesthetic not approved for human use. There is little known about effects of xylazine upon repeated administration, interactions between fentanyl and xylazine, and how xylazine may alter withdrawal from fentanyl. In this work, we established a precipitated withdrawal procedure with the goal of understanding withdrawal from xylazine and how it may impact withdrawal from fentanyl.

Methods: Mice received fentanyl, xylazine, or both, followed by antagonists naloxone, idazoxan, or both 2h later. Mice were then placed into a large glass beaker and observed for two 60s intervals at 9- and 17-min post injection, and presence of withdrawal signs was recorded in each interval.

Results: Injections of fentanyl or xylazine followed by antagonists naloxone or idazoxan, respectively, each produced a unique set of precipitated withdrawal signs. Both produced significant grimace and wet dog shakes; however, precipitated fentanyl withdrawal also produced paw tremors and jumps whereas xylazine withdrawal produced scratching. Xylazine coadministration with fentanyl increased the frequency of some signs of fentanyl precipitated withdrawal while decreasing others.

Conclusion: This work suggests that the addition of xylazine to illicit fentanyl supplies is changing the somatic state of fentanyl withdrawal, which may impact patients in clinical settings.

Shepherd B, Cakir K, Walker EA

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Pooled prevalence of infectious diseases among first responders in the prehospital setting: A systematic review with meta-analysis by occupation
item.description:
Objectives: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers.

Methods: Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using I², τ², and 95% prediction intervals. Meta-regression was used to examine potential sources of between-study heterogeneity, and small-study effects and potential publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Risk of bias was investigated using the AXIS tool.

Results: Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%- 5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonisation. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%- 25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%- 12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, p = 0.039.

Conclusions: Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Prehospital Whole Blood Resuscitation in Pediatric Patients: A San Antonio Cohort Descriptive
item.description:
Objectives: The objective of this study is to describe the demographic, clinical, and prehospital care characteristics of pediatric patients receiving whole blood (WB) resuscitation by San Antonio Fire Department (SAFD).

Methods: We conducted an observational retrospective cohort study to evaluate pediatric patients who received prehospital low-titer group O positive WB transfusion through the SAFD prehospital blood program between October 2018 and June 2025. The objective was to characterize patient demographics, injury patterns, resuscitative interventions, shock physiology, and outcomes among pediatric recipients in a mature civilian emergency medical services WB program.

Results: Of 1703 WB transfusions, 73 (4.3%) were pediatric. Most patients were male (76%), age range 1-17 years old with a mode of 17 years, adolescents represented 78%. Trauma accounted for 96% of cases, firearm injury (74%); all penetrating (84%), blunt (12%), with the remainder classified as medical/unknown. Vascular access was intravenous (73%), intraosseous (26%). Tranexamic acid was co-administered in 39%; 12% received ceftriaxone. When analyzed using age-adjusted Shock Index Pediatric Age-Adjusted (SIPA) thresholds (>1.2 for 1-6 years, >1.0 for 7-12 years, and >0.9 for 13-17 years), based on the initial available prehospital heart rate and systolic blood pressure, 45% of patients had an elevated SIPA, 22% had a normal SIPA, 20% were pulseless and therefore could not undergo SIPA calculation, and 14% lacked sufficient vital-sign data for classification. Survival was 50%; died 39%, and unknown outcomes 11%. Mean delta shock index values were most negative in toddlers (1-4 years) -0.97 ± 1.29, followed by children (5-11 years) -0.76 ± 1.07 and adolescents (12-17 years) -0.16 ± 0.46, indicating a greater physiologic response to resuscitation among younger pediatric patients.

Conclusions: Pediatric WB recipients were predominantly adolescent males who sustained penetrating trauma and presented with moderate-to-severe shock. Younger age groups had larger descriptive decreases in shock index during the prehospital encounter; however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small subgroup sizes and observational design.
