item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Automated Clinical Decision Support and Electronic Health Record Tracking of Patients With Adenomas Found on Colonoscopy
item.description:
Importance: Surveillance colonoscopy following adenoma detection is essential for colorectal cancer prevention, yet systematic tracking within electronic health record (EHR) systems remains challenging, as they rely on manual data entry.

Objective: To determine if implementation of an automatic tool in the EHR is associated with improved health care maintenance table updates for patients needing repeat colonoscopy for cancer screening after adenoma detection.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study at a single tertiary care center within a large health care organization with EHR functionality included patients undergoing colonoscopy between November 2017 and December 2024. Eligible participants were adults aged 50 to 75 years undergoing colonoscopy for screening, surveillance, or diagnostic indications. Exclusion criteria included patients with inflammatory bowel disease, known colorectal cancer, or hereditary cancer syndromes. Data were analyzed between January and May 2025.

Exposure: A decision support tool was implemented that allowed gastroenterologists completing colonoscopies for patients with adenoma to choose follow-up intervals that would automatically populate the health maintenance tab.

Main outcomes and measures: Rate of updates of the health maintenance table and percentage completion from gastroenterology vs primary care.

Results: A total of 35 802 patients met criteria (20 049 female [56.0%]; median [range] age: preintervention, 61 years [50-75 years]; postintervention, 62 years [50-75 years]); adenomas were detected in 8004 of 18 027 patients (44.4%) in the preintervention period and 8396 of 17 775 patients (47.2%) in the postintervention period. Health maintenance updates for patients with adenomas requiring closer surveillance increased significantly, from 83.4% (6672 of 8004 patients) to 94.2% (7913 of 8396 patients) following the intervention (P < .001). Gastroenterology team completion of health maintenance updates increased postintervention from 67.6% (5413 of 8004 patients) to 91.9% (7717 of 8396 patients). Conversely, primary care team updates decreased significantly from 9.3% (746 of 8004 patients) to 1.4% (118 of 8396 patients) following the intervention (P < .001 for both). Population health automatic updates occurred in a small number of patients in both periods.

Conclusions and relevance: Implementation of automatic updates to the health maintenance section of the EHR was associated with significantly increased the reliability of postadenoma surveillance documentation; after the intervention, gastroenterology reporting increased while the primary care burden was reduced. These findings suggest that clinical decision support implementation is critical for accurate adenoma surveillance intervals.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Inhaled Corticosteroids and Sickle Cell Disease Severity in Adults Without Asthma: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: People living with sickle cell disease (SCD) who have episodic cough and wheeze (ECW) without a diagnosis of asthma have high rates of pain episodes and acute chest syndrome. A previous trial, in which patients with SCD and ECW without asthma received 15 weeks of inhaled mometasone or placebo, showed that inhaled mometasone improved daily pain and reduced soluble vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1), a marker of disease severity in SCD.

Objective: To examine the biologic effects and safety of long-term daily inhaled mometasone in patients without asthma but with SCD and ECW.

Design, setting, and participants: This placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial recruited patients with SCD from December 2018 to May 2022. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either inhaled mometasone or placebo for 48 weeks. Data analyses followed the modified intention-to-treat principle and were performed between July and November 2023.

Interventions: The inhaled mometasone group received 220 μg of inhaled mometasone furoate dry powder once daily. The placebo group received a matching placebo inhaler.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was percentage change in soluble VCAM-1 levels from baseline to end of study. Secondary outcomes included laboratory results, functional outcomes, patient-reported outcomes, and health care utilization.

Results: Of the 77 patients who received the intervention and were included in the analysis, 40 were assigned to inhaled mometasone (mean [SD] age, 36.0 [11.6] years; 26 females [65%]) and 37 were assigned to placebo (mean [SD] age, 31.5 [8.6] years; 19 males [51%]). Compared with the placebo group, the inhaled mometasone group increased their soluble VCAM-1 levels by 42% (95% CI, -11% to 96%; P = .02). Point estimates for clinical outcomes favored the placebo group, although the findings were not statistically significant.

Conclusions and relevance: In this trial of adults with SCD and ECW, extended courses of inhaled mometasone were associated with worsened markers of disease severity. Inhaled mometasone should not be used long-term in patients with SCD and ECW without a definitive diagnosis of asthma.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03758950.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Ibuprofen Use and Acute Kidney Injury Among Adults Admitted to the Hospital
item.description:
Importance: Although nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the most effective nonopioid analgesics for acute pain, they may be underused in the inpatient setting due to uncertainty regarding the risk of acute kidney injury (AKI). Whether inpatient exposure to NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, substantially increases AKI risk and how ibuprofen-associated AKI varies across patient subgroups remain unknown.

Objective: To determine whether ibuprofen use is associated with AKI in hospitalized patients and whether the finding varies across AKI risk factor subgroups.

Design, setting, and participants: A retrospective active-comparator cohort study of hospitalized patients (aged ≥18 years) without end-stage kidney disease or contraindications to NSAID treatment admitted from January 1, 2004, to June 30, 2017, in a large academic health system including 3 hospitals in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, with follow-up until 48 hours after treatment end, hospital discharge, or 14 days elapsed, whichever occurred first. Analyses were conducted from March 2023 through August 2026.

Exposures: At least 24 hours of treatment with ibuprofen or oxycodone for acute pain.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was AKI, defined by changes in serum creatinine and incident kidney replacement therapy (KRT). Balancing weights were used to adjust for baseline covariates and weighted Poisson regression used to estimate incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% CIs.

Results: This study included 78 656 patients (median age, 59 [IQR, 47-69] years; 38 092 females [48%]) treated with ibuprofen (n = 6313) or oxycodone (n = 72 343). There were 4799 AKI events (79% stage 1) during 270 472 days of follow-up (17.7 events per 1000 days). After adjustment for baseline differences, patients treated with ibuprofen had a higher rate of any AKI (IRR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.09-1.38), severe AKI (IRR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.08-1.72), and KRT (IRR, 3.29; 95% CI, 1.35-8.03). IRRs were greater in postoperative (IRR, 1.70 [95% CI, 1.28-2.27] vs 1.12 [95% CI, 0.98-1.28]) and critically ill (IRR, 1.65 [95% CI, 1.29-2.11] vs 1.16 [95% CI, 1.02-1.33]) patients. In patients at low risk (those non-critically ill, nonpostoperative, aged <60 years without kidney dysfunction; ibuprofen, n = 2966; oxycodone, n = 20 440), ibuprofen was not associated with higher AKI risk (IRR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.75-1.18).

Conclusions and relevance: This study in an inpatient cohort found that ibuprofen was associated with higher rates of AKI and KRT, but this excess risk was concentrated in patients at high risk. Patients at low risk may be able to receive ibuprofen safely yet were often prescribed oxycodone.

Thelen HE, Keele LJ, Brotman C, Shashaty MGS, Miano TA

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: High-Sensitivity Troponin Pathway and Emergency Department Length of Stay
item.description:
Importance: High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays are the diagnostic standard for acute coronary syndrome but present significant implementation and workflow complexity.

Objective: To evaluate whether implementation of a structured, electronic health record (EHR)-integrated hs-cTn pathway was associated with changes in emergency department (ED) length of stay (LOS) and serial troponin testing times.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective quality improvement study compared preimplementation conventional cTn assay (June 1, 2021, to March 31, 2022) with a postimplementation integrated hs-cTn pathway (June 1, 2022, to March 31, 2023) in 4 urban EDs within a single health system. Participants were adults (aged ≥18 years) presenting with chest pain and at least 1 troponin assay result. Data analysis was performed from April to September 2024.

Exposures: Implementation of an hs-cTn assay within an EHR-integrated clinical pathway.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was ED LOS, defined as time from patient registration to ED departure. Secondary outcomes included time from first clinician evaluation to disposition (discharge or admission) and interval from the first troponin assay order to the second troponin assay result in patients with serial assays.

Results: Of the 16 094 patient encounters analyzed (9151 [56.9%] female; mean [SD] age, 49.5 [17.4] years), 8486 (52.7%) were in the hs-cTn and 7608 (47.3%) were in the conventional cTn cohort. Overall, hs-cTn implementation with workflow integration was associated with decreased mean ED LOS, from 6.18 (95% CI, 6.10-6.26) hours to 5.64 (95% CI, 5.57-5.71) hours. Compared with conventional cTn, implementation of the hs-cTn pathway was associated with shorter mean ED LOS in admitted patients (9.60 [95% CI, 9.35-9.87] hours vs 10.50 [95% CI, 10.22-10.78] hours; P = .003) and discharged patients (5.02 [95% CI, 4.96-5.08] hours vs 5.33 [95% CI, 5.26-5.40] hours; P = .006). Pathway implementation was also associated with shorter time from evaluation to disposition in patients receiving 2 or more troponin measurements (5.06 [95% CI, 4.97-5.15] hours vs 6.68 [95% CI, 6.52-6.85] hours; P < .001) and time from first troponin order to second troponin result in both admitted patients (3.18 [95% CI, 3.11-3.25] hours vs 5.16 [95% CI, 5.01-5.31] hours; P < .001) and discharged patients (2.78 [95% CI, 2.75-2.82] hours vs 4.54 [95% CI, 4.46-4.62] hours; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this quality improvement study, an EHR-integrated hs-cTn pathway was associated with significantly reduced ED LOS and, in patients with serial troponin measurements, reduced time from evaluation to disposition and reduced time to serial assay results. The findings suggest this structured EHR approach may mitigate operational challenges of hs-cTn adoption and could serve as a scalable model to improve ED efficiency for patients with chest pain.

Jia LZ, Israelyan N, Shofer FS, Saleh S, Moon J, Epps M

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Opioid Use and Overdose in Patients With Solid Tumor Cancers
item.description:
Importance: Opioids are essential for symptom control, but few studies have evaluated the association between prescription opioids and opioid overdose in oncology.

Objective: To describe opioid overdose in adults with solid tumor cancers and examine how opioid overdose rates vary by patient factors, cancer characteristics, and opioid prescribing.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based, retrospective cohort study of adults in Ontario, Canada, used linked ICES data from January 1, 2013, to December 31, 2020. Participants entered the cohort at the time of newly diagnosed solid tumor cancers and were followed up from diagnosis to the first opioid overdose event, death, or December 31, 2024. Data analysis was performed from August to December 2025.

Exposure: Exposure was outpatient opioid prescription dose and duration reassessed every 30 days.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was a fatal or the first nonfatal opioid overdose event.

Results: Among 554 316 adults with cancer (mean [SD] age, 63.8 [16.2], 57.1 [17.2], and 45.8 [13.7] years for the no, nonfatal, and fatal opioid overdose groups, respectively; 308 903 [55.9%], 921 [59.5%], and 116 [60.7%] female for the no, nonfatal, and fatal opioid overdose groups, respectively), 1591 (0.3%) had 1 or more nonfatal opioid overdoses, and 191 (0.03%) had a fatal opioid overdose. In the first year after diagnosis, patients with stage III and IV cancers had substantially higher rates of any opioid overdose than those with stage I (stage III vs I: hazard ratio [HR], 2.55; 95% CI, 1.96-3.31; stage IV vs I: HR, 6.24; 95% CI, 4.68-8.31). After adjustment, any opioid prescription in the prior 30 days was associated with 71% higher combined nonfatal and fatal opioid overdose rate (HR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.47-2.00), and approximately 3.5 times higher if prescribed high-dose opioids (≥50-mg morphine-equivalent daily dose; HR, 3.47; 95% CI, 2.97-4.05). Recently prescribed opioids were associated with increased opioid overdose risk in patients with cancer without opioid use disorder (any dose: HR, 1.80; 95% CI, 1.54-2.11; high dose: HR, 3.76; 95% CI, 3.21-4.41).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of adults with solid tumor cancers, opioid overdose was rare and highest in the first year after diagnosis and in patients with advanced cancer; opioid overdose risk increased with every month high-dose opioids were prescribed. The findings suggest that opioids should be prescribed at the lowest effective dose for symptom management, with close monitoring and routine assessment for opioid overdose risk.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Chemotherapy-Induced Biological Age Acceleration and Lifetime Outcomes in Breast Cancer Survivors
item.description:
Importance: Growing evidence suggests some breast cancer survivors may experience accelerated aging (biological age in excess of chronological age) after receiving chemotherapy.

Objective: To quantify the range of lifetime changes in accelerated aging following chemotherapy.

Design, setting, and participants: This comparative effectiveness study used an established Cancer Intervention and Surveillance Modeling Network breast cancer model integrating biological aging with breast cancer epidemiology. Biological aging was modeled using data on distributions of postchemotherapy senescence measured by p16INK4a levels, and the model assumed chemotherapy-induced senescence only affected non-breast cancer mortality. The simulated population included US women diagnosed with breast cancer at ages 30 to 79 years between 1990 and 2030, with follow-up until death. Two model simulations were run; the first assumed all women who developed breast cancer received anthracycline, and the second assumed all received nonanthracycline treatment. Modeling was conducted from November 2025 to April 2026. Results were validated by comparing model-predicted trends with findings from the Anthracycline for Early Breast Cancer (ABC) trials.

Exposures: More vs less cytotoxic chemotherapy, using exemplar anthracycline-based vs nonanthracycline regimens.

Main outcomes and measures: Lifetime outcomes included the age at which the risk of non-breast cancer mortality exceeded the risk of breast cancer mortality by chemotherapy regimen, posttreatment life-years, and all-cause mortality by age group at diagnosis and median senescence levels.

Results: The study included a simulated population of 400 million US women aged 30 to 79 years diagnosed with breast cancer. Breast cancer survivors who received anthracycline lost 9.4 (IQR, 7.6-11.2) years of remaining life years. Overall, among anthracycline recipients, the risk of non-breast cancer mortality was projected to exceed breast cancer mortality 16 (IQR, 12-19) years earlier than expected based on chronological age. There was heterogeneity in results, with greater variability for women diagnosed at younger vs older ages. Women receiving more vs less cytotoxic regimens were estimated to lose a median difference of 7.6 (IQR, 7.0-8.0) more years of life due to earlier ages at onset of aging-related diseases. The model closely replicated all-cause and 8-year breast cancer survival trends in the ABC trials.

Conclusions and relevance: In this simulation model of chemotherapy-induced biological aging, increased breast cancer survival was seen with more (vs less) cytotoxic regimens, but this was paired with greater potential risk of earlier non-breast cancer mortality due to age acceleration. These results suggest the value of integrating knowledge about biological aging into survivorship care and could inform future research to address accelerated aging among breast cancer survivors.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Differences in Health and Access to Care Between Heterosexual and Sexual Minority Health Care Professionals
item.description:
Importance: Little is known about the health and access to care of sexual minority health care professionals (HCPs).

Objective: To compare health outcomes, health insurance coverage, and access to care between sexual minority and heterosexual HCPs.

Design, setting, and participants: For this survey study, cross-sectional data analysis of the 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024 National Health Interview Surveys was performed. The study population included nationally representative household probability samples of noninstitutionalized US civilian adults aged 18 years or older, restricted to HCPs working in health care settings. Data analysis was conducted between February 2024 and August 2026.

Exposure: Self-reported sexual orientation, categorized as sexual minority (gay, lesbian, bisexual, or another nonheterosexual identity) or heterosexual.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes included cigarette smoking, lifetime diagnosis of depression, moderate to severe psychological distress, selected physical health conditions, primary source of health insurance coverage, and delayed or forgone medical care, mental health care, and prescription medications due to cost. Multivariable logistic regression models compared outcomes while adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics.

Results: The sample included 2890 HCPs (2731 heterosexual and 159 sexual minority; mean [SE] age, 44.9 [0.7] years; 74.7% [0.9%] female [survey weighted]). Sexual minority individuals represented 5.7% (95% CI, 4.8%-6.7%) of HCPs and were more likely to be younger (aged 26-34 years: 38.8% [95% CI, 30.1%-48.3%] vs 24.0% [95% CI, 22.2%-25.9%]), never married (32.7% [95% CI, 24.7%-41.8%] vs 14.6% [95% CI, 13.0%-16.4%]), and living in households below the federal poverty level (7.4% [95% CI, 3.4%-15.4%] vs 1.1% [95% CI, 0.7%-1.7%]) compared with heterosexual HCPs. Sexual minority HCPs were significantly more likely to report a lifetime diagnosis of depression (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 3.05 [95% CI, 2.02-4.59]), moderate to severe psychological distress (AOR, 2.06 [95% CI, 1.23-3.46]), arthritis (AOR, 2.45 [95% CI, 1.42-4.22]), and delayed medical care due to cost (AOR, 2.06 [95% CI, 1.14-3.72]). Sexual minority HCPs faced greater disparities in access to care: they were more likely to forgo mental health care (AOR, 3.74 [95% CI, 2.11-6.63]) and to forgo prescription medications (AOR, 4.81 [95% CI, 2.52-9.15]) due to cost than their heterosexual peers.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional survey study of HCPs, sexual minority HCPs were more likely than heterosexual HCPs to report depression, psychological distress, and financial barriers to health care. These findings highlight disparities in health and access to care among sexual minority HCPs and the need for workplace supports to address factors contributing to these disparities.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Social Determinants of Health and Long-Term, Device-Based Sleep Health
item.description:
Importance: Prior research on social determinants of health (SDOH) and sleep health has largely relied on subjective sleep measures, primarily self-reported sleep duration. Evidence remains limited on the associations between SDOH and wearable-derived long-term sleep patterns in large-scale populations.

Objective: To examine how SDOH (overall and by domain) are associated with long-term, wearable-derived sleep duration and variability.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study included participants from the All of Us Research Program enrolled between 2018 and 2023 who contributed at least 180 days of wearable data, including pre-enrollment historical records, and completed the SDOH survey. Data analysis was conducted from September 2025 to June 2026.

Exposures: Measures of overall and domain-specific SDOH, including social and community context, economic stability, neighborhood environment, and health care access and quality, were derived from validated surveys and standardized to z scores.

Main outcomes and measures: Mean daily sleep duration (in minutes) and day-to-day sleep duration SD across all available days were calculated from device-estimated main sleep episodes.

Results: Among 12 403 participants (mean [SD] age, 57.8 [15.2] years; 8719 female [70.3%]; 10 946 White [88.3%] and 1457 members of minority racial groups [11.7%]; 756 Hispanic [6.1%]), 9052 individuals (73.0%) had a college degree or above, with a mean (SD) sleep duration of 406.1 (44.9) minutes and a mean (SD) sleep duration SD of 76.9 (20.6) minutes. Participants were monitored for a median (range) of 982 (180 to 4133) days. Compared with participants in the lowest SDOH tertile, those in the highest tertile (indicating more favorable social and structural conditions) had 5.82 minutes (95% CI, 3.84 to 7.80 minutes) longer sleep duration and 4.79 minutes (95% CI, -5.69 to -3.89 minutes) lower sleep duration SD in the fully adjusted model. When examining individual SDOH domains, economic stability showed the strongest associations with mean sleep duration (eg, 10.70 minutes; 95% CI, 5.30 to 16.10 minutes) and sleep duration SD (eg, -8.70 minutes; 95% CI, -11.20 to -6.26 minutes). Limited subgroup heterogeneity in the association was observed across age, sex, race, and ethnicity.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, more favorable SDOH conditions were associated with longer and more regular habitual sleep duration over the long term, emphasizing the importance of social and structural factors when evaluating sleep health.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Efficacy and safety of oliceridine versus remifentanil for analgesia in mechanically ventilated critically ill adults (CO-ROAM): a multicenter, assessor-blinded, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial
item.description:
Purpose: Remifentanil provides effective analgesia during invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), but its utility is limited by opioid-related adverse events. Oliceridine, a G protein-biased μ-opioid receptor agonist, may decouple analgesia from these effects, but lacks evidence in critically ill patients.

Methods: This multicentre, assessor- and patient-blinded, non-inferiority randomised controlled trial was conducted across 19 intensive care units (ICUs) in China. Adults receiving IMV were randomised 1:1 to oliceridine or remifentanil, titrated to a Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool score below 3. The primary endpoint was time in target analgesic range (TTR; non-inferiority margin -10%).

Results: Of 307 randomised patients, 304 comprised the modified intention-to-treat population (151 oliceridine, 153 remifentanil). Median TTR was 96.0% versus 92.3% (absolute difference 3.7%, 95% CI -0.3-5.7%). Oliceridine was associated with fewer mild-to-moderate adverse drug reactions (ADRs), occurring at 15.9 versus 22.2 events per 100 patient-days (IRR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52-1.00, P = 0.049), and a lower rate of respiratory depression during the study period (0% vs. 4.6%, P = 0.015). Post-extubation respiratory depression (0% vs. 7.9%, P = 0.005) and analgesic-sedation costs were both lower with oliceridine. IMV duration, ICU stay, and 28-day mortality did not differ. Subgroup analyses identified a nominal ADR benefit in patients with Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II > 17 and a larger nominal TTR difference in those without acute respiratory distress syndrome.

Conclusion: Oliceridine provides non-inferior analgesia to remifentanil with a more favourable respiratory safety profile and lower costs in critically ill adults.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06454292 (registered June 11, 2024).

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Violent Reinjury Trajectories Across Injury Mechanisms: A Multicenter Cohort Study
item.description:
Study objective: Survivors of violent injury often experience reinjury. We sought to identify demographic and clinical factors associated with violent reinjury across different injury types.

Methods: We conducted an observational cohort study of individuals with violent injury (ie, blunt assaults, stabbings, and firearm injuries) across 2 adult and 2 pediatric Level I trauma centers from 2016 to 2023. Covariates included age, sex, race, hospital type, insurance status, and social vulnerability. Our primary outcome was time to reinjury. We used multivariable Cox proportional hazards models to measure associations between each covariate and time to reinjury across injury types.

Results: There were 29,038 individuals with nonfatal violent injuries. Male sex (n=19,273; 66.4%), Black and other race (n=21,403; 73.7%), presentation to adult hospitals (n=24,200; 83.3%), public insurance (n=13,879; 47.8%), and living in an area with high social vulnerability (n=21,044; 72.5%) were associated with a greater risk of any violent reinjury, adjusting for covariates. For index firearm injuries, patients younger than18 years had greater risk of firearm reinjury than patients aged 18 to 26 years (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]:0.65 [0.47 to 0.91]) and for those older than 26 years (aHR:0.47 [0.34 to 0.66]). Although women with firearm injury had a lower risk of firearm reinjury compared with men (aHR:0.46 [0.36 to 0.58]), they had greater risk of blunt reinjury (aHR:1.77 [1.34 to 1.24]). Patients living in areas with high social vulnerability had a higher risk of escalating reinjury mechanism (eg, blunt to firearm; aHR:1.46 [1.11 to 1.90]) versus patients in areas with low/average social vulnerability.

Conclusion: This research underscores how sequelae of violent reinjury are shaped by certain demographic and clinical characteristics, highlighting opportunities to strengthen reinjury prevention in key subgroups.

item.description:
A 55-year-old man was admitted with a 2-year history of recurrent dyspnea and exertional breathlessness, accompanied by intermittent blood-tinged sputum. During this period, he had been hospitalized 7 times at external institutions, where he underwent extensive investigations including fiberoptic bronchoscopy, endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration, mediastinoscopy, thoracoscopy, and CT imaging-guided biopsy of a mediastinal mass. Empirical antituberculosis therapy also was administered, but no definitive diagnosis was established.

item.title: Chest: A 63-Year-Old Man With Dyspnea and Loculated Pleural Effusion
item.description:
A 63-year-old man with a past medical history of hypertension and end-stage renal disease receiving scheduled hemodialysis via a left upper extremity fistula sought treatment for shortness of breath of 1 to 2 years' duration that worsened acutely for 1 day after missing a hemodialysis session. In addition, the patient reported mild central chest pain without radiation. He otherwise was in his usual state of health and did not report fevers, chills, cough, sputum production, wheezing, abdominal pain, or hemoptysis. He reported history of tobacco use, having smoked one-half a pack of cigarettes for 15 years and quit about 15 years ago.

item.title: Chest: Persistent Severe OSA Despite Ongoing CPAP Therapy
item.description:
A 51-year-old man was referred to our sleep medicine clinic for reevaluation of previously diagnosed OSA. The diagnosis had been established approximately 4 years earlier, at a body weight of 105 kg (BMI, 31.7 kg/m2). At that time, cardiorespiratory polygraphy documented severe OSA, with an apnea-hypopnea index of 97 events/h. Mean nocturnal oxygen saturation (Spo2) was 91%, and the cumulative time spent with Spo2 < 90% accounted for 38% of the total recording time, indicating a substantial nocturnal hypoxemic burden. Nocturnal CPAP therapy had been prescribed, delivered through an oronasal mask at a fixed pressure of 11 cm H2O.

item.title: Chest: Bilateral Pulmonary Nodules After Lung Transplantation: A Rare Diagnosis
item.description:
A 64-year-old man who underwent bilateral orthotopic lung transplant for emphysema related to α1-antitrypsin deficiency 8 months ago presented to the clinic for assessment of bilateral pulmonary nodules identified on routine postlung transplant surveillance without any symptomatic concerns. The donor was positive for cytomegalovirus and positive for Epstein-Barr virus, and the recipient was negative for cytomegalovirus and positive for Epstein-Barr virus. He denied any fever, chills, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, weight loss, or night sweats. The patient lived in South Florida with no recent travel history outside the United States or infectious contacts. His posttransplant course was complicated with antibody-mediated rejection at 1.5 months after lung transplant. Antibody-mediated rejection was successfully treated with our institutional multimodal regimen, including a combination of plasmapheresis, carfilzomib, and anti-thymocyte globulin followed by monthly IV immunoglobulin and tocilizumab injections. Also, because of calcineurin inhibitor (CNI)-related renal dysfunction, the patient's immunosuppression was converted to a belatacept-based CNI-sparing regimen in addition to prednisone, with a tacrolimus goal trough of 4 to 6 ng/mL. He was also placed on mycophenolic acid, which was soon held because of neutropenia.

item.title: Chest: A Young Man With Hypereosinophilia and Pseudochylothorax
item.description:
A 31-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dry cough, progressive dyspnea, intermittent fever, and unintentional weight loss of 8 kg. He had no wheezing, hemoptysis, chest pain, palpitations, or skin rashes. He did not smoke and reported occasional alcohol intake. One year earlier, he had been diagnosed elsewhere with pleuro-pericardial TB based on an ultrasound showing right-sided pleural effusion, and 2-dimensional echocardiography showed pericardial effusion. Pleural fluid analysis showed a lymphocytic exudative pleural effusion with elevated adenosine deaminase levels (46 IU/mL). The patient received anti-tubercular therapy along with tapering corticosteroids, showing initial clinical improvement. He was employed as a soldier in the army, and his last posting was in northeast India, where he frequently consumed raw crabs pickled in alcohol. There was no other significant environmental history.

item.title: Lancet: Cardiovascular outcomes with survodutide in adults with obesity at increased cardiovascular risk (SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
item.description:
Background: Survodutide, a glucagon receptor and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, improved markers of cardiometabolic health in people with obesity, but cardiovascular safety for this new class remains to be established.

Methods: SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT was a global, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, multicentre, event-driven, cardiovascular safety trial conducted at 524 clinical sites in 34 countries. We included participants aged 18 years or older with a BMI of 27 kg/m2 or greater and established cardiovascular disease or at least two obesity complications or risk factors for cardiovascular disease; participants with chronic kidney disease were eligible if they also had a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or greater. Participants were randomly assigned by interactive response technology (1:1:1) to once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide (up-titrated to 3·6 mg or 6·0 mg) or placebo. The primary endpoint was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event (targeting 189 primary endpoint events). We assessed the non-inferiority of pooled survodutide compared with placebo with a margin of 1·65 for the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI of the hazard ratio (HR). Efficacy and safety analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of survodutide or placebo. The primary analysis was performed according to the treatment-regimen estimand, which assessed treatment effects regardless of any early discontinuation of survodutide or placebo, temporary stop, the use of protocol-prohibited obesity medications, or a prolonged dose-escalation period. This completed trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06077864.

Findings: From Nov 20, 2023, to Nov 8, 2024, we screened 7753 participants, of whom 5530 (71·3%) participants were recruited and randomly assigned to treatment. 23 (0·4%) participants were not treated; 1836 (33·3%) of 5507 participants received survodutide 3·6 mg, 1835 (33·3%) received 6·0 mg, and 1836 (33·3%) received placebo; 2194 (39·8%) were female, 3313 (60·2%) were male, and 4332 (78·7%) were White. Median time in study was 22·0 months (IQR 20·1-23·7). 1029 (56·0%) in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 1039 (56·6%) in the survodutide 6·0 mg group, and 1083 (59·0%) in the placebo group remained on treatment until study closeout. The primary endpoint occurred in 136 (3·7%) of 3671 participants in the survodutide group and in 76 (4·1%) 1836 participants in the placebo group (HR 0·89 [95% CI 0·67-1·18; p<0·0001 for non-inferiority). Adverse events occurred in 1708 (93·0%) of 1836 participants with survodutide 3·6 mg, 1708 (93·1%) of 1835 with survodutide 6·0 mg, and 1571 (85·6%) of 1836 with placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with survodutide than in the placebo group (nausea occurred in 882 [48·0%] of 1836 participants in the 3·6 mg group and 900 [49·0%] of 1835 in the 6·0 mg group vs 223 [12·1%] of 1836 in the placebo group, and vomiting occurred in 582 [31·7%] participants in the 3·6 mg group and 623 [34·0%] in the 6·0 mg group vs 89 [4·8%] in the placebo group). Gastrointestinal adverse events leading to treatment discontinuations occurred in 354 (19·3%) participants in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 381 (20·8%) in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 34 (1·9%) in the placebo group. Serious adverse events occurred at similar rates across treatment groups (413 [22·5%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 381 [20·8%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 439 [23·9%] in the placebo group). Fatal adverse events were similar across treatment groups (16 [0·9%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 16 [0·9%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 11 [0·6%] in the placebo group) and were primarily due to cardiac disorders (six [0·3%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, seven [0·4%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and six [0·3%] in the placebo group).

Interpretation: In participants with obesity with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease or at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, survodutide was not associated with increased risk for the primary composite endpoint of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event compared with placebo. This cardiovascular safety trial provides clinicians with reassuring data that treatment with survodutide, a novel glucagon receptor-GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, is not associated with increased cardiovascular risk.

Funding: Boehringer Ingelheim.

Bozkurt B, le Roux CW, Wharton S, Butt JH, Startseva E, Sumin M

item.title: Lancet: Efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and stage 2-3 fibrosis: a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled study
item.description:
Background: Efinopegdutide is a pharmacologically distinct once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist with a relative receptor potency balance of approximately 2:1 under development for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). We aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with non-cirrhotic MASH.

Methods: We did a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind study conducted at 176 academic and community centres in 26 countries. We included adults (aged ≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage 2 or stage 3 fibrosis. Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1:1) to receive either efinopegdutide (4 mg, 7 mg, or 10 mg), placebo, or open-label semaglutide 2·4 mg, all administered subcutaneously once weekly. Randomisation was performed centrally. The primary endpoint was MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis at week 52. The key secondary histological endpoint was fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis. Missing end-of-treatment biopsies were considered as failure for the primary analysis. This study is registered with EU CT, 2022-502647-35-00, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05877547, and is complete.

Findings: Between June 23, 2023, and Dec 29, 2025, we screened 1704 participants. We randomly assigned 386 (23%) participants, of whom 381 (99%; 194 [51%] women and 187 [49%] men) received at least one dose of study intervention and were included in the analysis. Baseline characteristics were similar across groups; 239 (63%) of 381 participants had F2 fibrosis and 142 (37%) had F3 fibrosis; the mean age of participants was 53 years (SD 13). At week 52, MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 31 (56%) of 55 participants in the 4 mg efinopegdutide group, 31 (63%) of 49 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 35 (61%) of 57 participants in the 10 mg efinopegdutide group versus seven (13%) of 53 participants in the placebo group (difference vs placebo 43·0 percentage points [95% CI 25·7 to 57·8; p<0·0001] for 4 mg, 49·5 percentage points [31·4 to 64·2; p<0·0001] for 7 mg, and 47·8 percentage points [30·7 to 62·0; p<0·0001] for 10 mg); 26 (53%) of 49 participants receiving semaglutide met this endpoint. For the key secondary endpoint, fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis occurred in 32 (43%) of 75 participants in the efinopegdutide 4 mg group, 39 (52%) of 75 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 26 (34%) of 77 participants in the efinopegdutide 10 mg group versus 16 (21%) of 77 participants receiving placebo (difference vs placebo 21·7 percentage points [7·1 to 35·7; p=0·0038] in the efinopegdutide 4 mg group, 30·4 percentage points [15·4 to 44·3; p<0·0001] in the efinopegdutide 7 mg group, and 13·0 percentage points [-1·2 to 26·8; p=0·072] in the efinopegdutide 10 mg group); 16 (25%) of 65 participants receiving semaglutide met this endpoint. The most frequently reported adverse events with efinopegdutide were gastrointestinal, with the highest rates among participants receiving efinopegdutide 10 mg. Adverse events leading to discontinuation of study intervention occurred more frequently among participants receiving efinopegdutide 10 mg (nine [11%] of 79 participants) compared with the other doses of efinopegdutide (range 3-4%) or placebo (one [1%]).

Interpretation: Treatment with efinopegdutide resulted in a significantly greater proportion of participants with MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis compared with placebo. The 7 mg dose showed the most favourable benefit-risk profile, improving fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis in approximately half of participants after 1 year of treatment. These findings support the potential utility of efinopegdutide as a once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist in MASH.

Funding: Merck Sharp & Dohme, a subsidiary of Merck & Co.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade in geriatric patients with multiple rib fractures and flail chest: A national analysis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: It remains unclear whether direct ICU admission benefits geriatric patients compared with delayed floor-to-ICU upgrade. The study evaluated the association of direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade with clinical outcomes in geriatric trauma patients with flail chest and thoracic injury, stratified by oxygenation compromise, frailty, and rib fracture burden.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study used the 2017-2024 ACS-TQIP-PUF to identify patients aged 65 years or older with blunt trauma, flail chest, at least three rib fractures, an Injury Severity Score of 9 or greater, and thoracic injury. Patients were classified as floor admission without ICU upgrade, direct ICU admission, or floor-to-ICU upgrade. The primary adjusted analysis compared direct ICU admission with floor-to-ICU upgrade, using floor-to-ICU upgrade as the reference group.

Results: A total of 6743 patients were included. Mortality did not differ significantly between direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade in the primary adjusted analysis (aOR 0.732, 95% CI 0.467-1.148, p = 0.174). Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation (aOR 0.355, 95% CI 0.251-0.502, p < 0.001), ARDS (aOR 0.412, 95% CI 0.172-0.987, p = 0.047), sepsis (aOR 0.352, 95% CI 0.171-0.725, p = 0.005), and DVT (aOR 0.444, 95% CI 0.209-0.942, p = 0.034). Mortality was lower with direct ICU admission among patients with 3-5 documented rib fractures (aOR 0.535, 95% CI 0.296-0.969, p = 0.039), and the association with fewer unplanned intubations persisted across all subgroups. In the secondary analysis, both direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade were associated with higher mortality, lower odds of discharge home, and fewer ventilator-free days than floor admission without ICU upgrade.

Conclusion: Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation, ARDS, sepsis, and DVT compared with floor-to-ICU upgrade. These findings support identifying at-risk geriatric rib fracture patients for direct ICU admission before deterioration occurs.

Nasef Y, Nishida C, Bundschu I, Hus A, Kumar S, Rogers L

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Cost and operational impact of a molecular point-of-care test for sexually transmitted infections in the emergency department
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Female patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with suspected sexually transmitted infections (STIs) have historically been evaluated using centralized laboratory testing (CLT), with results unavailable during the visit. Point-of-care (POC) tests enable real-time diagnosis but have higher direct costs than CLT.

Objective: To compare hospital and societal costs of CLT and POC STI testing (chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomonas) among female ED patients with suspected infection, and to assess effects on underdiagnosis, overtreatment, undertreatment, and ED recidivism.

Design: Decision analysis through cost tables using data from a pre-post implementation study.

Setting: Large urban academic ED (Johns Hopkins Hospital).

Interventions: CLT (nucleic acid amplification test [NAAT]/wet preparation) versus molecular POC STI testing.

Measurements: Direct testing costs, follow-up costs for informing patients after discharge, costs of overtreatment/undertreatment, and ED return visits within 30 days. Analyses were conducted from hospital and societal perspectives over 12-month horizon.

Results: Direct POC testing costs for 1000 women exceeded CLT by $16,502. This difference was not offset by lower follow-up costs for undertreatment or by societal costs of under- or overtreatment. From the hospital perspective, costs may be offset by increased margins from maximizing ED Examination room utilization. Threshold analysis shows room time need not be fully occupied, nor margins equal full revenue, to achieve net revenue gain.

Conclusions: POC testing for STIs, given current pricing and unchanged reimbursement, increases societal costs and reduces hospital revenue versus CLT. However, EDs and hospitals may increase net revenue, by improved patient throughput thereby generating revenue if ED wait times are long.

Paul-Ledesma A, Dashler G, Hsieh YH, Maliszewski K, Saheed M, Mann E

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Predicting survival in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Development and internal validation of risk scores
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in the pediatric population is associated with poor survival and neurological outcomes. We aimed to develop and internally validate risk scores to predict survival to discharge in pediatric OHCA patients.

Methods: We included pediatric OHCA patients in the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival from 2013 to 2023. We used logistic regression (LR) and classification and regression trees (CART) to develop risk scores using 70% of the data and validated them using the remaining 30% of the data. We used discrimination and predictive accuracy to evaluate model performance.

Results: We included 26,895 pediatric patients, of whom 27.8% survived to hospital admission and 11.9% survived to hospital discharge. We developed three separate risk scores for i) infants ii) preschool and school-age children, and iii) adolescents. The most important predictor variables were gender, arrest location, witness status, etiology of arrest, bystander CPR, use of prehospital AED, and first rhythm. Models developed using both LR and CART approaches had good classification accuracy (AUROCC for LR: 0.81, 0.77 and 0.82, AUROCC for CART: 0.78, 0.76, 0.82 for the three age groups) However, we found CART models to be the most useful because they are simpler to follow, classified more patients in low and high survival categories using a smaller number of predictors. The average survival probability in infants for each risk group was 3%, 13%, and 33%, for preschool and school-age children it was 4%, 11%, and 29%, whereas for adolescents it was 4%, 13%, and 48% for the low, moderate, and high survival categories.

Conclusion: Pediatric patients experiencing OHCA can be classified into low, moderate, and high survival categories using a simple risk score and easily identified prehospital variables. These risk scores can facilitate research, monitor the quality of medical services and can potentially support clinical decision-making.

Mawani M, McNally B, Knight J, Shen Y, Ebell M

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Integration of multimodal large language models into point-of-care ultrasound documentation: A pilot study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: There are no studies evaluating the potential to deploy artificial intelligence in the interpretation of cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) documentation. Telexy Health developed an image interpretation and documentation system using multimodal model extensions with video capabilities (MLLM) and deployed it on the POCUS manager QpathE. This study evaluated the MLLM's agreement to experts in identifying cardiac POCUS views and interpreting normal and abnormal examinations.

Methods: This was a retrospective pilot study using cardiac POCUS studies stored in QPathE. The MLLM was applied to POCUS examinations until 350 examinations were reached, 100 normal, and 250 with pathology. MLLM view identification and interpretation were recorded using Qualtrics, with expert image review serving as the gold standard.

Results: The MLLM was applied to 370 examinations, with 20 failures. View identification agreed with expert review in 151 examinations (43.1%). Cohen's kappa showed fair agreement for apical four-chamber views between expert and MLLM, with moderate agreement for parasternal long axis, parasternal short axis, subxiphoid, and inferior vena cava views. The MLLM agreed with expert interpretation 86 of 100 normal examinations; the agreement varied by pathology with pericardial effusion, ejection fraction, aortic outflow tract, chamber size, and inferior vena cava having an agreement of 8%, 4%, 70%, 0%, and 12% respectively.

Conclusion: While agreement in image interpretation was poor, this vendor agnostic workflow demonstrated the ability to integrate an MLLM model into image interpretation. While it should not be incorporated into clinical practice in this state, future model improvement may enable automated POCUS interpretation and documentation.

item.title: Ann Intern Med: Doxycycline and Risk for Pregnancy Loss : A Multi-database, Multi-indication Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: Doxycycline is commonly prescribed to reproductive-aged women, but evidence about safety during pregnancy is limited.

Objective: To evaluate the risk for pregnancy loss after doxycycline exposure in the first trimester.

Design: Retrospective active-comparator cohort study.

Setting: Merative MarketScan commercial (2005-2021) and Medicaid (1999-2019) claims data.

Participants: Pregnancies ending in loss or live birth among women aged 12 to 55 years.

Intervention: 3 cohorts of pregnancies with first-trimester oral doxycycline or comparator antibiotic prescription fills and concomitant diagnoses of respiratory tract infection (RTI) or acne.

Measurements: Pregnancy loss was evaluated using validated algorithms. Doxycycline-exposed pregnancies were matched on propensity score and gestational age to comparator pregnancies (exposed to amoxicillin or a macrolide for RTI or topical clindamycin for acne). Adjusted risk differences and adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) were estimated via binomial and modified Poisson regression separately for each database and comparison.

Results: The study included 218 234 pregnant participants with RTI (110 254 in MarketScan, 107 980 in Medicaid) and 6636 with acne (4719 in MarketScan, 1917 in Medicaid). Among those with RTI, doxycycline use was associated with an increased risk for pregnancy loss compared with amoxicillin use (MarketScan aRR, 1.54 [95% CI, 1.41 to 1.68]; Medicaid aRR, 1.40 [CI, 1.28 to 1.53]). Results were similar for the comparison with macrolides (MarketScan aRR, 1.39 [CI, 1.28 to 1.51]; Medicaid aRR, 1.36 [CI, 1.25 to 1.48]). Among patients with acne, the comparison with topical clindamycin was statistically significant in MarketScan (aRR, 1.49 [CI, 1.26 to 1.76]) but not Medicaid (aRR, 1.03 [CI, 0.80 to 1.33]). Among cohorts with statistically significant aRRs, risk differences ranged between 7 and 11 percentage points.

Limitation: Residual confounding and exposure or outcome misclassification are possible, and congenital malformations were not evaluated.

Conclusion: Doxycycline use for RTI or acne during early pregnancy was associated with an increased risk for pregnancy loss. Clinicians may use this information to weigh risks and benefits when prescribing doxycycline to reproductive-aged women.

Primary funding source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Emergency Response and Patient Transport in Remote Indigenous Communities: A Scoping Review
item.description:
Objectives: Prehospital and inter-facility transport, such as air medical retrieval and pre-birth evacuation, often move Indigenous patients in rural and remote settings out of their communities, where care is already shaped by fragmented funding and structural inequities; no review has mapped these pathways globally. This scoping review mapped evidence on prehospital emergency response and patient transport for this population.

Methods: A librarian-assisted PubMed, Embase, and Scopus search was conducted for English-language publications on March 9, 2026. Eligible studies included an explicit rural Indigenous population with a defined prehospital pathway. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts, and a third reviewer resolved disagreements. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively.

Results: Across eight countries, 76 studies met the inclusion criteria, primarily from Australia (n = 29) and Canada (n = 23). Air transport and medical evacuation was the most frequently described pathway (71%), followed by ground transport (51%). Explicit description of paramedic or emergency medical services (24%) and dispatch/9-1-1 (12%) were depicted less frequently. Additionally, pathways were commonly described but rarely evaluated: only 12/76 (16%) publications used an evaluative design, and no pathway was evaluated in more than 7 of 76 publications (9%). The most reported barriers were infrastructure and communications (92%), cost and jurisdiction (87%), and distance to definitive care (83%). All percentages describe how often a topic was reported across the 76 included publications, and not its prevalence in practice. An explicit cultural-safety framework was applied in 9% of the publications, and community-led governance of the research in 7%.

Conclusions: The published evidence disproportionately described transporting patients out of their communities. Community first response and tele-support were described more often than their standing in the literature suggests; however, they were rarely evaluated, and Indigenous-led governance of the research itself was reported in 7% of publications. Low reporting frequency does not establish that these models are uncommon in application and practice. Future priorities include community-partnered evaluation of community-based capacity and telehealth-supported care, alongside the development of patient and family cultural safety.

item.title: JAMA Intern Med: Reducing Low-Value Care Through the Smarter Care Virginia Initiative
item.description:
Importance: Low-value care costs more than $100 billion annually and remains pervasive despite decades of evidence documenting its clinical and financial harms. While several US states have begun discouraging its use, the feasibility of such statewide interventions in partnership with large health systems remains unknown.

Objective: To investigate the effectiveness of a clinician-led, multistakeholder, statewide initiative to reduce low-value care in the Commonwealth of Virginia.

Design, setting, and participants: This quality improvement study used a difference-in-differences analyses comparing low-value service changes among patients attributed to 6 health systems vs 12 control systems in the Commonwealth of Virginia preintervention (January 1 to December 31, 2019) vs postintervention (January 1 to December 31, 2022). Any patient eligible to receive 1 or more of the 9 measured low-value services in the 18 health systems evaluated were included. Data were analyzed between December 1, 2023, and September 1, 2026.

Exposure: The intervention, Smarter Care Virginia, included health system financial support, clinician education, and quarterly peer-comparison performance scorecards.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the percentage of patients receiving any of 9 selected low-value services: (1-3) preoperative laboratory, imaging, and cardiac testing; (4-5) electrocardiogram/cardiac screening and cardiac stress testing; (6-7) diagnostic imaging and opioids for acute back pain; (8) advanced diagnostic eye imaging; and (9) peripherally inserted central catheter lines for patients with chronic kidney disease. Secondary outcomes included adverse events (eg, myocardial infarction-related hospitalization) and per-capita spending on the 9 low-value services.

Results: A total of 17 223 clinicians (7222 in the intervention group and 10 001 in the control group) and 4.5 million patients (approximately 68% of Virginia's adult population) were identified. In 2019, 10.5% of patients in the intervention group and 10.7% of patients in the control group received 1 or more low-value services; in 2021 to 2022, rates declined to 8.5% and 9.1%, respectively. The intervention was associated with 10.4% fewer patients receiving 1 or more low-value services (absolute reduction, -1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.1 to -0.1 percentage points; P = .04). There was no statistically significant change in adverse events (0.03%; 95% CI, -0.02% to 0.03%; P = .84) or spending on the 9 low-value services ($0.33; 95% CI, -$3.43 to $4.11).

Conclusions and relevance: In this quality improvement study, a statewide, clinician-led initiative was associated with a small but statistically significant reduction in low-value care delivery without evidence of harm. Achieving larger reductions may require combining such health system-driven efforts with additional strategies, such as payment reform and physician and hospital accountability, that discourage the use of low-value care.

item.title: JAMA Intern Med: Drug Burden Index Stewardship to Deprescribe Anticholinergic or Sedative Drugs in Older Inpatients: A Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Anticholinergic and sedative medications contribute to poor clinical outcomes in older inpatients. Evidence-based deprescribing strategies are needed.

Objective: To evaluate whether an intervention bundle increases deprescribing of anticholinergic and sedative medications in older inpatients.

Design, setting, and participants: This stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 6 Australian public hospitals from January 2022 to July 2023. Participants were patients 65 years and older with Drug Burden Index (DBI; a measure of anticholinergic and sedative medication exposure) score greater than 0 at admission and hospitalized for 48 hours or more. Data were analyzed from October 2023 to May 2026.

Interventions: The intervention bundle had 2 components. The informational component (automated DBI score calculation displayed in the electronic medical record, deprescribing guides, patient leaflets, and education module) was present in all trial phases, although clinicians were not informed of it during the control phase. The stewardship component (study stewardship pharmacists who promoted the informational component and made patient-level deprescribing recommendations to attending teams) was delivered in the intervention phase. The informational component was promoted 1 to 2 times monthly during the sustainability phase.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with 1 or more DBI-contributing medications deprescribed (ceased or dose reduced) at discharge compared with admission. Secondary outcomes included deprescribing recommendations in discharge summaries and in-hospital adverse events.

Results: Among 4827 included patients, 2798 (58.0%) were female, and the median (IQR) age was 83.0 (76.0-88.0) years. The proportion of patients with 1 or more DBI-contributing medications deprescribed was 38.1% (788 of 2069) in the control phase, 41.4% (326 of 788) in the intervention phase, and 37.0% (729 of 1970) in the sustainability phase. The adjusted absolute difference (aAD) between intervention and control was 5.3 percentage points (95% CI, 0.1-10.6), smaller than hypothesized. Deprescribing was predominantly by cessation; in the intervention phase, 256 of 788 patients (32.5%) had 1 or more DBI-contributing medications ceased, 91 (11.5%) had 1 or more doses reduced, and 21 (2.7%) had both. The aAD between the sustainability and intervention phase estimates was -5.3 percentage points (95% CI, -10.9 to 0.3). Deprescribing recommendations in discharge summaries were more prevalent in the intervention (176 of 751 admissions [23.4%]) than the control phase (287 of 1968 admissions [14.6%]; aAD, 10.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.0-15.1) and were lower in the sustainability phase (362 of 1910 [19.0%]; aAD, -4.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -8.7 to 0.8). In-hospital adverse events were similar across phases.

Conclusions and relevance: In this stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial, the intervention bundle increased deprescribing less than hypothesized, and the increase was not sustained once the stewardship component ended.

Trial registration: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12622000374763.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Inforatio Technique and Foot Ulcer Closure Among Patients With Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are common complications of diabetes, a disease increasing in prevalence worldwide. Novel adjunctive treatments that are affordable and feasible to implement in both high- and low-income settings are urgently needed.

Objective: To assess whether the inforatio technique promotes healing of DFUs compared with standard of care (SOC).

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter, evaluator-blinded randomized clinical trial was conducted at 4 outpatient clinics specializing in wound care in Denmark from February 15, 2022, to December 18, 2024. One-year medical record follow-up was completed August 14, 2025. Participants included patients with noninfected Wagner grade 1 DFUs.

Interventions: Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive the inforatio technique every third week for 12 weeks with SOC or SOC only. The inforatio technique involved making incisions on wound beds with 2-mm biopsy punch tools.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the proportion of ulcers achieving closure within 20 weeks. Secondary outcomes were health-related and disease-specific quality of life. Safety outcomes included serious and target ulcer-related adverse events.

Results: A total of 101 patients were randomized, of whom 100 had DFUs and were included in the primary analysis (49 in the inforatio group and 51 in the SOC only group; 85 men; mean [SD] age, 64.4 [11.4] years; median ulcer size, 0.76 [range, 0.09-23.23] cm2). Twenty-four patients in the inforatio group (49.0%) vs 14 in the SOC-only group (27.5%) achieved ulcer closure within 20 weeks (adjusted odds ratio, 3.01 [95% CI, 1.20-7.58]; P = .02). No between-group difference was found in quality of life change from baseline to 20 weeks. Within 20 weeks, 7 patients in the inforatio group vs 13 in the SOC-only group experienced the serious adverse events, including death, amputation, or target ulcer-related hospitalization (relative risk, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.24-1.29]; P = .25), and 16 patients in the inforatio group vs 30 in the SOC-only group experienced target ulcer-related adverse events (relative risk, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.88]; P = .02).

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial, the inforatio technique improved DFU healing compared with SOC alone. Fewer ulcer-related adverse events were also observed with the inforatio technique, although this exploratory finding should be interpreted cautiously.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05189470.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Neighborhood Social Disadvantage and Lung Aging and Mortality
item.description:
Importance: Neighborhood social disadvantage (NSD) is increasingly recognized as being associated with health disparities. However, its associations with longitudinal lung function decline, health-related quality of life (HRQOL), and mortality remain incompletely understood.

Objective: To evaluate associations of NSD with lung function, HRQOL, and all-cause mortality and to explore potential mediators of any association.

Design, setting, and participants: Prospective cohort study of current and former smokers aged 40 to 75 years with at least 10 pack-years of smoking history in the Lovelace Smokers Cohort. Participants underwent repeated spirometry approximately every 18 months from 2001 through 2017. Mortality was ascertained through October 2020 using the National Death Index. Data were analyzed from January to May 2025.

Exposures: Census tract-level Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and Social Deprivation Index (SDI) assigned to residential addresses.

Main outcomes and measures: Baseline and longitudinal lung function (forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1], forced vital capacity [FVC], and the FEV1:FVC ratio), baseline HRQOL assessed by the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), with higher scores indicating poorer respiratory health status, and the 36-item Short Form Survey, and all-cause mortality. Formal mediation analyses evaluated educational attainment, current smoking status, and dietary patterns, whereas baseline lung function and HRQOL were considered as potential mediators for associations of NSD with all-cause mortality.

Results: Among 2362 included participants, the mean (SD) baseline age was 56.3 (9.4) years, and 1738 (73.58%) were female. A 1-IQR increase in SDI was associated with lower baseline FEV1 (β, -0.09 [95% CI, -0.13 to -0.06] L) and FEV1:FVC ratio (β, -1.21 [95% CI, -1.80 to -0.62] percentage points). Higher SVI was associated with faster annual decline in FEV1 (β, -3.11 [95% CI, -5.86 to -0.36] mL/y) and FEV1:FVC ratio (β, -0.05 [95% CI, -0.11 to -0.001] percentage points/y), worse baseline HRQOL, including a higher SGRQ total score (β, 4.46 [95% CI, 3.26-5.65] points), and higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.08-1.53]). Current smoking status and 2 dietary pattern scores mediated 4.4% (95% CI, -1.2% to 12.8%) to 31.0% (95% CI, 13.0%-51.6%) and 4.5% (95% CI, 0.2%-12.9%) to 17.0% (95% CI, 5.5%-113.7%), respectively, of selected associations between NSD and lung health outcomes; baseline lung function and HRQOL mediated 6.7% (95% CI, 0.6%-22.8%) to 38.6% (95% CI, 19.9%-125.3%) of selected associations with all-cause mortality.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, worse NSD was associated with faster lung function decline, worse HRQOL, and higher all-cause mortality among ever smokers. Mediation analyses suggested that current smoking status and dietary patterns may partially account for associations of NSD with lung function and HRQOL.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Perioperative Antibiotic Use in Head and Neck Surgery
item.description:
Importance: Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis in head and neck surgery remains poorly standardized internationally, despite evidence supporting short-course regimens and showing no benefit in low-risk procedures. Contemporary international data on prescribing practice are limited.

Objectives: To characterize international patterns of perioperative antibiotic use in endocrine and oncologic head and neck surgery and to identify discrepancies between reported practice and evidence-based recommendations.

Design, setting, and participants: In this survey study, a cross-sectional survey was distributed electronically between October 1, 2024, and December 31, 2025, through national and international professional societies. Respondents were classified by country of practice into Europe, North America, and rest of world. Data were analyzed in June 2026.

Main outcomes and measures: Routine antibiotic use, agent selection, and duration of prophylaxis across 6 procedure categories (conventional thyroidectomy, completion thyroidectomy, complex thyroidectomy, low-risk head and neck squamous cell carcinoma [HNSCC], low-complexity HNSCC, and complex clean-contaminated HNSCC). Secondary outcomes were departmental guideline availability and circumstances prompting antibiotic use.

Results: Of 468 respondents (310 of 419 [74%] with available data reported male sex or gender, 32 of 432 [82%] otolaryngologists-head and neck surgeons and 283 of 431 [66%] in academic practice), routine antibiotic use for conventional thyroidectomy was reported by 12% (95% CI, 8%-19%) of European, 35% (95% CI, 27%-44%) of North American, and 56% (95% CI, 39%-71%) of rest of world respondents. For clean-contaminated HNSCC, prophylaxis use ranged from 93% to 99%, with aminopenicillin plus a β-lactamase inhibitor preferred in Europe (66%) and North America (64%); cefazolin predominated in North America (47%) and cefuroxime in Europe (31%). For low-complexity clean-contaminated procedures, 24-hour regimens were reported by 43% (95% CI, 34%-53%) of North American vs 11% (95% CI, 7%-16%) of European respondents, whereas 7-day courses were reported by 23% (95% CI, 17%-29%) of European vs 8% (95% CI, 4%-15%) of North American respondents. Departmental HNSCC guidelines were more available in Europe than North America (83% vs 38%).

Conclusions and relevance: In this survey study of 468 head and neck surgeons, perioperative antibiotic prescribing was heterogeneous internationally, with routine use in clean procedures and prolonged regimens for clean-contaminated surgery. Departmental guideline availability did not correspond to shorter reported prophylaxis duration, suggesting that implementation rather than guideline existence may be the target for antimicrobial stewardship.

item.title: N Engl J Med: ANGPTL4 Inhibition in Adults with Elevated Triglyceride Levels
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Angiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4) inhibits lipoprotein lipase and regulates triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism. MAR001 is a monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL4 that is being evaluated for lowering triglyceride levels.

Methods: We conducted a two-part, phase 2b, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. In part A, the focus of this report, we enrolled adults who had a nonfasting triglyceride level of at least 175 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 35 mg per deciliter at initial screening, followed by a fasting triglyceride level of at least 150 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 30 mg per deciliter on confirmatory screening. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to receive MAR001 at a dose of 300, 450, or 900 mg or matching placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 24 weeks. The primary end point was the percent change from baseline in the fasting triglyceride level at week 12, reported as the difference between each MAR001 dose group and the placebo group (placebo-adjusted change).

Results: A total of 236 participants were enrolled in the trial, with 177 assigned to receive MAR001 and 59 to receive placebo; a total of 235 participants received at least one dose of MAR001 or placebo and were included in the primary efficacy analyses. The mean age of the participants was 60.4 years, and 39% were women. The median triglyceride level at baseline was 249.5 mg per deciliter (interquartile range, 210.0 to 313.0). At week 12, in an intention-to-treat analysis, the placebo-adjusted least-squares mean percent changes in the fasting triglyceride level were -39.1 percentage points, -40.5 percentage points, and -45.3 percentage points for the 300-mg, 450-mg, and 900-mg doses, respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons). Adverse events occurred in 123 of 177 participants (69%) in the pooled MAR001 group and in 45 of 58 participants (78%) in the placebo group.

Conclusions: Inhibition of ANGPTL4 with MAR001 significantly reduced fasting triglyceride levels at 12 weeks. (Funded by Marea Therapeutics; TYDAL-TIMI 78 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT07028749.).

item.title: JAMA: Orforglipron for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Results From 2 Randomized Clinical Trials (ATTAIN-OSA)
item.description:
Importance: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder characterized by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep that is associated with reduced quality of life and increased incidence of cardiometabolic disease.

Objective: To assess the effects of orforglipron on moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity or overweight, compared with placebo.

Design, setting, and participants: Two 52-week, phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials were conducted at 66 sites in the US, Argentina, Brazil, China, Czech Republic, Germany, Japan, Mexico, and Taiwan. Adults with moderate to severe OSA and body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 27 or higher were enrolled between November 11, 2024, and July 23, 2025. Final follow-up occurred on July 30, 2026. Trial 1 included patients not receiving positive airway pressure treatment and trial 2 included patients receiving positive airway pressure treatment.

Intervention: Patients were randomized (1:1) to receive either once-daily orforglipron (maximum tolerated dose: equivalent to 9-, 14.5-, or 17.2-mg tablet dose) or placebo.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary end point was change in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, events/h) from baseline to week 52. Seven key multiplicity-controlled secondary end points included change in sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Short Form Sleep-Related Impairment T-score, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein.

Results: A total of 363 patients were randomized in trial 1 (mean age, 48.4 years; BMI, 37.4; AHI, 50.7 events/h; 31.4% female) and 349 patients were randomized in trial 2 (mean age, 51.1 years; BMI, 38.6; AHI, 57.6 events/h; 26.9% female). For the treatment regimen estimand, in trial 1, the mean AHI change was -17.8 for orforglipron compared with -4.5 for placebo (difference, -13.2 [95% CI, -17.7 to -8.7]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. In trial 2, the mean AHI change was -17.3 for orforglipron and -5.3 for placebo (difference, -12.0 [95% CI, -17.1 to -6.9]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. Of 7 key secondary end points, 6 were statistically significant, favoring orforglipron. Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 123 (68.0%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 68 (37.4%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 1 and in 125 (70.6%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 63 (36.6%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 2.

Conclusions and relevance: These results provide evidence for the potential use of oral orforglipron to improve sleep-disordered breathing in adults with moderate to severe OSA and obesity or overweight.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06649045.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Unintended Exposure to Medical Aid in Dying Drug Mixtures: Principles of Emergency Care
item.description:
Medical Aid in Dying (MAID) is a legal medical option for terminally ill patients with decision-making capacity to self-administer prescription medication to cause death. MAID has expanded across the United States, with New York becoming the most recent state to legalize it in August 2026. As these medications become more available in the community, typically administered outside controlled medical settings, such as the home, rare but consequential unintended exposures can occur. MAID is distinct from euthanasia in that the patient must have decision-making capacity and must be able to self-administer the medication; this requirement contributes to the presence of highly lethal drug mixtures in nonclinical environments. Although MAID formulations are designed to be lethal, unintended recipients may ingest only a partial dose (eg, a "sip"), making survival possible with prompt medical care. We review the background and common components of MAID mixtures, which typically combine a sedative (benzodiazepine and/or barbiturate), an opioid, and cardiotoxic agents such as digoxin, β-blockers, and/or tricyclic antidepressants. We propose preliminary management guidelines for suspected unsanctioned MAID exposures: early regional poison center consultation; supportive resuscitation; activated charcoal when safe; targeted diagnostics, including serum digoxin concentration and serial electrocardiograms; gastric aspiration, when feasible; use of digoxin immune Fab when indicated; avoidance of flumazenil and naloxone in mixed ingestions; and substance-specific therapies, such as high-dose insulin for propranolol toxicity and sodium bicarbonate for tricyclic antidepressants-induced QRS widening.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Association Between the Neutrophil:Lymphocyte Ratio After Hospitalization for Sepsis and Long-Term Outcomes: A Population-Based Cohort Study
item.description:
Objectives: Long-term outcomes after sepsis survival remain poor. No clinical laboratory tests are in use for stratifying long-term risk after sepsis, limiting the development of secondary prevention. The peripheral blood neutrophil:lymphocyte ratio (NLR) reflects innate and adaptive immune cell balance, and may reflect an immune milieu which is associated with long-term risk after sepsis. Accordingly, we evaluated the association between the NLR in the weeks after sepsis hospitalization discharge-a time when patients are routinely seen in post-ICU clinics-and long-term outcomes.

Design: Population-based cohort study.

Setting: Ontario, Canada, 2010-2020.

Patients: Adults discharged alive from a sepsis hospitalization.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: The exposure was the first outpatient NLR-derived from the complete blood count-measured 15-90 days after sepsis discharge. Among 37,250 survivors with available NLR, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) time-to-measurement was 34 days (22-54 d), and the median NLR was 2.7 (1.8-4.2). Within 1 year, 17,732 patients (47.6%) were rehospitalized or died (median [IQR] time-to-event, 82 d [27-185 d]). The frequency of rehospitalization or death increased across increasing NLR quartiles: 34.2%, 41.5%, 50.3%, and 64.4% (ptrend < 0.001). Compared with the lowest quartile, adjusted hazard ratios (95% CI) were 1.24 (1.18-1.29), 1.54 (1.48-1.62), and 2.25 (2.15-2.35) across higher quartiles. For most patients, NLR after sepsis returned to its patient-specific presepsis ambient level, which was itself prognostic.

Conclusions: Among sepsis survivors, outpatient NLR measured 15-90 days after discharge is strongly associated with 1-year risk of rehospitalization or death. As a simple, widely available biomarker, the NLR may support early postsepsis risk stratification and inform development of secondary prevention strategies.
