item.title: N Engl J Med: Left Bundle-Branch Pacing versus Right Ventricular Pacing for Atrioventricular Block
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Right ventricular pacing is associated with cardiac dyssynchrony and left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Left bundle-branch pacing preserves left ventricular electrical and mechanical synchrony, but its clinical benefits relative to right ventricular pacing in patients with atrioventricular block remain unclear.

Methods: In this investigator-initiated, international, open-label, randomized, controlled trial, we assigned patients with atrioventricular block in a 1:1 ratio to receive left bundle-branch pacing or right ventricular pacing. The primary outcome was a composite of death from any cause, hospitalization for heart failure, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.

Results: A total of 702 patients underwent randomization, with 348 assigned to receive left bundle-branch pacing and 354 to receive right ventricular pacing; 17 patients (6 in the left bundle-branch pacing group and 11 in the right ventricular pacing group) were excluded before device implantation. A total of 685 patients (342 in the left bundle-branch pacing group and 343 in the right ventricular pacing group) were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The mean age of the patients was 68.4 years, and 57.5% were men. At the prespecified interim analysis, the data monitoring committee recommended early termination of the trial. At a median follow-up of 35.1 months (interquartile range, 23.6 to 40.7), a primary-outcome event had occurred in 16 patients in the left bundle-branch pacing group and in 35 patients in the right ventricular pacing group (Kaplan-Meier 4-year cumulative incidence, 8.5% and 19.2%, respectively; hazard ratio, 0.41; 95% confidence interval, 0.23 to 0.75; P = 0.003 by a stratified log-rank test). Serious adverse events unrelated to implantation procedures occurred in 39 patients (11.8%) who had received left bundle-branch pacing and in 33 patients (9.3%) who had received right ventricular pacing (P = 0.32).

Conclusions: Among patients with atrioventricular block, left bundle-branch pacing was superior to right ventricular pacing in reducing the risk of a composite of death from any cause, hospitalization for heart failure, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. (Funded by Project on New Technology of Jiangsu Province and others; OptimPacing ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04624763.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Community and EMS Interventions to Improve Survival in Cardiac Arrest
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Early cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation improve survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but evidence from randomized trials about whether community-based implementation strategies improve outcomes is lacking.

Methods: We conducted a registry-based, cluster-randomized trial involving adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by emergency medical services (EMS) in North Carolina counties. The counties were grouped into clusters, which were then randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to implement a multifaceted intervention or administer usual care. The intervention included four components: training of 911 telecommunicators to improve rapid recognition of cardiac arrest, training of 911 telecommunicators to improve delivery of CPR instructions from telecommunicators to bystanders, community CPR training, and enhanced use of automated external defibrillators by first responders or bystanders before EMS arrival. Data were collected through the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome (Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2; range, 1 to 5, with higher scores indicating worse neurologic outcome).

Results: From July 1, 2022, to June 30, 2026, a total of 28 clusters comprising 11,615 patients were assigned to the intervention group, and 27 clusters comprising 10,844 patients were assigned to the usual-care group. The median age of the patients was 64.0 years, and 36.7% were women. The percentage of patients who survived to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome was 9.0% (1048 of 11,608 patients) in the intervention group and 9.4% (1017 of 10,839 patients) in the usual-care group (adjusted odds ratio, 0.97; 95% confidence interval, 0.75 to 1.26; P = 0.80).

Conclusions: Among adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, implementation of a multifaceted strategy involving the community and EMS did not result in a greater percentage of patients who survived to hospital discharge with a favorable neurologic outcome than usual care. (Funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute of the National Institutes of Health; RACE-CARS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04660526.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for the treatment of painful knee osteoarthritis in persons with obesity.

Methods: In two phase 3 trials, adults without diabetes who had painful knee osteoarthritis and a body-mass index of at least 27 were randomly assigned to receive once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide (9 or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-4 and 4, 9, or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-1-OA) or placebo. In TRIUMPH-4, the primary end points were the change in the WOMAC pain score (range, 0 to 10, with higher scores indicating worse pain) and the percent change in body weight at week 68. In TRIUMPH-1-OA, the primary end point was the change in the WOMAC pain score at week 80. For non-pain-related end points, intercurrent events were handled with a treatment-policy strategy. For pain-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy for intercurrent events that suggested treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy elsewhere. We also report results for an intention-to-treat (ITT) estimand.

Results: A total of 445 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-4 and 574 in TRIUMPH-1-OA. At 68 weeks, the mean changes in the WOMAC pain score (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-4 were -3.96 (9 mg) and -3.74 (12 mg), versus -2.12 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -1.83 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -2.37 to -1.30] and -1.61 [95% CI, -2.16 to -1.07], respectively). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -1.70 (95% CI, -2.19 to -1.22) and -1.38 (95% CI, -1.91 to -0.85) (P<0.001 for all comparisons). The mean percent changes in body weight with retatrutide were -20.0% (9 mg) and -23.7% (12 mg), versus -4.6% with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -15.4 percentage points [95% CI, -18.7 to -12.1] and -19.2 percentage points [95% CI, -22.4 to -15.9]; P<0.001 for both comparisons). At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the WOMAC pain score (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OA were -3.22 (4 mg), -3.48 (9 mg), and -3.64 (12 mg), versus -1.87 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -1.35 [95% CI, -1.92 to -0.78], -1.61 [95% CI, -2.20 to -1.02], and -1.77 [95% CI, -2.34 to -1.20], respectively). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -0.96 (95% CI, -1.61 to -0.30), -1.41 (95% CI, -2.07 to -0.75), and -1.64 (95% CI, -2.26 to -1.02) (P≤0.005 for all comparisons). In both trials, serious adverse events were more common with retatrutide than with placebo, and the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal.

Conclusions: In participants with painful knee osteoarthritis and obesity, treatment with retatrutide resulted in significantly greater reductions in both the WOMAC pain score and body weight than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-4 and -1 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05931367 and NCT05929066.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: The inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 is hypothesized to be a therapeutic target for patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Whether neutralizing interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab, a monoclonal antibody, reduces the risk of adverse cardiovascular events remains unknown.

Methods: We conducted a multinational, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation (defined by a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [CRP] level of ≥2 mg per liter). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ziltivekimab (15 mg once monthly) or placebo. The primary efficacy end point was a 3-point major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE). This composite end point included death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke.

Results: A total of 6376 patients were included in the full analysis population: 3184 were assigned to receive ziltivekimab and 3192 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 69.4 years, and 27.5% were women. At 24 months, the between-group difference in the median percent change in the levels of inflammatory biomarkers among patients receiving ziltivekimab as compared with those receiving placebo was -76 percentage points for free interleukin-6 and -64 percentage points for high-sensitivity CRP. During a median follow-up of 33 months, a primary end-point event occurred in 561 patients (17.6%) in the ziltivekimab group and in 565 patients (17.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.99; 95% confidence interval, 0.88 to 1.11; P = 0.84). Serious adverse events occurred in 54.6% of the patients in the ziltivekimab group and in 54.8% of those in the placebo group; serious infections occurred in 20.4% and 17.9%, respectively.

Conclusions: Among patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation, a strategy of lowering interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab did not result in a lower risk of cardiovascular events than placebo. (Funded by Novo Nordisk; ZEUS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05021835.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Uncertainty persists regarding the effects of intensive blood-pressure lowering in patients with type 2 diabetes.

Methods: In this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted in Brazil, patients with elevated blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and high cardiovascular risk received intensive therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or standard therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary end point was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure.

Results: Of the 9476 ethnically diverse patients who were enrolled, 4745 were assigned to receive intensive therapy and 4731 to receive standard therapy. The mean (±SD) age was 64.7±8.2 years, and 5871 of the patients (62.0%) were women. The mean systolic blood pressure during follow-up (with exclusion of the first 3 months) was 121.8±10.8 mm Hg in the intensive-therapy group and 135.4±8.2 mm Hg in the standard-therapy group. During a median follow-up of 4.0 years (interquartile range, 3.9 to 4.0), a primary-outcome event occurred in 286 patients (6.0%; 1.65 events per 100 person-years) in the intensive-therapy group and in 315 patients (6.7%; 1.83 events per 100 person-years) in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; 95% confidence interval, 0.77 to 1.06; P = 0.20). Serious adverse events occurred in 706 patients (14.9%) with intensive therapy and in 693 patients (14.6%) with standard therapy.

Conclusions: Among patients with type 2 diabetes, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg, as compared with less than 140 mm Hg, did not reduce the occurrence of major cardiovascular events. (Funded by Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and the Brazilian Ministry of Health; OPTIMAL-DIABETES ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04040634.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Whether discontinuing statin therapy in older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease affects the time to a first cardiovascular event is not well characterized.

Methods: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized, controlled trial that enrolled adults at least 70 years of age who were taking statins for primary prevention. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either discontinue or continue statin therapy and other lipid-lowering therapies. The primary outcome was a composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. The primary analysis assessed noninferiority on the basis of the between-group difference in restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years, with a noninferiority margin of -5.2 weeks.

Results: A total of 1880 participants underwent randomization: 938 were assigned to the discontinuation group and 942 to the continuation group. The mean age of the participants was 77.5 years, and 46.9% were women. The between-group difference in the restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years was -2.0 weeks (95% confidence interval, -3.7 to -0.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Over a median follow-up of 103 weeks, 119 participants (12.7%) in the discontinuation group and 87 (9.2%) in the continuation group had a primary-outcome event. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 43.0% of the participants in the discontinuation group and in 39.8% in the continuation group.

Conclusions: Among older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease, discontinuation of statin therapy was noninferior to continuation with respect to major cardiovascular events or death from any cause at 2 years. (Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation; STREAM ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05178420.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Whether intensive blood-pressure control reduces cardiovascular risk after cerebrovascular events remains uncertain.

Methods: In this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 30 sites in Brazil, we assigned participants with elevated blood pressure and previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack to receive intensive treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or to receive standard treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary outcome was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure.

Results: A total of 4368 participants were enrolled, with 2172 assigned to intensive treatment and 2196 to standard treatment. The mean (±SD) age of the participants was 63.9±11.2 years, and 2093 (47.9%) were women. During the follow-up period, excluding the first 3 months, the mean systolic blood pressure was 122.0±11.5 mm Hg (median, 119.6 mm Hg) in the intensive-treatment group and 135.2±9.7 mm Hg (median, 135.0 mm Hg) in the standard-treatment group, with a between-group mean difference of 13.1 mm Hg (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.5 to 13.8). Over a median follow-up of 3.9 years, a primary-outcome event occurred in 236 participants (10.9%; 3.25 events per 100 person-years) with intensive treatment and in 297 (13.5%; 4.11 events per 100 person-years) with standard treatment (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.94; P = 0.007). The composite renal outcome (sustained reduction of ≥50% in the estimated glomerular filtration rate or progression to end-stage renal disease) was more common with intensive treatment. The overall incidence of serious adverse events was similar in the two groups.

Conclusions: Among participants with previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg resulted in a lower incidence of major cardiovascular events than targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. (Funded by Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and the Brazilian Ministry of Health; OPTIMAL-STROKE ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04036409.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: In patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can be performed to establish reperfusion. Data comparing prehospital ECPR with conventional care regarding survival until hospital discharge among patients who are 50 years of age or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest are limited.

Methods: In a nationwide, nonrandomized study conducted in the Netherlands, we evaluated the outcomes in young adults who were attended by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) that were equipped to deliver prehospital ECPR (intervention group) as compared with those attended by HEMS without ECPR capability (conventional group). The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge.

Results: A total of 144 patients were included in the intervention group, and 87 were included in the conventional group. In the intervention group, 57 of 144 patients (40%) survived until hospital discharge, as compared with 17 of 87 patients (20%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 2.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.59 to 4.66; P = 0.002). At 6 months, a favorable neurologic outcome was reported in 51 of 141 patients (36%) in the intervention group and in 11 of 85 patients (13%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 4.22; 95% CI, 2.82 to 6.32). There were 32 adverse events in the intervention group and 11 in the conventional group.

Conclusions: Among patients who were 50 years of age or younger with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, incorporating ECPR into HEMS was associated with improved survival until hospital discharge, as compared with conventional care. (Funded by the Dutch Ministry of Health; OnScene ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04620070.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a)
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide, reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). However, the effect of pelacarsen on cardiovascular outcomes remains uncertain.

Methods: We conducted an international, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and a lipoprotein(a) level of at least 70 mg per deciliter. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous pelacarsen (80 mg) administered monthly or matching placebo. The primary end point was a major adverse cardiovascular event, defined as a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization.

Results: A total of 8350 patients underwent randomization, with 8322 included in the efficacy analysis; 4157 patients were assigned to receive pelacarsen, and 4165 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 59.7 years, and 27.0% were women. The median lipoprotein(a) level at baseline was 236 nmol per liter. At 12 months, the lipoprotein(a) level was 64.4 nmol per liter in the pelacarsen group and 233.4 nmol per liter in the placebo group. The median follow-up was 4.7 years. A primary end-point event occurred in 511 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 503 (12.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90 to 1.15, P = 0.76). Among patients with a baseline lipoprotein(a) level of at least 90 mg per deciliter, a primary end-point event occurred in 402 of 3266 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 403 of 3274 (12.3%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.15; P = 0.99). Serious adverse events occurred in 1553 of 4166 patients (37.3%) who received pelacarsen and in 1709 of 4154 (41.1%) who received placebo.

Conclusions: Pelacarsen did not result in a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events than placebo at a median follow-up of 4.7 years. item.title: J Addict Med: Locked Out or Linked Up: Lessons in Cross-agency Data Linkage and a Call for State-based Measures for Substance Use Surveillance
item.description:
As the durability of federal public health surveillance is called into question, state and local health departments are increasingly central to monitoring the overdose crisis. From interviews with stakeholders leading data linkage initiativesin 7 states, we identified pragmatic strategies for building capacity, including legislative mandates paired with funding and privacy safeguards, academic-government partnerships, and visible champions who build cross-agency trust. Two categories of opportunities emerged: linking person-level data across agencies within states and standardizing measures across states. Standardization of local addictions surveillance measures is critical for both local quality improvement and national benchmarking, and we propose the proportion of nonfatal overdoses followed by treatment as a first shared metric and offer actionable steps for advancing substance use surveillance locally.

item.title: J Addict Med: Variation in Prenatal and Newborn Toxicology Testing Policies in Michigan Hospitals
item.description:
Objectives: This study examines hospital policies on prenatal and newborn toxicology testing, and subsequent referral to child protective services (CPS) for suspected abuse and neglect in Michigan. We assessed variability between hospitals, alignment with state law, and consistency with professional guidelines.

Methods: This cross-sectional survey was conducted between February 1, 2024, and September 1, 2024. All 76 birth hospitals in Michigan were invited to participate. The 10-question survey addressed hospital protocols for prenatal and newborn toxicology testing, indications for testing in risk-based protocols, informed consent policies, protocols for reporting to child protective services, and specific policies for cannabis exposure and patients receiving medication treatment for opioid use disorder.

Results: Of 76 birth hospitals in Michigan, 25 completed the survey (response rate 33%). Hospitals reported variability in prenatal and newborn toxicology testing policies. Of respondents, 28% (7/25) reported universal prenatal toxicology testing and 68% (17/25) reported risk-based testing. Most hospitals (23/25) used a risk-based testing strategy for newborns. The most common risk-based indication was no prenatal care (12/17). Although guidelines recommend informed consent for all prenatal toxicology tests, only 56% (14/25) of hospitals required informed consent for prenatal toxicology testing and only 20% (5/25), required informed consent from a parent for newborn toxicology testing.

Conclusions: Variability in hospital prenatal and newborn toxicology testing policies, even within a single state's regulatory framework, highlights opportunities for quality improvement at the level of hospital policy to improve the ethical treatment of birth parents and newborns with potential exposures to substance use during pregnancy.

item.title: JAMA: Implementation of Single-Pill Combination Therapy Through Team-Based Care for Hypertension Control in Resource-Constrained Settings: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Single-pill combination therapy improves medication adherence and hypertension control. However, limited evidence is available on its implementation in routine clinical practice.

Objective: To assess the long-term effectiveness, implementation, and sustainability of single-pill combination therapy through team-based care for blood pressure reduction among patients with uncontrolled hypertension in primary care settings in Colombia and Jamaica.

Design, setting, and participants: Multicountry, unblinded, pragmatic, cluster randomized clinical trial. Twenty primary care clinics in Jamaica and 20 in Colombia were randomly assigned to either the single-pill combination therapy group or the standard care group. A total of 1706 adults with uncontrolled hypertension were enrolled between February 23, 2023, and September 12, 2024. The final follow-up visit occurred on September 9, 2026.

Interventions: In the intervention group (n = 869), a team-based care approach that included physician and nurse training, health coaching, home blood pressure monitoring, and blood pressure audit and feedback was used to implement single-pill combination therapy. Single-pill combinations were purchased locally and provided to patients. In the standard care group (n = 837), patients received monotherapy or polytherapy with guideline-recommended medications covered by health insurance or government programs. The intervention lasted 18 months, with additional follow-up at 24 months.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in systolic blood pressure from baseline to 18 months. Three blood pressure measurements were obtained at each of 2 visits at each time point using a standard protocol.

Results: Among the 1706 enrolled participants, at baseline, the mean age was 61.4 years, 69.9% of participants were female, and 98.2% were taking antihypertensive medications. Among the 1574 participants included in the primary analysis, systolic blood pressure decreased by 19.1 mm Hg, from 145.9 mm Hg at baseline to 126.8 mm Hg at 18 months, in the intervention group and by 9.0 mm Hg, from 145.0 mm Hg to 136.1 mm Hg, in the standard care group, with a between-group difference of -10.1 mm Hg (95% CI, -13.3 to -6.9 mm Hg; P < .001). At 18 months, 69.5% of patients in the intervention group and 29.2% in the standard care group achieved systolic blood pressure less than 130 and diastolic blood pressure less than 80 mm Hg. Serious adverse events (death and hospitalization) occurred at similar frequencies in the intervention (7.9%) and standard care (9.9%) groups.

Conclusions and relevance: Implementing single-pill combination therapy through team-based care significantly reduced blood pressure over 18 months among adults with uncontrolled hypertension in Colombia and Jamaica. This comprehensive strategy integrating single-pill combination therapy with team-based care could be widely adopted and scaled up for hypertension control, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05405920.

item.title: JAMA: Low-Voltage Area Ablation for Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: The COAST-AF Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) for persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) has demonstrated modest success rates. Ablation of atrial low-voltage areas (LVA) has shown potential results, but more data are required.

Objective: To determine whether PVI plus LVA ablation is superior to PVI alone in reducing atrial arrhythmia recurrence in patients with AF.

Design, setting, and participants: Single-blind randomized clinical trial in 14 AF ablation centers in Canada. Adults with persistent AF of more than 3 months were enrolled between August 2018 and September 2024 and followed up for 18 to 36 months through April 2026.

Intervention: Patients were randomized to PVI plus LVA ablation or PVI alone.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was atrial arrhythmia recurrence beyond 90 days after a single catheter ablation procedure. Secondary outcomes included repeat ablation for AF, atrial flutter, or atrial tachycardia, emergency visits or hospitalization, arrhythmia recurrence over 18 months, procedure duration, total ablation delivery time, AF burden, and safety outcomes. The primary efficacy analysis was based on the modified intention-to-treat principle for patients who received the intervention.

Results: Among 508 enrolled patients, 253 were randomized to PVI plus LVA ablation and 255 to PVI alone. Mean (SD) age was 65.2 (9.0) years, 386 (76%) were male and 268 (54%) had LVA. After a mean (SD) follow-up of 21 (15) months, 124 (49.4%) randomized to PVI plus LVA and 146 (57.5%) randomized to PVI reached the primary outcome (hazard ratio [HR], 0.82; 95% CI, 0.65-1.04; P = .11). In the prespecified principal subgroup analysis of 268 patients with LVA, arrhythmia recurrence occurred in 68 of 138 patients (49.3%) following PVI plus LVA ablation compared with 90 of 130 patients (69.2%) following PVI alone (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.66-0.91; P = .002). Arrhythmia recurrence over 18 months (37.0% vs 56.2%; HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.64-0.92) and AF burden were lower after PVI plus LVA ablation in this group. Among patients without LVA, recurrence was similar between ablation groups (56 of 113 [49.6%] vs 51 of 113 [45.1%]; HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.90-1.32). Procedure duration and ablation delivery time were longer in the PVI plus LVA ablation group. Safety outcomes were similar between groups.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, among patients with persistent AF, adjunctive LVA ablation did not significantly reduce atrial arrhythmia recurrence in the overall population over a mean 21-month follow-up. A prespecified principal subgroup analysis of patients with LVA suggested that adjunctive LVA ablation was consistent with reduced recurrence of atrial arrhythmias in this group.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, Identifier: NCT03347227.

item.title: Lancet: Cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (DAPT-SHOCK-AMI): a randomised, double-blind trial
item.description:
Background: Acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) can compromise the administration and absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors and carries high ischaemic and mortality risks. This trial assessed whether intravenous cangrelor was non-inferior to crushed oral ticagrelor for short-term clinical outcomes and whether it provided faster and more consistent platelet inhibition in patients with AMI-CS.

Methods: DAPT-SHOCK-AMI was a double-blind trial conducted at 29 hospitals across five European countries (Czech Republic, France, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia). Patients older than 18 years with AMI-CS were randomly assigned (1:1 ratio, stratified by centre, age, sex, presence or absence of ST-segment elevation, and mechanical ventilation) to cangrelor (30 μg/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 4 μg/kg per min for at least 2 h) or crushed ticagrelor (180 mg loading dose). The primary laboratory endpoint was a platelet reactivity index of less than 50% at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. The primary clinical endpoint was death, myocardial infarction, or ischaemic stroke at 30 days. The primary clinical endpoint was analysed for non-inferiority with a prespecified margin of 1 percentage point among all randomly assigned patients who received study treatment. The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03551964) and EudraCT (2018-002161-19); recruitment and 1-year follow-up are complete, and 5-year follow-up is ongoing.

Findings: Between Aug 1, 2018, and Jan 19, 2024, 605 patients (137 [23%] were female) were randomly assigned to cangrelor (n=298) or ticagrelor (n=307); no surviving patients were lost to the 1-year follow-up. The primary laboratory endpoint was analysed in 56 (19%) patients in the cangrelor group and 68 (22%) in the ticagrelor group, and was achieved in 56 (100%) of 56 patients receiving cangrelor and 15 (22%) of 68 receiving ticagrelor (p<0·0001). The 30-day primary clinical endpoint occurred in 112 (38%) of 298 patients receiving cangrelor and 126 (41%) of 307 receiving ticagrelor; non-inferiority was not demonstrated (difference -4 percentage points [90% CI -10 to 3]; Pnon-inferiority=0·13). Major bleeding at 30 days occurred in 19 (6%) of 298 patients receiving cangrelor and 16 (5%) of 307 receiving ticagrelor.

Interpretation: To our knowledge, this is the first randomised trial to compare P2Y12 inhibitor strategies specifically in patients with AMI-CS. Cangrelor achieved effective platelet inhibition more frequently than crushed ticagrelor at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Non-inferiority of cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor was not demonstrated for the primary 30-day clinical endpoint. These trial findings can inform future trials of P2Y12 inhibition strategies in patients with AMI-CS.

Funding: Czech Republic Ministry of Health, Charles University (Czech Republic), and NextGenerationEU.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Perceived sleep disruption and opioid consumption in chronic low back pain: Craving as a mediating pathway
item.description:
Background: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) affects more than 600 million people worldwide, many of whom receive long-term opioid therapy (LTOT). Sleep disturbance, particularly wake after sleep onset (WASO), may contribute to opioid craving and use, yet the temporal relationships among WASO, craving, and opioid dose in chronic pain populations remain poorly understood.

Methods: Adults with CLBP receiving LTOT (N = 81) completed 14 days of ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and overnight actigraphy monitoring. WASO was assessed using sleep diaries and overnight actigraphy, while morning and nocturnal craving, pain severity, and daily opioid dose (morphine milligram equivalents) were assessed using EMA. Linear mixed-effects models examined main and interactive effects of WASO and pain severity on craving and opioid dose. Multilevel mediation models tested whether craving mediated the relationship between WASO and opioid dose.

Results: Greater diary-based WASO was associated with higher nocturnal opioid craving. Pain severity emerged as a strong predictor of both nocturnal and morning craving and moderated the association between WASO and opioid dose, such that greater WASO was associated with higher opioid dose on high-pain days. Mediation analyses demonstrated significant indirect effects of WASO on opioid dose through both nocturnal and morning craving. Exploratory analyses using actigraphy-derived WASO showed minimal associations with craving or opioid dose.

Conclusions: Perceived sleep disruption was associated with opioid craving and opioid consumption among individuals with CLBP receiving LTOT. Craving may represent a cognitive-affective pathway linking disrupted sleep to opioid use, highlighting sleep disturbance as a potentially modifiable intervention target in chronic pain populations.

Towers EB, Denoue C, Reid MJ, Thrul J, Huhn AS, Dunn KE

item.title: JAMA: Long-Term Survival After Initial Invasive or Conservative Management of Stable Coronary Disease in ISCHEMIA-EXTEND
item.description:
Importance: It is unknown whether routine invasive management of chronic coronary disease improves long-term survival when added to guideline-directed medical therapy.

Objective: To compare the effects of initial invasive and conservative strategies on long-term mortality in patients with chronic coronary disease.

Design, setting, and participants: In this long-term follow-up study of the International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness with Medical and Invasive Approaches (ISCHEMIA), an international trial of patients with chronic coronary disease, moderate or severe ischemia, left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or more, and no left main coronary artery disease, unacceptable angina, or recent acute coronary syndrome, participants were randomized at 320 sites in 37 countries beginning August 2012 and followed up through December 2025. Data were analyzed using the intention-to-treat principle.

Intervention: ISCHEMIA randomized patients to an initial invasive strategy of guideline-directed medical therapy plus coronary angiography and revascularization (when feasible) or an initial conservative strategy with guideline-directed medical therapy alone, with invasive management for failure of medical therapy.

Main outcomes and measures: All-cause, cardiovascular, and noncardiovascular mortality were analyzed using cumulative incidence estimates, Cox and Fine-Gray models, bayesian analysis, and restricted mean survival time.

Results: Among 5179 participants, median age was 64 (IQR, 58-70) years; 23% were female, 42% had diabetes, and median ejection fraction was 60% (IQR, 55%-65%). During 9-year median follow-up (range, 1 day to 13.4 years), 1071 deaths occurred (782 during extended follow-up): 672 cardiovascular, 359 noncardiovascular, and 40 unclassified. All-cause 11-year mortality was not significantly different between groups (25.8% invasive vs 26.9% conservative; estimated difference, -1.0 percentage point [95% CI, -4.2 to 2.1 percentage points]; adjusted hazard ratio [AHR], 0.97 [95% CI, 0.86-1.09]). By bayesian analysis, the posterior probability of more than 1 percentage-point survival benefit to invasive vs conservative was low (18%). Cardiovascular mortality at 11 years was 15.8% in the invasive group vs 17.1% in the conservative group (estimated difference, -1.4 percentage points [95% CI, -4.0 to 1.3 percentage points]; AHR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.75-1.02]). Noncardiovascular mortality at 11 years was 9.1% in the invasive group vs 8.1% in the conservative group (estimated difference, 1.0 percentage point [95% CI, -0.9 to 2.9 percentage points]; AHR, 1.18 [95% CI, 0.96-1.45]). Eleven-year restricted mean survival was not significantly different (estimated difference, 14 days [95% CI, -41 to 70 days]).

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, long-term all-cause mortality in patients with high-risk chronic coronary disease was not significantly different after routine invasive vs initial conservative management.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04894877.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Trends in Care and Outcomes Among Emergency Department Patients With Chest Pain Without Myocardial Infarction
item.description:
Study objective: To characterize trends in hospitalization, downstream care, and outcomes among emergency department (ED) patients with chest pain without acute myocardial infarction (AMI) diagnosis.

Methods: We analyzed claims data from a large national commercial insurer (2007-2021) and identified ED visits with a principal diagnosis of chest pain. We excluded visits with secondary diagnoses of AMI or other significant cardiopulmonary conditions and those preceded by cardiac testing, coronary procedures, AMI admissions, or chest pain ED visits within 6 months. Usage outcomes included index hospitalization (principal), 7-day cardiac testing, and 30-day coronary revascularization. The principal clinical outcome was 180-day postindex AMI hospitalization. Adjusted annual rates were estimated using generalized estimating equations, and trends were assessed using inverse-variance-weighted linear regression.

Results: We included 773,250 index chest pain ED visits (mean age 54.2 years; 54.3% women). Adjusted hospitalization rates declined from 42.7% to 18.6%, and 7-day noninvasive testing decreased from 26.7% to 9.1%. Revascularization within 30 days declined from 5.8% to 3.6%. Overall, 180-day postindex AMI hospitalization showed no significant temporal trend, ranging from 0.8% to 1.2%. However, a modest increasing trend was observed among patients aged 70 years and older.

Conclusion: Among ED patients with chest pain without AMI diagnosis, hospitalization, cardiac testing, and revascularization declined substantially from 2007 to 2021. Overall, downstream AMI hospitalization remained stable, although those in older adults experienced modest rises. Although efforts continue to identify additional low-risk patients for safe discharge, future research should quantify the potential benefits of hospitalization and cardiac testing, particularly for older adults and high-risk patients.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Concepts in Practice: Understanding and Addressing Name-Based Microaggressions in Health Care
item.description:
Names are important markers of identity, culture, and belonging. In health care settings, individuals with ethnically distinct names may experience repeated mispronunciations, unsolicited nicknames, or avoidance of their names. Repeated mispronunciations without sincere efforts to learn or improve, as well as the avoidance, dismissal, or replacement of names with unsolicited nicknames, may function as name-based microaggressions and can negatively affect psychological safety, professional identity formation, and workplace inclusion. In this manuscript, we discuss the effect of name-based microaggressions on health care professionals and trainees, with particular focus on the emergency department. We review the 3 major categories of microaggressions-microassaults, microinsults, and microinvalidations-and use clinical vignettes to demonstrate how these behaviors may appear in both interpersonal and institutional settings. We also propose practical interpersonal and institutional strategies to promote more inclusive workplaces and foster respectful engagement with ethnically distinct names. By encouraging greater awareness, curiosity, humility, and intentionality around names, health care organizations can help cultivate clinical environments where individuals feel respected, included, and valued.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Survival From Traumatic Cardiac Arrest After Sequential Decompression of Dual-Tension Thoracic Physiology Without Chest Compressions
item.description:
Traumatic pulseless electrical activity arrest from simultaneous dual-tension thoracic physiology-bilateral tension pneumothorax and tension pneumomediastinum-with concurrent oropharyngeal hematoma causing airway obstruction has not been described as a unified presentation in the published literature. We report a 28-year-old male who sustained penetrating machete injuries producing this presentation and arrested in pulseless electrical activity on arrival. A sequential surgical resuscitation was performed without external chest compressions: hemostasis and evacuation of an oropharyngeal hematoma restored ventilation, with return of peripheral photoplethysmographic signal consistent with pseudo-pulseless electrical activity physiology; bilateral finger thoracostomies achieved pleural decompression; digital exploration through the manubrial wound vented tension pneumomediastinum, producing an audible air rush, immediate resolution of jugular venous distension, and confirmed return of spontaneous circulation. The patient ambulated independently within hours of arrest and was discharged neurologically intact on day 7. This case illustrates that mechanically mediated pulseless electrical activity arrest from dual thoracic obstructive physiology may be reversible by sequential surgical decompression, and that persistent jugular venous distension following pleural decompression may signal residual mediastinal tension warranting urgent decompression.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Live Versus Delayed Video-Based TEAM Assessment During Real-World Cardiac Arrest: Agreement and Exploratory Differences by Rater Experience
item.description:
Study objective: To evaluate agreement between immediate live and delayed video-based assessment of nontechnical skills during real-world adult cardiac arrest resuscitation, and whether agreement differed by rater experience.

Methods: We conducted a prospective observational study of adult cardiac arrest resuscitations in a tertiary emergency department in Taiwan in 2024. For each event, one trained physician or nurse who participated in the resuscitation completed the Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) immediately afterward and re-rated the same event from video approximately 30 days later. Live-video agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analysis.

Results: Of 105 recorded resuscitations, 80 had complete paired assessments. Mean global ratings were similar between modalities (8.25 versus 8.22; mean paired difference, -0.03; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.25 to 0.20), whereas teamwork scores were modestly lower on video review (mean paired difference, -1.00; 95% CI -1.77 to -0.23). Event-level agreement was limited: intraclass correlation coefficients were 0.21 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.41) for total TEAM score and 0.16 (95% CI -0.06 to 0.37) for global rating. Total TEAM video ratings averaged 1.24 points lower than live ratings, with limits of agreement from -12.28 to 9.80. Agreement was higher among senior raters.

Conclusion: Delayed video-based TEAM assessment produced similar group-level scores but limited event-level agreement during real-world cardiac arrest. Agreement appeared higher among senior raters. Video review may support debriefing and monitoring, but appraisal of a specific resuscitation or other higher stakes use likely requires experienced raters and structured safeguards.

item.title: Am J Respir Crit Care Med: Systemic Inflammation in Bronchiectasis: Data from the EMBARC-BRIDGE Study
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Background: Neutrophilic inflammation in the airways is associated with exacerbation risk in patients with bronchiectasis. Systemic inflammation and neutrophil function are less characterised. The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between systemic inflammation and neutrophil function with severity of disease and clinical outcomes.

Methods: Observational international multi-centre study of adults with bronchiectasis (EMBARC-BRIDGE). Serum inflammatory profiling was performed in 487 patients using Olink® proteomics, and associations with key clinical and patient reported outcomes, including severe exacerbations during follow-up, were analysed. In a sub-study, peripheral blood neutrophils from bronchiectasis patients and controls were analysed for surface activation and functional markers, and functional responses including degranulation and neutrophil extracellular trap formation.

Results: Systemic inflammatory profiling revealed a dominant neutrophil-endothelial signature. Several proteins including PR3, AZU1, MPO, the soluble IL-33 receptor ST2, and the cellular stress marker GDF-15 were associated with increased disease severity using the bronchiectasis severity index, lower lung function, increased symptoms and for many markers, higher rates of severe exacerbations during follow-up. Neutrophils from bronchiectasis patients exhibited reduced surface CD11b and increased CXCR2, with lower CD11b correlating with lower lung function. Basal degranulation was reduced in bronchiectasis, whereas responsiveness to LPS stimulation was preserved.

Conclusion: Bronchiectasis is associated with a systemic neutrophil and endothelial inflammatory signature linked to disease severity and risk of severe exacerbations, alongside altered but functionally-responsive circulating neutrophils.

Hughes C, Long MB, Stobo J, Johnson ED, Viligorska K, Lind H

item.title: Crit Care: Structural imbalances in open-access critical care research: a bibliometric analysis of abstracts from ICU database studies, 2018-2025
item.description:
Background: Open access intensive care unit (ICU) databases, including MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD), AmsterdamUMCdb, HiRID-high time resolution ICU data set, and the Salzburg Intensive Care Database (SICdb), have fundamentally transformed critical care research over the past decade. Despite their widespread use, no comprehensive bibliometric analysis has systematically mapped the scientific output generated by studies relying on these resources.

Methods: A structured search was conducted in PubMed and Web of Science covering 2018 to 2025, retrieving original articles citing at least one of six defined open access ICU databases in title or abstract. Database selection followed the methodology of two prior systematic reviews of publicly available adult ICU datasets. Structured fields covering database used, machine learning (ML) methods, study design, clinical outcomes, AUROC values and patient counts were extracted via a semi-automated AI pipeline (DeepSeek API, multi-label JSON schema). The extraction pipeline was validated against a manually coded reference sample of 110 publications. Bibliometric analyses used R (bibliometrix v4.0.1) and Python. Citation counts, open-access status and SCImago journal quartile were retrieved via OpenAlex and SCImago to characterise the visibility and venue quality of the corpus. Four network analyses were performed: database-to-ML-method co-occurrence, country-to-database, international collaboration, and clinical topic co-occurrence networks.

Results: A total of 4,648 publications were included. Annual publication counts increased 45-fold from 42 (2018) to 1,907 (2025), accelerating markedly after 2021 following the release of MIMIC-IV. MIMIC-IV dominated database attributions (54.6%), followed by MIMIC-III (30.0%) and eICU-CRD (13.5%); European databases (AmsterdamUMCdb, HiRID, SICdb) collectively accounted for only 1.9%. China contributed 65.6% of publications (n = 3,048) and the USA 10.6%. Median citations per paper were 5.0 (1.50 per year). 76.4% of publications were open access and 49.3% appeared in a Q1 SCImago-ranked journal. AUROC showed no meaningful correlation with citation impact (p = 0.10). Logistic regression was the most frequent ML method (38.5%), followed by neural networks (15.6%) and gradient boosting (13.8%). Retrospective observational designs dominated (67.9%), with mortality prediction in sepsis as the primary research focus. Median AUROC among 1,263 publications with extractable values was 0.798.

Conclusion: Open access database-based critical care research is growing almost exponentially, driven primarily by Chinese groups using MIMIC-IV for retrospective mortality studies. European databases remain underutilized. The field exhibits methodological homogeneity and a heavy bias toward US-American clinical practice patterns, with cross-dataset external validation rarely foregrounded in study abstracts. Greater use of European databases, systematic external validation and topical diversification are key priorities.

item.title: Crit Care: Fluid-intolerance signals as bedside safety limits during early septic shock resuscitation: a multicenter randomized trial
item.description:
Background: Fluid resuscitation in early septic shock has a narrow therapeutic index. Signals of fluid intolerance are frequently present during early resuscitation, yet current resuscitation strategies do not incorporate them to guide when to limit fluid administration. We evaluated whether integrating fluid-intolerance signals as safety limits could reduce fluid-induced harm without compromising hypoperfusion resolution.

Methods: In this multicenter, open-label randomized trial in three Chilean ICUs, mechanically ventilated adults with septic shock, persistent hypoperfusion, fluid responsiveness, and at least one high-risk criterion for fluid-induced harm were randomized 1:1 to a fluid-intolerance-limited resuscitation strategy or standard care during a 6-hour protocol window. In the intervention arm, before each bolus, fluid-intolerance signals (lung ultrasound score, VExUS, E/lateral e', and central venous pressure) were graded as traffic-light: green received a 500-mL bolus, yellow 250 mL, and red no further fluid. Standard care delivered 500-mL boluses while hypoperfusion and fluid responsiveness persisted. The primary outcome was the change in PaO2:FiO2 from baseline to 6 h (ΔPaO2:FiO2).

Results: Recruitment was discontinued before the planned sample size was reached because continued enrollment was no longer feasible. Among 113 screened patients, 36 of a planned 62 were randomized, and 35 were analyzed (18 standard care, 17 intervention). The intervention group received a lower protocol bolus volume during the 6-hour intervention window than the standard-care group (250 [125-500] vs. 650 [500-1500] mL; between-group difference, - 500 mL [95% CI, - 750 to - 250]). Cumulative fluid exposure from pre-randomization through the end of the protocol window was similar between groups (3375 [2375-3875] vs. 3750 [1875-4851] mL; between-group difference, - 150 mL [95% CI, - 1470 to 1250]). The primary outcome favored the intervention: median ΔPaO2:FiO2 was 40.5 [24.0-58.5] versus - 37.9 [-69.2 to -12.5]; p < 0.001 (between-group median difference + 78.3 points; 95% CI 50.5 to 110.0), and 0-6-hour changes in lactate and capillary refill time did not differ.

Conclusion: Because the trial was stopped early, the effect of a fluid-intolerance-limited resuscitation strategy on oxygenation remains uncertain. A larger trial would be needed to determine whether this strategy improves oxygenation. Such a trial appears feasible.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT06568744, registered August 21, 2024.
